docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 17 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Śilpa–Kāru: Crafts and Textiles. It is about the knowledge of those who made things in the Indian subcontinent: smiths and bronze-casters, spinners, weavers, dyers and printers, tailors, potters, carpenters and carvers, jewellers, glass- and lac-workers, painters, embroiderers, instrument-makers and basket-makers. It follows their work from the craft quarters of the Indus cities to the workshops, cooperatives and design studios of the present, and it asks how that knowledge was organised, transmitted, valued and, at times, devalued.

Primary texts are quoted only where the wording and the reference could be confirmed, and figures are given only where a source can be named; where the evidence is uncertain, the text says so. Popular myths, such as the story that the East India Company cut off the thumbs of Bengal’s muslin weavers, are discussed and corrected rather than repeated. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such.

Two themes run through the book. The first is the sheer range and sophistication of Indian craft knowledge, much of it never written down, which is documented here from archaeology, inscriptions, Sanskrit, Pali, Tamil and Persian texts, the records of European trading companies and modern ethnography. The second is the social setting of that knowledge. Most crafts were practised by hereditary occupational communities (jāti), within a hierarchy that ranked many artisans low and treated some, above all leather-workers, as untouchable. The book tries to give both themes their due: to describe the artisans’ achievements and their own traditions, such as those of the Viśvakarma communities, without romanticising the system of caste in which they worked. Leather, the clearest case of the second theme, therefore has a chapter of its own.

Chapters on materials and processes are followed by a regional survey and by three chapters on guilds and caste, the colonial economy and the present; schematic line diagrams show the main processes, and photographs show representative objects, monuments and tools.

References to the standard studies (among others those of Stella Kramrisch, Ananda Coomaraswamy, John Irwin, Rosemary Crill, Ruth Barnes, Giorgio Riello, Prasannan Parthasarathi, Tirthankar Roy, Sharada Srinivasan and Paul Craddock) are given in the text and collected in the select bibliography. A glossary of the principal terms is provided at the end. Metallurgy and chemistry are treated more fully in Volume 14, architecture and sculpture in Volume 16, and trade in Volume 19 of this series.

No survey of this size can be complete, and specialists will find much to add and correct. Readers should treat it as an introduction, and turn to the works cited for the evidence itself.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: A Note on Transliteration and Names
docs.text:
Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST): śilpa, kāru, Arthaśāstra. Tamil words follow the conventions of the Tamil Lexicon (Madras), which marks the letters peculiar to Tamil: Kammāḷar, Paṭṭiṉappālai. Words from Hindi, Urdu, Persian, Bengali, Gujarati, Marathi, Assamese and other modern languages are given with long vowels and retroflex consonants marked, in the form most used for the craft concerned (bāndhaṇī, kānthā, paṭolā, mugā); Persian and Arabic terms of the court workshops are given in a simplified scholarly form (kārkhāna, nastaʿlīq). Where a craft term has a regional variant, the variant is noted at its first appearance, as with Gujarati ajrakh and Sindhi ajrak; the glossary marks the language of each term.

Modern place-names are given in their current official or customary English spelling without diacritics (Varanasi, Kolkata, Kumbakonam), except for a few places, such as Kāñcīpuram, whose classical names recur in the history of a craft; older forms (Banaras, Calcutta, Madras, Cawnpore) are used where they are the names of the period under discussion. The names of registered Geographical Indications, firms, institutions and laws are given exactly as registered, even where they differ from the spelling used elsewhere (“Kancheepuram silk”, “Muga silk of Assam”).

docs.title: Chapter 1: Śilpa and Kāru: Makers and Making in India
docs.text:
From the bead-makers of Harappa to the Dhokra casters of Bastar and the silk weavers of Kāñcīpuram, the Indian subcontinent has one of the longest and best-documented histories of craft production in the world. This volume is about that history and about the knowledge it embodied: how materials were chosen and transformed, how techniques were organised and taught, how objects were traded, and how the people who made them were placed in society. It covers metals, textiles, dyeing and printing, pottery, wood, ivory and stone, bamboo and plant fibres, leather, jewellery, glass, lac and perfume, painting and the arts of the book, festival crafts, and the regional crafts of the present, and it ends with the guilds and craft knowledge, the colonial economy and the revival movements of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

Two cautions are needed at the start. First, most craft knowledge in India was never written down. It was carried in hands, eyes and workshop routines, and passed from parent to child or master to apprentice. Texts in Sanskrit and other languages tell us a good deal about how crafts were classified, taxed and valued, and the technical treatises on architecture and image-making (śilpaśāstra) record proportional systems and procedures; but for most crafts the evidence is archaeological, inscriptional, commercial or ethnographic. Second, the continuity of Indian crafts is real but should not be exaggerated. Techniques such as lost-wax casting or mordant dyeing have very long histories in the subcontinent, but the communities, markets and meanings of craft changed constantly. Phrases such as “five thousand years of unbroken tradition” describe a hope rather than a documented lineage.

docs.title: 1.1.1 Śilpa
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word śilpa means skill, art or craft, and also the work produced by skill. In the Vedic Brāhmaṇas the word already refers to works of art and ornament; in classical usage a śilpin is any skilled maker, from a sculptor to a weaver. The technical literature on building and image-making came to be called śilpaśāstra (“the science of craft”), and vāstuśāstra (“the science of building”); these two overlapping bodies of text are discussed below and in Volume 16 of this series.

The best-known classification of the arts is the list of sixty-four kalās given in the Kāmasūtra (1.3) and explained by its commentator Yaśodhara (13th century). It mixes what we would call fine arts, crafts, accomplishments and games: singing, instrumental music and dance stand beside painting (ālekhya), needlework (sūcīvānakarma), carpentry (takṣaṇa), architecture (vāstuvidyā), the testing of silver (rūpyaparīkṣā), metallurgy (dhātuvāda) and the colouring of gems, alongside riddles, cock-fighting and the teaching of parrots. The list was meant to describe the accomplishments of a cultivated city-dweller (nāgaraka), not the work of professional artisans, and it should not be read as a technical curriculum. It shows, however, that a wide range of making skills was recognised as vidyā, a body of knowledge.

docs.title: 1.1.2 Kāru
docs.text:
The word kāru has an interesting history. In the Ṛgveda it usually means a singer or poet, the “maker” of hymns. In a well-known humorous hymn (RV 9.112) the poet lists the different aims of different people: the carpenter (takṣan) looks for what is broken, the physician for the injured, the priest for someone who presses soma; and the speaker says that he himself is a kāru, his father a physician, and his mother a grinder of grain (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The passage is valuable evidence that occupations were differentiated in Vedic society, and it suggests that they were not yet necessarily fixed by birth within a family. In later Sanskrit, kāru came to mean an artisan in general; the lexicons treat kāru and śilpin as near-synonyms, and the law-books speak of kārus and śilpins together.

Some Terms for Makers

takṣan carpenter, woodworker (Vedic) rathakāra chariot-maker karmāra smith kulāla, kumbhakāra potter tantuvāya, kuvinda weaver rajaka washerman (dyers are rañjaka, raṅgakāra) suvarṇakāra goldsmith maṇikāra jeweller, bead-maker carmakāra leather-worker sthapati master builder, architect sūtradhāra “holder of the cord”, architect or carpenter citrakāra painter

docs.title: 1.2 Artisans in Vedic Literature
docs.text:
The earliest Indian texts already know a variety of craftsmen. The Ṛgveda mentions the carpenter and the chariot-maker, the smith (karmāra), and the weaving of cloth; it uses craft as a source of images for the poet’s own work, which is “fashioned” like a chariot or “woven” like a garment. A famous verse compares the creator Brahmaṇaspati to a smith who “blew together” the births of the gods like a karmāra at his bellows (RV 10.72.1–2). The hymns to Viśvakarman, “the maker of all” (RV 10.81–82), ask from what wood and what tree heaven and earth were hewn, and picture the one god who has eyes, faces, arms and feet on every side blowing heaven and earth together with his arms and wings (RV 10.81.3–4) (Jamison and Brereton 2014). These cosmological images are discussed in Chapter 2.

The Yajurveda gives two remarkable lists. The Śatarudrīya litany to Rudra (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 16; Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5) pays homage, among many others, to carpenters and chariot-makers, potters and smiths. The list of victims for the symbolic “human sacrifice” (puruṣamedha) in book 30 of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā names dozens of occupations, among them the jeweller, the goldsmith, the arrow-maker, the bow-maker, the rope-maker, the dyer and the embroiderer; several of these, such as the dyer and the embroiderer, are women. The lists are ritual, not sociological, but they are the earliest Indian record of a highly specialised division of labour.

Women’s craft work is visible in these early sources. Besides the dyer and the embroiderer of the puruṣamedha list, Vedic texts mention women weaving and stitching, and the image of the weaving woman is used of Night and Dawn, who weave the day. In the Arthaśāstra women spin yarn for the state (Chapter 4); in Buddhist texts, women prepare thread and cloth for the robes of monks and nuns. Throughout Indian history, much of the labour of craft, especially spinning, embroidery, basketry and the preparation of materials, has been done by women, though it has usually been less visible in the sources than the work of men.

The status of the chariot-maker became a famous problem for ritual theory. Vedic texts allow the rathakāra to set up the sacred fires, in the rainy season. Since the chariot-maker was not one of the three “twice-born” classes, later Mīmāṃsā exegetes debated who exactly the rathakāra was and how he could have this right. From an early date, then, craftsmen occupied an uncertain place in the scheme of the four varṇas.

docs.title: 1.3 Artisans in Buddhist, Jain and Tamil Sources
docs.text:
The Buddhist canon in Pali, much of it composed in the last centuries BCE, gives a lively picture of the urban and village artisans of the Ganga valley. Its stories mention villages of smiths, carpenters and potters, heads (jeṭṭhaka) of groups of craftsmen, and the “eighteen guilds” (aṭṭhārasa seṇiyo) as a conventional total (Chapter 13). The Buddha’s last meal, according to the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, was taken in the house of Cunda, a smith’s son (kammāraputta) of Pāvā, whom the Buddha took care to exonerate from any blame for his final illness. The monastic rules (Vinaya) regulate the cloth that monks may accept, listing six permitted materials (linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp and mixed fibres), and give detailed instructions for cutting and sewing robes in a pattern of patches said to resemble the fields of Magadha (Horner 1951). Buddhist monasteries were also major patrons of builders, carvers and painters, as the rock-cut halls of western India and the paintings of Ajanta show.

Jain texts approached craft from the point of view of non-violence. The lay vows of the Jain tradition forbid fifteen “occupations that bind karma” (karmādāna), including trades that involve fire and the destruction of living beings, such as charcoal-burning, clearing forests, digging and trading in lac, ivory, poisons and animal products. Such rules helped to steer Jain laymen away from many crafts and towards commerce, banking and the jewellery trade, and Jain merchants became important patrons of temple building, manuscript production and textile trade in western India (Jaini 1979).

The earliest Tamil poetry, the Caṅkam anthologies of the early centuries CE, describes busy markets and harbours (Ramanujan 1985; Zvelebil 1973). The long poems Maturaikkāñci and Paṭṭiṉappālai picture the streets of Madurai and of the port of Pukār (Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam), crowded with craftsmen, merchants and foreign traders, and Tamil poets often compare fine cloth to the cast-off skin of a snake or to steam or smoke. The fullest early literary picture of an Indian craft city is in the Tamil epic Cilappatikāram, probably composed in the middle of the first millennium CE. Its fifth canto describes the two quarters of Pukār during the festival of Indra: the houses of foreign traders and the warehouses by the sea, and streets in which particular trades lived and worked together, among them weavers of silk, wool and cotton, dealers in perfumes, gems and gold, and workers in metal and wood (Parthasarathy 1993). Its sequel, the Buddhist Maṇimēkalai, is set in the same city. These descriptions are literary, but they agree with archaeological evidence from sites such as Kodumanal, Arikamedu and Alagankulam for bead-making, iron-working and trade in this period.

docs.title: 1.4 The Archaeological Record: Craft in the Indus Cities
docs.text:
The earliest systematic evidence for specialised craft production in South Asia comes from the cities of the Indus or Harappan civilisation, whose mature phase is usually dated c. 2600–1900 BCE (Allchin and Allchin 1982; Kenoyer 1998). Excavations at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Chanhudaro, Dholavira and Lothal have revealed workshops and production debris for a wide range of crafts:

  • Shell working. Bangles and inlays were cut from the conch shell Turbinella pyrum, using bronze saws; the debris allows the whole sequence of production to be reconstructed.

  • Stone beads. Long carnelian beads were drilled with specially made stone drills, and carnelian was bleached and “etched” with white designs. Etched carnelian beads of Indus type have been found in Mesopotamia, including the royal tombs at Ur.

  • Faience and stoneware. Indus craftsmen made glazed faience beads, figurines and seals, and a very hard fired stoneware used for bangles. Faience was made earlier in Egypt and Mesopotamia; the Indus industry was a sophisticated regional tradition rather than the world’s first.

  • Metalwork. Copper and bronze were cast and hammered into tools, vessels and ornaments. The bronze “dancing girl” from Mohenjo-daro was cast by the lost-wax method.

  • Weights and seals. Standardised cubical stone weights and carved steatite seals point to an organised system of exchange and control.

Kenoyer’s work at Harappa shows that many of these crafts were practised by specialists in particular parts of the city, and that some products, such as stoneware bangles and fine seals, were made under close control (Kenoyer 1997). The Indus evidence also includes some of the earliest cotton cloth and some of the earliest silk in the Old World (Chapter 4).

Scholarly Note: Lothal: Dock or Reservoir?

The large brick-lined basin at Lothal in Gujarat, about 214–219 metres long and 35–37 metres wide (published figures vary), was interpreted by its excavator S. R. Rao as a dockyard for ships coming from the Gulf of Khambhat. Some archaeologists regard the basin instead as a water reservoir or tank; its function — dock or reservoir — remains debated. A seal of Persian Gulf type found at Lothal and the many Indus objects found in the Gulf and Mesopotamia show that there was sea-borne trade, but “the world’s first dockyard” should be treated as a hypothesis, not a fact.

The lost-wax casting of the Mohenjo-daro bronzes is often linked with the lost-wax casting still practised by Dhokra smiths in central and eastern India. The technique is the same in principle, but there is no documented chain of transmission over four thousand years, and lost-wax casting was practised in many parts of the ancient world. It is better to speak of a long history of the technique in the subcontinent than of an unbroken lineage of craftsmen.

docs.title: 1.5.1 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra attributed to Kauṭilya is a composite work, probably compiled between about 50 BCE and 300 CE (its attribution to Cāṇakya, minister of Candragupta Maurya c. 300 BCE, is traditional) (Olivelle 2013). Its second book describes the duties of a series of superintendents, several of whom control craft production: the superintendent of mines (2.12), who also runs metal workshops; the superintendent of gold (2.13) and the state goldsmith (2.14); the superintendent of forest produce (2.17); and the superintendent of yarn (2.23), who organises spinning by women and weaving in state workshops. Another chapter (2.11) describes the precious goods to be received into the treasury, including pearls, gems, diamonds, coral, sandalwood and fine textiles, with notes on their sources and qualities. Book 4 opens with a chapter on “keeping watch over artisans” (kārukarakṣaṇa), which regulates the dealings of weavers, washermen, goldsmiths and other craftsmen with their customers and fixes penalties for fraud (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). The text thus gives a precise picture of the state’s interest in craft: taxation, quality control, the prevention of fraud and the supply of the royal household and army.

docs.title: 1.5.2 The Śilpaśāstra Literature
docs.text:
The technical literature on architecture and image-making developed from the middle of the first millennium CE. Among the most important works are:

Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira (6th century CE) An encyclopaedia of omens and natural knowledge with chapters on houses, temples, images, the selection of timber, gems, and perfumes (Bhat 1981–1982). Mayamata (c. 9th–12th century) A South Indian treatise on houses, temples, towns and images, important for its description of the master builder and his team; its editor and translator, Bruno Dagens, places it in the Tamil country between the ninth and the twelfth century (Dagens 1994). Mānasāra (medieval; date disputed) A South Indian treatise in seventy chapters on architecture and image-making, edited and translated by P. K. Acharya, who dated it to c. 500–700 CE; most later scholars place it after the Mayamata, though no firm date can be given (Acharya 1934). Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra (11th century) An architectural treatise attributed to King Bhoja of Dhārā. Mānasollāsa (c. 1131 CE) A royal encyclopaedia composed for the Cālukya king Someśvara III, in five sections of twenty chapters each, covering kingship, the royal household, pleasures and arts (Shrigondekar 1925–1961). Aparājitapṛcchā (12th–13th century) A western Indian treatise in the Māru-Gurjara tradition, attributed to Bhuvanadeva. Viśvakarmaprakāśa A popular text on house-building attributed to Viśvakarman, of uncertain date. Śilparatna of Śrīkumāra (16th century) A Kerala treatise on architecture, image-making and painting, relevant to the timber architecture of Kerala (Chapter 7).

These texts were written by and for learned specialists, and how far working builders and sculptors used them is debated. Stella Kramrisch, whose The Hindu Temple (1946) remains the classic synthesis, emphasised that in these texts measurement, ritual and meaning are inseparable: the proportional grid of a temple is also a map of the cosmos (Kramrisch 1946). Her later essay on “Traditions of the Indian Craftsman” stresses the craftsman’s dependence on received forms and on the workshop rather than on books (Kramrisch 1958). Most crafts, such as weaving, dyeing, pottery and smithing, have no comparable Sanskrit literature at all.

docs.title: 1.6 Craft in Indian Thought
docs.text:
Craft supplied Indian philosophers with some of their most familiar examples. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.1.4–6) explains how knowledge of a single underlying reality gives knowledge of all its forms by three craft analogies: by one lump of clay everything made of clay is known, the modification being “a name, a matter of words”, while “clay” alone is real; likewise with a copper (or gold) ornament and with an iron nail-cutter. The example of the pot and the clay became a standard illustration of the relation between cause and effect in Sāṃkhya and Vedānta. The Sāṃkhyakārikā (67) compares the liberated person who continues to live to a potter’s wheel that keeps turning after the potter has stopped. These are philosophical uses of craft, not statements about the status of craftsmen; but they show how familiar craft processes were to the thinkers who used them.

The Bhagavad Gītā defines yoga as “skill in action” (yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam, BG 2.50). In context the phrase means the skill of acting without attachment to the results of action, not craftsmanship in the ordinary sense; but modern writers on Indian craft, from Coomaraswamy onwards, have often applied it to the artisan’s absorbed attention to work (Coomaraswamy 1909). The Gītā’s teaching that it is better to do one’s own duty (svadharma) badly than another’s well (BG 3.35), and its account of the duties of the four varṇas (BG 18.41–48), have a more ambiguous legacy: they could give dignity to every kind of work, but they were also read as sanctioning a social order in which occupation was fixed by birth.

docs.title: 1.6.1 The Six Limbs of Painting
docs.text: The clearest piece of classical theory about the visual arts is the list of six “limbs” (ṣaḍaṅga) of painting quoted by Yaśodhara in his commentary on the Kāmasūtra’s list of arts: rūpabheda (the distinction of forms), pramāṇa (proportion), bhāva (expression of feeling), lāvaṇyayojana (the infusion of grace), sādṛśya (likeness) and varṇikābhaṅga (the handling of colour). The Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa, whose third book contains a substantial treatise on painting and image-making (the Citrasūtra), discusses similar qualities. These lists apply to painting and sculpture, but they suggest the standards by which skilled work in general was judged: correct proportion and form, expressive life, and beauty.

docs.title: 1.7 Tools and Workshops
docs.text:
Indian craftsmen worked mostly with simple tools, used with great skill. The carpenter’s adze, saw, chisel and bow-drill; the smith’s bellows of goatskin or bamboo, tongs, hammers and anvil; the potter’s wheel, paddle and anvil; the weaver’s loom, shuttle and reed; the bow-lathe, turned with one hand by a bow while the other hand guides the tool, used by turners and toy-makers; the goldsmith’s blowpipe, crucible and touchstone; the jeweller’s bow-drill and polishing wheel; the block-printer’s carved blocks and the painter’s brushes of squirrel hair: these were the basic equipment of Indian crafts. Many tools were made or maintained by the craftsmen themselves, and many were treated with respect and worshipped once a year (Chapter 2).

Workshops were usually in or beside the home, and work often took place sitting on the ground, with the feet used as well as the hands to hold or operate tools. Western visitors were often struck by the contrast between the simplicity of the equipment and the refinement of the product. The contrast is misleading if it suggests that technique did not matter: the sophistication of Indian crafts lay less in machinery than in the organisation of processes, the knowledge of materials and the skill of hands trained from childhood.

docs.title: 1.8 Artisans and Caste
docs.text: Any honest account of Indian crafts must deal with caste. For most of the last two thousand years, the great majority of crafts were practised by hereditary occupational groups (jāti), each associated with a particular occupation, marrying within itself, and ranked within a local hierarchy. Potters, smiths, carpenters, weavers, oil-pressers, washermen, barbers, leather-workers and many others formed distinct jātis, though the names, ranks and occupations of these groups varied greatly from region to region and changed over time (Bayly 1999).

docs.title: 1.8.1 What the Law-Books Say
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstras both recognised artisans and ranked them low. Manu (c. 2nd century CE) allows the king to exact one day’s labour a month from artisans and craftsmen instead of taxes (Manu 7.138), and declares that “the hand of an artisan is always pure” while he is at work (Manu 5.129), a practical rule that allowed artisans’ products to be used by people of higher rank (Olivelle 2005). The same text includes smiths, goldsmiths, basket-makers, washermen and others among the people whose food a Brahmin should not accept (Manu 4.210–219), and in its account of the “mixed” castes (Manu 10) it assigns occupations such as leather-work, carpentry and fishing to groups born of unions between varṇas. The law-books also recognised the customs of guilds and occupational groups as binding on their members (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 1.8.2 Untouchability and Craft
docs.text: The lowest place in this hierarchy was given to groups whose work involved death, dirt or animal remains: leather-workers and tanners, scavengers, sweepers, and in some regions weavers of coarse cloth, basket-makers and drummers. Communities such as the Chamārs and Mochīs of north India, the Mādigas of Andhra and Karnataka, the Cakkiliyars (Aruntatiyars) of Tamil Nadu and the Dhors and Chāmbhārs of Maharashtra were treated as untouchable, excluded from temples, wells and schools, and subjected to violence. B. R. Ambedkar’s Annihilation of Caste (1936) remains the most forceful critique of the idea that caste is merely a rational division of labour; in his words, the caste system “is not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers” (Ambedkar 1936). Chapter 13 treats untouchability, the historians’ critique of the “polluting occupation” stereotype and the artisans’ own responses more fully.

docs.title: 1.8.3 Artisans’ Own Traditions
docs.text: Artisans did not simply accept the places assigned to them. The Viśvakarma communities of the South (the Kammāḷar of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, the Pāñcāla of Karnataka and Andhra), who comprise smiths, carpenters, bronze-casters, stone-carvers and goldsmiths, claim descent from the divine craftsman Viśvakarman and a Brahmanical status of their own, and have long disputed the precedence of Brahmins (Chapter 2) (Brouwer 1995). Potters in north India call themselves Prajāpati after the creator. Many of the most important poet-saints of the bhakti movements were artisans, from Kabīr the weaver to Raidās the leather-worker, and their songs speak with the authority of working people (Chapter 13). These traditions should be represented on their own terms, as part of India’s craft heritage.

docs.title: 1.9 Art and Craft
docs.text:
Modern English distinguishes “art”, made by individual artists for contemplation, from “craft”, made by artisans for use. The distinction took shape in Europe in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and colonial institutions in India applied it, classifying textiles, metalwork and pottery as “industrial arts” or “art manufactures” and placing them below painting and sculpture (Chapter 14). Indian languages did not divide the field in the same way: śilpa covered the work of the temple sculptor and the weaver alike, and the sixty-four kalās mixed painting with needlework and carpentry. Ananda Coomaraswamy argued that in traditional societies there was no distinction between fine art and craft, and that every made thing was meant to be both useful and beautiful (Coomaraswamy 1934). The argument is attractive, but the absence of a single word for “fine art” did not mean the absence of hierarchy. Indian society ranked different kinds of makers very differently, and the sculptor who carved temple images or the goldsmith who served a king enjoyed a status very different from that of the basket-maker or the tanner.

The present volume uses “craft” in a broad sense, for all skilled making by hand, and avoids treating any one craft as more “artistic” than another. Painting and sculpture as arts are treated in other volumes of this series; here they appear as crafts, with attention to materials, techniques and the people who practised them.

docs.title: 1.10 Craft and Environment
docs.text: Every craft depended on local materials: clays, ores, fuels, fibres, dye plants, woods, grasses and water. Craft traditions were therefore closely adapted to their environments, and changes in land use, forest law, water supply and agriculture have often affected them more than changes in fashion. It is sometimes claimed that traditional crafts were inherently “sustainable”. Many were indeed economical in their use of energy and materials, reusing and recycling waste; but some, such as iron smelting and lime and brick burning, consumed large quantities of wood and charcoal, and others, such as tanning, dyeing and metalworking, produced pollution and exposed workers to harm. A realistic history of crafts must consider both their ecological wisdom and their costs.

docs.title: 1.11 Sources for the History of Crafts
docs.text:
Because craftspeople rarely wrote about their own work, the historian of Indian crafts must piece together evidence of many kinds. Archaeology provides excavated objects, workshops, kilns, slag heaps and debris, analysed by scientific methods and dated by radiocarbon; it supplies most of the evidence for the Indus period and much for later periods, including the zinc retorts of Zawar and the printed cottons of Fustat. Surviving objects (textiles, jewellery, metalwork and other things preserved in temples, palaces, families and museums, many of them now outside India) show what was made and for whom. Inscriptions name craftsmen and guilds as donors, list artisans’ rights and duties in temples, and record grants on copper plates.

Texts in Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit, Tamil, Persian and other languages describe, regulate, classify and praise crafts, though seldom from the craftsman’s point of view. Greek, Chinese, Arab, Persian and European travellers wrote about what they saw, and from the seventeenth century the vast archives of the European trading companies record prices, qualities, quantities and the organisation of production. Around 1900 district gazetteers, census reports, industrial surveys and provincial monographs on particular crafts described crafts and craft communities through the categories of colonial administration, and anthropologists have continued the work since. Last, the knowledge of present-day craftspeople can often explain techniques that texts and objects leave obscure, and archaeologists increasingly study living crafts, such as bead-making at Khambhat or village pottery, to interpret ancient evidence.

Each kind of source has its biases: texts reflect the views of elites, company records the interests of merchants, colonial surveys the assumptions of administrators. The history of crafts is therefore always partly a reconstruction.

docs.title: 1.12 Craft, Trade and the Wider World
docs.text:
Indian craft products travelled very far. Carnelian beads of Indus type reached Mesopotamia in the third millennium BCE. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek merchant’s handbook of the mid-first century CE, lists Indian cotton cloth of many grades, including the “Gangetic” muslins of Bengal, and Indian iron and steel, among the exports of Indian ports (Casson 1989). Glass beads made at Arikamedu and other South Indian sites were traded across the Indian Ocean (Francis 2002). Block-printed Indian cottons of the tenth to fifteenth centuries have been excavated in large numbers in Egypt (Barnes 1997), and Indian textiles were the principal medium of exchange for spices in the Indonesian archipelago (Guy 1998). From the seventeenth century the European trading companies carried Indian cottons to Europe, West Africa and the Americas (Riello and Roy 2009; Riello 2013). Table 1.1 summarises these exports by period. These trades are surveyed in the chapters that follow and, for maritime commerce, in Volume 19.

Table 1.1. Some Indian craft exports in long-distance trade (approximate periods) Period Products Destinations and evidence c. 2600–1900 BCE Carnelian beads, shell, other Indus goods Mesopotamia and the Gulf (excavated objects, cuneiform texts on Meluhha) 1st century CE Cotton cloth, muslins, iron and steel, gems, pepper Red Sea and Roman Egypt (Periplus) c. 2nd century BCE onwards Glass beads Southeast Asia and East Africa (excavated beads) 10th–15th centuries Block-printed and resist-dyed cottons (mainly Gujarat) Egypt and the Red Sea (Fustat, Quseir al-Qadim) 14th–18th centuries Paṭolā, printed and painted cottons Southeast Asia (heirloom textiles in Indonesia) 17th–18th centuries Calicoes, chintz, muslins Europe, West Africa, the Americas (company records)

How large was this craft economy? Economic historians agree that before the nineteenth century South Asia was one of the world’s great manufacturing regions, and that its share of world manufacturing fell drastically in the colonial period; but the figures usually quoted are rough estimates whose basis is discussed in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 1.13 An Outline History
docs.text:
The chapters that follow are organised by material and theme. A brief chronological outline may help the reader to place them.

Before c. 1900 BCE Neolithic and Chalcolithic villages of Baluchistan and the Indus region (Mehrgarh) develop pottery, copper working, cotton and bead-making; the mature Harappan cities (c. 2600–1900 BCE) support highly specialised crafts and long-distance trade. c. 1900–600 BCE Regional Chalcolithic and early Iron Age cultures; Vedic texts describe carpenters, chariot-makers, smiths and weavers; iron comes into common use. c. 600 BCE–300 CE The second urbanisation of the Ganga valley and the Deccan; coinage; guilds; Buddhist and Jain monasteries as patrons; the Arthaśāstra; Indian Ocean trade with the Roman world, Southeast Asia and East Africa; crucible steel and glass beads in the south. c. 300–1200 Gupta and post-Gupta kingdoms; the growth of temple architecture and image-making; the śilpaśāstras; land grants on copper plates; regional kingdoms in the south (Pallava, Cola) and east (Pāla); the beginnings of zinc distillation; Indian textiles traded to Egypt and Southeast Asia. c. 1200–1550 The Delhi Sultanate and regional sultanates introduce or spread paper, the spinning wheel, new weaving and dyeing techniques, glazed tiles and Persian design; Gujarat and the Coromandel coast dominate Indian Ocean textile trade; Vijayanagara in the south. c. 1550–1750 The Mughal empire and Rajput, Deccani and southern courts; imperial workshops; carpets, jewellery and painting at their height; European companies begin large-scale export of Indian textiles. c. 1750–1947 The East India Company and the British Raj; coercion of weavers; competition from British factory goods; decline and adaptation of crafts; colonial collecting and art schools; Svadeśī and khādī. After 1947 State support for handicrafts and handlooms; the craft revival; design schools; Geographical Indications; globalisation and new markets.

docs.title: 1.14 The Structure of This Volume
docs.text:
The book moves from ideas about making to materials, then to places, and finally to the institutions and history that shaped the makers’ lives. Chapter 2 follows Viśvakarman, the divine craftsman, from the Vedic hymns to the festival of Viśvakarma Pūjā and the artisan communities who claim him as ancestor. Chapters 3 to 11 are organised by material and process. Metals come first (Chapter 3): bronze-casting and the image-maker’s workshop, iron and the Delhi pillar, crucible steel, zinc, gold and silver, Bidrī ware and brass. Two chapters on textiles follow, the first on fibres, looms, the regional woven traditions, embroidery, garments and their makers (Chapter 4), the second on dyeing, printing, the chintz trade and Indian cloth in Asia, Africa and the Atlantic world (Chapter 5). Pottery and terracotta (Chapter 6) are followed by the hard materials that are cut and carved, wood, ivory and stone, including the makers of musical instruments (Chapter 7), and by bamboo, cane and the other plant fibres (Chapter 8). Leather has a chapter of its own (Chapter 9), because its makers were placed at the bottom of the caste order and its history shows most clearly the theme of this book. Chapter 10 treats the crafts of adornment: jewellery and gems, beads, glass, lac and perfume. Chapter 11 treats painting as a craft together with the arts of the book, and the crafts of festivals, toys, games and masks.

Chapter 12 surveys living crafts region by region, with a brief look at Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and Pakistan, and its closing table serves as a finding aid to the rest of the book. The last three chapters are analytical. Chapter 13 examines guilds, caste, the organisation of production, the nature of craft knowledge and the notations artisans devised, the relation between craft and science, and the work of women and children. Chapter 14 treats crafts in the colonial economy, including the debate on “deindustrialisation”, the myth of the muslin weavers’ thumbs and the making of khādī, and Chapter 15 the revival, protection and present condition of the crafts, including the design schools. Line diagrams of the main processes (the loom, resist-dyeing, the chintz sequence, lost-wax casting, crucible steel and zinc, the potter’s wheel and firing, and tanning) accompany the chapters that describe them. Photographs show representative objects, from a Harappan storage jar and a Cola bronze to a Kashmir shawl and a box spinning wheel, and some of the monuments discussed; their sources are listed under Image Credits at the end of the volume.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the Indus crafts, Kenoyer (1998); for the Arthaśāstra, Olivelle (2013); for the śilpaśāstras and the temple, Kramrisch (1946), with Acharya (1927) for technical terms; for Indian art as a whole, Kramrisch (1954); for Coomaraswamy’s influential theory of traditional art, Coomaraswamy (1934); for a regional encyclopaedia of contemporary crafts, Ranjan and Ranjan (2007); for a classic survey by a leader of the craft revival, Chattopadhyay (1975); for caste, Bayly (1999) and Ambedkar (1936).

docs.title: Chapter 2: Viśvakarman: The Divine Craftsman and His Communities
docs.text: In many workshops of India, from engineering works in Howrah to goldsmiths’ shops in Kerala, an image or print of Viśvakarman, the divine craftsman, receives worship once a year, and tools and machines are garlanded in his honour. Viśvakarman (in modern Indian languages usually Viśvakarmā) is the patron deity of craftsmen across much of India, and the ancestor claimed by several large artisan communities. This chapter follows the figure from the Vedic hymns, where “Viśvakarman” is a name for the creator, through the epics and Purāṇas, where he is the architect of the gods, to the religious and social life of the communities who claim him as their own.

docs.title: 2.1 Viśvakarman and Tvaṣṭṛ in the Veda
2.1.1 The Viśvakarman Hymns
docs.text:
The name Viśvakarman means “maker of all” or “whose work is everything”. In the Ṛgveda it is used as an epithet of Indra and the Sun, and in two late hymns of the tenth book (RV 10.81 and 10.82) it names the creator himself. These hymns are among the earliest Indian speculations on the origin of the world, and they think about creation in the language of craft (Jamison and Brereton 2014):

Ṛgveda 10.81.3

viśvataścakṣur uta viśvatomukho viśvatobāhur uta viśvataspāt sam bāhubhyāṃ dhamati sam patatrair dyāvābhūmī janayan deva ekaḥ

“With eyes on every side and faces on every side, with arms on every side and feet on every side, the one god, generating heaven and earth, blows them together with his arms and with his wings.”

The verb sam dhamati, “blows together”, is the smith’s word for working the bellows (the same verb is used of the smith in RV 10.72.2), and the “wings” may be the fans used to blow a fire. The next verse asks a carpenter’s question:

Ṛgveda 10.81.4

kiṃ svid vanaṃ ka u sa vṛkṣa āsa yato dyāvāpṛthivī niṣṭatakṣuḥ

“What was the wood, and what the tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth?”

The verb takṣ-, “to fashion, to hew”, is the root of takṣan, the carpenter. Creation is imagined as the work of a smith and a carpenter; the questions are left open, as befits the speculative hymns of the late Ṛgveda.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Tvaṣṭṛ and the Ṛbhus
docs.text:
In the Ṛgveda the craftsman of the gods par excellence is Tvaṣṭṛ, “the fashioner”. He forges Indra’s mace, the vajra (RV 1.32.2), and he is the god who shapes forms (rūpa) in the womb; a hymn for conception asks that Tvaṣṭṛ “fashion the forms” of the child (RV 10.184.1). Beside him stand the three Ṛbhus, divine artisans who became immortal through their skill: they renewed their aged parents, fashioned a chariot for the Aśvins and a cow that gave milk, and made four cups out of Tvaṣṭṛ’s single cup (RV 1.161 and the Ṛbhu hymns of the fourth book). In later tradition Tvaṣṭṛ and Viśvakarman are often identified.

The Ṛbhus are especially interesting as divine artisans who were not born gods but earned immortality and a share in the sacrifice through their craftsmanship. They are called “skilful” and “good workers”, and their achievements are all craft achievements: the chariot, the cup, the cow, the renewal of their parents. In the ritual, they receive their share of soma at the third pressing of the day. Some scholars have seen in them a reflection of the honour in which skilled craftsmen were held in early Vedic society; others emphasise that they remain, in the hymns, figures of slightly lower rank than the great gods, admitted to the sacrifice only late (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Either way, the Vedic poets of the Ṛbhu hymns treated the making of things, like the making of hymns, as an activity of the highest significance.

docs.title: 2.2 The Architect of the Gods
docs.text:
In the epics and Purāṇas Viśvakarman becomes the architect and engineer of the gods. According to the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (1.15.118–119) he is the son of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus, and of Yogasiddhā, the sister of Bṛhaspati (Mani 1975). His daughter Saṃjñā married the Sun; unable to bear her husband’s brilliance, she fled, and Viśvakarman, according to the same Purāṇa (3.2.2–12), trimmed the Sun on his lathe and from the filings made the discus of Viṣṇu, the trident of Śiva and other divine weapons.

The works attributed to Viśvakarman in the epics and Purāṇas include the city of Laṅkā, the aerial chariot Puṣpaka, and Kṛṣṇa’s city of Dvārakā; in some versions he fashions Indra’s thunderbolt from the bones of the sage Dadhīca. In the Rāmāyaṇa the bridge to Laṅkā is built by the monkey Nala, “son of Viśvakarman”. In the Mahābhārata the wonderful assembly-hall of the Pāṇḍavas, with its floors that look like water and its pools that look like floors, is built not by Viśvakarman but by Maya, the architect of the Dānavas. These stories express admiration for skilled building on a heroic scale; they are not, as is sometimes claimed, coded records of ancient aircraft or other lost technologies.

In Pali literature the divine craftsman appears as Vissakamma, a god (devaputta) who builds palaces and other works for Sakka (Indra), the king of the gods, and who in some stories descends to earth to build for kings and holy men. Jain narratives describe the gods building the assembly-hall (samavasaraṇa) in which a Tīrthaṅkara preaches after attaining omniscience, a wonderful circular structure of walls, gateways and terraces that is often represented in Jain painting and sculpture. With the spread of Indian religions, the divine craftsman travelled to Southeast Asia: in Thailand, Phra Witsanukam (Viśvakarman) is revered as the patron of craftsmen and builders.

docs.title: 2.2.1 The Person of the Site
docs.text: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā tells how the vāstupuruṣa came to lie beneath every building. A formless being, blocking heaven and earth, was seized and pressed face down to the ground by the gods, who remained seated on its limbs; Brahmā placed it there as the “person of the site”, to be honoured whenever a building is laid out (Bhat 1981–1982). Each god presides over the square of the grid on which he sits, and the builder must avoid placing pillars or walls on the vulnerable points (marman) of the body. The myth links the measuring and dividing of the ground, the first task of the builder, with the cosmic ordering of chaos by the gods.

docs.title: 2.2.2 The Craftsman’s Vow
docs.text: The śilpaśāstras present the work of the image-maker as a ritual discipline. The craftsman was to begin work on an auspicious day, purify himself, worship the deity of the image and his own tools, and visualise the form described in the meditation verses (dhyāna-śloka) of the deity before carving or modelling it. These prescriptions are ideals stated in learned texts; they are also, in modified form, part of the living practice of many sthapati families, who worship their tools and begin major work with rituals.

docs.title: 2.3 Viśvakarman in the Śilpaśāstras
docs.text: The treatises on architecture and image-making present themselves as revealed by divine or semi-divine authors: the Mayamata by Maya, other texts by Viśvakarman, Kāśyapa or Agastya. In this tradition Viśvakarman is the archetypal sthapati, and craft knowledge descends from him.

docs.title: 2.3.1 The Master Builder and His Team
docs.text:
The Mayamata and the Mānasāra describe the qualifications of the master builder and a team of four craftsmen (Dagens 1994; Acharya 1934):

Sthapati The master builder, who must know the treatises, be skilled in all the crafts and of good character, and who directs the whole work. Sūtragrāhin “He who holds the cord”, the surveyor and draughtsman, often the son or pupil of the sthapati. Takṣaka The carver, who cuts wood or stone to size. Vardhakin The joiner or assembler, who fits together what the carver has cut.

The sthapati was also a ritual figure: the building of a temple or the making of an image was punctuated by rites, and the completed image received its life through the rite of “establishing the breath” (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), performed by priests (Kramrisch 1946).

docs.title: 2.3.2 Measure and Proportion
docs.text:
The śilpaśāstras describe images in terms of a module, the tāla (roughly the length of the face), and classify figures by systems of ten, nine, eight or fewer tālas; the highest gods are typically made in the ten-tāla system. Temples and houses are laid out on grids of squares (pada) governed by the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala, the diagram of the “person of the site”. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā describes a grid of eighty-one squares with forty-five deities, Brahmā at the centre and the head of the vāstupuruṣa in the north-east (Bhat 1981–1982). These systems are discussed more fully in Volume 16.

Scholarly Note: Vāstu Today

Vāstu is today the subject of a large popular literature that presents it as a science of “energies” and makes claims about magnetism, health and prosperity. Such claims have no basis in the classical texts, which are concerned with ritual order, auspiciousness and proportion, nor in modern science. The modern uses and reinventions of vāstu are studied by Chakrabarti (1998); the planning of eighteenth-century Jaipur, often cited as a vāstu city, is examined by Sachdev and Tillotson (2002).

docs.title: 2.3.3 Texts in the Workshop: Odisha
docs.text: In at least one region we can see how śilpa texts were used by working craftsmen. In Odisha, families of hereditary stone-carvers kept palm-leaf manuscripts of architectural texts and drawings, which they consulted and copied. The Swiss artist and scholar Alice Boner, working with the Sanskrit scholar Sadāśiva Rath Śarmā, edited and translated one such text, the Śilpa Prakāśa attributed to Rāmacandra Kaulācāra, a manual of temple architecture and ornament in the Odishan tradition; its editors argued for an early medieval date, which others think too early (Boner and Rath Śarmā 1966). Its detailed instructions for laying out temple walls and for drawing figures and ornaments show a close connection between text and practice, and its vocabulary is still partly understood by Odishan carvers. Elsewhere, the relation between the Sanskrit treatises and the knowledge of working builders was looser: builders learned by apprenticeship, and the texts were often known to them through oral tradition and local manuals in regional languages.

docs.title: 2.3.4 Maya, Architect of the Asuras
docs.text: Viśvakarman has a counterpart in Maya, the architect of the demons (asuras or dānavas). In the Mahābhārata Maya, saved by Arjuna from the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest, builds the wonderful assembly-hall of the Pāṇḍavas in gratitude; in the Purāṇas he builds the three flying cities of the demons, which Śiva destroys with a single arrow. South Indian tradition made Maya the author of the Mayamata and of other works on architecture and astronomy, and the Sūryasiddhānta, the most important Indian astronomical text, is presented as revealed by the Sun to an Asura named Maya. Maya thus represents a rival, non-Vedic source of craft knowledge, honoured even though he belongs to the enemies of the gods.

docs.title: 2.4 Viśvakarma Pūjā
docs.text:
The festival of Viśvakarma Pūjā is celebrated in eastern India (Bengal, Odisha, Bihar, Jharkhand, Assam and Tripura) on the day of the Sun’s entry into Virgo (Kanyā saṅkrānti), at the end of the Bengali month of Bhādra, which usually falls on 16, 17 or 18 September. In parts of north India Viśvakarma is worshipped on the day after Dīpāvalī. In south India tools are worshipped on the ninth day of Navarātri (Āyudha Pūjā, Mahānavamī), when craftsmen, students and soldiers honour the instruments of their work.

On Viśvakarma Pūjā, workshops, factories and garages close; machines and tools are cleaned and decorated; and an image of the god is installed. In Bengal the image is typically a youthful, moustached, four-armed figure riding an elephant, holding tools such as a hammer and a measuring instrument. In much of India the god is shown as an older, bearded figure seated on a goose (haṃsa). Among south Indian Viśvakarma communities a five-faced form, representing the five crafts, is common. The festival has adapted readily to industrial work: it is observed in railway workshops, steel plants, shipyards and among taxi and auto-rickshaw drivers, who decorate their vehicles.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Āyudha Pūjā
docs.text: In south India and Maharashtra, the worship of tools and weapons (āyudha pūjā) on the ninth day of Navarātri plays a role similar to that of Viśvakarma Pūjā in the east. Soldiers worship their weapons, farmers their ploughs, craftsmen their tools, students their books and musicians their instruments; today vehicles, computers and machines are cleaned, marked with sandal paste and vermilion, and garlanded. The custom is connected with the worship of the goddess Durgā, who in the myth received her weapons from the gods, and with the epic story in which the Pāṇḍavas recover the weapons they had hidden in a tree during their year in disguise. The festival expresses, in a form shared by many social groups, the idea that the instruments of work deserve respect.

docs.title: 2.5.1 Five Crafts, Five Sons
docs.text:
Several large artisan communities claim descent from Viśvakarman. In south India the five crafts of iron, wood, brass and bronze, stone and gold are practised by the communities known in Tamil as Kammāḷar, in Kerala as Viśvakarma or by the names of the individual crafts, in Karnataka as Pāñcāla (“of the five”) and in Andhra as Viśvabrāhmaṇa. Their traditions hold that Viśvakarman had five sons, each the ancestor of one craft (Table 2.1).

Table 2.1. The five crafts of the south Indian Viśvakarma communities, as described in community tradition Ancestor Craft Tamil and Malayalam names Manu iron (smiths) Kollaṉ Maya wood (carpenters) Taccaṉ, Āśāri Tvaṣṭṛ brass, copper, bronze Kaṉṉāṉ; Mūśāri (Kerala) Śilpī stone (masons, sculptors) Kal-taccaṉ, Kallāśāri Viśvajña (Daivajña) gold, silver (goldsmiths) Taṭṭāṉ

In north India there is no single equivalent, but smiths (Lohār), carpenters (Baṛhaī, Khātī), goldsmiths (Sunār) and others have increasingly adopted the name Viśvakarma (often spelled Vishwakarma) as a common caste or community name in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and Viśvakarma associations are active in community and political life.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Claims to Status
docs.text:
The south Indian artisans’ claim to be “Viśvabrāhmaṇa”, Brahmins of Viśvakarman, is old. They had their own priests, wore the sacred thread, and in some places refused to accept the ritual precedence of Brahmins. Medieval Tamil society was divided into “right-hand” (valaṅkai) and “left-hand” (iṭaṅkai) caste groupings; the Kammāḷar belonged to the left hand, and disputes between the two divisions over processional and ritual privileges were frequent from the Cola period into the nineteenth century (Bayly 1999). Under British rule such disputes came before the courts, and censuses that ranked castes provoked petitions from Viśvakarma associations for recognition as Brahmins. Jan Brouwer’s study of the Viśvakarma artisans of Karnataka shows how their own texts, myths and rituals articulate an artisan view of the world, in which making is the primary sacred act and the craftsman, not the priest, stands closest to the creator (Brouwer 1995).

These claims are best understood on their own terms: as an artisan tradition asserting the dignity and sanctity of skilled work, in a society whose dominant texts ranked artisans low (Chapter 1). They were also, however, claims within the caste system rather than against it; Viśvakarma communities themselves observed rules of purity and distance towards groups they considered lower.

docs.title: 2.5.3 Builders and Their Names
docs.text:
Indian temples are usually remembered by the names of their royal patrons, but inscriptions sometimes name the builders. The great Rājarājeśvara (Bṛhadīśvara) temple at Thanjavur, completed c. 1010 CE, records the name of its chief architect, Kuñcaramallaṉ Rājarāja Peruntaccaṉ (in Sanskritised form Kuñjaramalla). At Pattadakal an eighth-century inscription names the architect of the Virūpākṣa temple. The Hoysaḷa temples of Karnataka (12th–13th centuries) are notable for the many sculptors’ signatures carved on the images, among them Mallitamma and Dāsoja. Such evidence makes it possible to glimpse individual craftsmen behind monuments usually credited to kings.

Temples were also permanent employers of craftsmen. The inscriptions of Rājarāja I at Thanjavur list the hundreds of people attached to the temple, among them carpenters, goldsmiths, braziers and potters as well as priests, musicians, dancers and accountants, with the shares of land or grain allotted to each. Temple endowments thus maintained families of artisans over generations, and the great temple towns of south India, such as Madurai, Kumbakonam and Kāñcīpuram, became centres of bronze-casting, weaving, jewellery and other crafts serving both the temple and its pilgrims.

docs.title: 2.5.4 Viśvakarma in Modern Public Life
docs.text:
In the twentieth century, Viśvakarma associations campaigned for education, for the reform of community customs and for representation in politics, and many artisan communities have been classified as “Other Backward Classes” for the purposes of reservation in education and government employment. The festival of Viśvakarma has become an occasion for public celebration of labour and skill, and in 2023 the name was given to a national scheme for traditional artisans (Chapter 15). The name has thus moved from Vedic cosmology through artisan genealogy to labour politics and welfare policy.

Modern Relevance: The Sthapatis Today

The tradition of the hereditary sthapati continues, above all in Tamil Nadu. Bronze-casting families at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam make images by the lost-wax method for temples in India and abroad. The government college of architecture and sculpture at Mamallapuram, founded in the 1950s, trains young sculptors in the traditional canons; its long-serving principal was V. Gaṇapati Sthapati (1927–2011), whose works include the statue of Tiruvaḷḷuvar at Kanyakumari. Hindu temples built in North America, Europe and elsewhere often employ sthapatis and craftsmen from south India.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the Vedic hymns, Jamison and Brereton (2014); for the śilpaśāstras, Dagens (1994) and Acharya (1934); for the south Indian Viśvakarma artisans, Brouwer (1995); for caste in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Bayly (1999).

docs.title: Chapter 3: Loha: Metals and Metalworkers
docs.text: Metalworking is one of the oldest specialised crafts of the subcontinent and one of the best studied by archaeologists and metallurgists. Indian smiths forged massive objects of wrought iron, made high-carbon crucible steel that was exported across western Asia, distilled zinc on an industrial scale, and cast bronze images of great refinement. This chapter surveys these achievements from the point of view of the craftsman and his products. The history of metallurgy and of the chemical tradition of rasaśāstra is treated more fully in Volume 14 of this series (Rasāyana: Chemistry and Metallurgy), to which the reader is referred for technical detail.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Early Copper
docs.text:
A copper bead from an early burial at Mehrgarh in Baluchistan, perhaps of the sixth millennium BCE, is among the earliest metal objects in South Asia; the mineralised cotton fibres preserved inside it are discussed in Chapter 4 (Jarrige et al. 1995). Copper working became common in the fourth millennium, and the cities of the mature Harappan period (c. 2600–1900 BCE) used copper and bronze for tools, weapons, vessels and ornaments. Indus smiths used both arsenical copper and tin bronze, cast metal in open and closed moulds, and made small figures by the lost-wax process, of which the bronze “dancing girl” of Mohenjo-daro is the best known (Kenoyer 1998). The sources of Indus tin are uncertain; Afghanistan and Central Asia are possible sources, since the subcontinent itself has little tin.

In the Ganga–Yamuna Doab and further east, the so-called Copper Hoards of the early second millennium BCE include flat axes, harpoons, “antennae-hilted” swords and enigmatic anthropomorphic figures of thick copper sheet. Their makers are still debated; the copper may have come from the Khetri belt of Rajasthan or from the ores of Jharkhand and Odisha.

docs.title: 3.1.2 Bronze Casting by the Lost-Wax Process
docs.text:
Lost-wax casting (Sanskrit madhūcchiṣṭa-vidhāna, “the method of beeswax”) produces a unique metal copy of a wax model (Figure 3.1). The model is coated in fine clay, the clay is dried and heated so that the wax melts out, and molten metal is poured into the cavity; the mould is then broken to release the casting. For hollow castings the wax is modelled over a clay core. The Mānasāra includes a chapter on casting images in wax, and the method is described in a number of later texts (Acharya 1934).

Figure 3.1. Solid casting by the lost-wax process, as practised by the sthapatis of Swamimalai (schematic). Each wax model yields one casting, since the mould must be broken to release it. Dhokra casters model the wax over a clay core and seal the crucible of metal to the mould itself, so that the metal runs in when the heated mould is turned over.

The most celebrated Indian bronzes are those of the Cola period in Tamil Nadu (10th–13th centuries CE), made for processions in temples: images of Śiva as Naṭarāja, of Pārvatī, of the saints and of Viṣṇu and his consorts. They are cast solid, and their metal is usually a leaded copper or bronze; the “five-metal” alloy (pañcaloha) of gold, silver, copper and other metals spoken of in ritual texts is more an ideal than a description of the actual composition of most images. The hereditary sthapatis of Swamimalai in the Kaveri delta still make images by the same method (below).

The Cola bronze of Śiva as Naṭarāja, the lord of dance, shows what the method could achieve (Figure 3.2). The god dances within a ring of flames, one leg raised across his body, the other trampling a dwarf who personifies ignorance; one hand holds the drum whose sound accompanies creation, another the fire of destruction; one hand is raised in the gesture of protection, and another points to the raised foot, the refuge of the devotee; his locks fly out to either side with the river Gaṅgā caught in them. The image was usually cast in one piece, balanced on a single foot, with the flying hair and the ring of fire joined to the body at only a few points, and then carried in procession. Coomaraswamy’s essay “The Dance of Śiva” (1918) made this image famous in the West as a symbol of the rhythm of the universe (Coomaraswamy 1918); its interpretation draws on the Tamil devotional literature of Chidambaram as well as on Sanskrit texts.

Figure 3.2. Śiva as Naṭarāja, the lord of dance: a Cola bronze from Tamil Nadu of about 1000 CE, 113 cm high, cast solid by the lost-wax process. The god dances on the dwarf of ignorance within a ring of flames, with the drum in one upper hand and the fire in the other (Cleveland Museum of Art). Photo: Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Other regions had their own metal-image traditions. The Buddhist monasteries of Bihar and Bengal under the Pālas (8th–12th centuries) produced bronze images of the Buddha, bodhisattvas and Tantric deities, many found in hoards such as that of Kurkihar, which influenced the art of Nepal, Tibet and Southeast Asia. An earlier copper image of the standing Buddha, more than two metres high, found at Sultanganj in Bihar and now in the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery, shows that very large castings were made in the Gupta or post-Gupta period. Kashmir, the western Himalaya and Nepal developed brass and copper image traditions of their own; the Newar metalworkers of the Kathmandu valley became the leading image-makers of the Himalayan Buddhist world. In western India, Jain temples commissioned large numbers of metal images of the Tīrthaṅkaras, many inscribed with the date and the name of the donor.

Lost-wax casting is also practised by the Dhokra or Dokra metalworkers of West Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh. They build the wax model from threads of wax wound over a clay core, which gives their figures of animals, deities and people their characteristic ribbed surfaces (Chapter 12). Their metal is usually scrap brass, melted in a crucible sealed into the clay mould itself, so that when the mould is heated and inverted the molten metal flows directly into the cavity left by the wax. The Dhokra smiths were traditionally itinerant, making measuring bowls, lamps, bells, ornaments and images of local deities for village customers; since the mid-twentieth century, encouraged by craft boards and designers, they have made figures for urban and foreign buyers. Many Dhokra families are poor and landless, and the rising cost of brass and wax has made their craft precarious.

docs.title: 3.1.3 The Image-Maker’s Workshop Today
docs.text:
The canonical proportions and iconography of images are treated in Volume 16. Here we look at how a modern bronze workshop is organised and what it sells. At Swamimalai, near Kumbakonam, the bronze workshops are family enterprises of the Viśvakarma sthapatis (Chapter 2), ranging from a master working with his sons to larger studios employing dozens of hired workers. The work is divided by skill. The master sets out the proportions of a new image with a measuring strip graduated in the units of the texts, follows the dhyāna verse of the deity for its iconography, and usually models or at least finishes the face, the part on which the reputation of a workshop depends. Assistants prepare the wax, a mixture of beeswax, a resin and a little oil, which is softened by warming and rolled into sheets and rods. They model ornaments and attributes separately and fix them to the figure, and they attach the wax runners and vents. Other workers coat the model with several layers of fine alluvial clay from the river, the first very fine to take the detail and the later ones coarser and reinforced; they then heat the mould, drain the wax, and pour the metal melted in a crucible into the hot mould. Large images are cast in parts and joined. The longest stage is often the last. Chasing, engraving and filing the rough casting, sharpening the details of face, hands and ornaments, can take longer than modelling and casting together, and it is done by specialists with sets of fine chisels and files. The canon fixes the proportions, but the movement and modelling that distinguish a good image come from the skill of the craftsman and the conventions of his workshop.

The metal is usually copper with tin and lead. Customers who ask for pañcaloha often have token amounts of gold and silver added at the casting. The workshops produce for several markets at once: temples in Tamil Nadu and elsewhere in India, which have new images consecrated before worship; Hindu temples abroad; households, which buy small images for domestic shrines; and collectors and decorators in India and abroad. The name “Swamimalai bronze icons” has been registered as a Geographical Indication (Chapter 15). Because Cola and later bronzes have been stolen from temples and sold abroad, new images are subject to legal checks. Under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act of 1972, objects more than a hundred years old may not be exported except by the government or its authorised agencies, so a newly made image needs a certificate that it is not an antiquity before it leaves the country. The return to India in 2014 of a Cola Naṭarāja stolen from a temple at Sripuranthan and bought by the National Gallery of Australia showed how close the line can be between the market for new work in the old style and the trade in stolen originals.

Stone image-making shows the same pattern of continuity and change. At Mamallapuram, workshops line the streets near the Pallava monuments. Some are run by hereditary sculptors and others by graduates of the Government College of Architecture and Sculpture (Volume 16). They carve granite images and architectural elements for temples in India and overseas, using pneumatic hammers and diamond-disc cutters to rough out the block and hand chisels for the finish. The use of power tools has greatly increased output, and it has also increased the danger from silica dust (Section 7.10).

docs.title: 3.1.4 Bell Metal and Brass
docs.text:
Bell metal (kāṃsya, Hindi kāṃsā) is a high-tin bronze, typically with roughly one part of tin to three or four of copper, used for gongs, cymbals, bells and dishes. In Kerala, high-tin bronze is also used for the famous metal mirrors of Āṟanmuḷa, which are cast and then polished to a reflective surface (Chapter 10). Brass (pittala, rīti), an alloy of copper and zinc, was made in the subcontinent from the late centuries BCE, at first probably by heating copper with zinc ore, and later by alloying copper with metallic zinc (Craddock 2017).

Hammered brass and copper utensils are made by raising a disc of sheet metal over an anvil, with repeated cycles of hammering and annealing. The craft of the Ṭhaṭherās of Jandiala Guru in Punjab, who make vessels entirely by hand-hammering, was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2014. Moradabad in Uttar Pradesh is the largest centre of the brassware industry today, producing mainly for export.

docs.title: 3.2.1 The Beginnings of Iron
docs.text:
The date at which iron came into use in India is debated. Iron objects are common at sites of the Painted Grey Ware and related cultures of the early first millennium BCE, and Dilip Chakrabarti argued that iron technology developed independently in several regions of India (Chakrabarti 1992). Excavations at Malhar, Raja Nala-ka-Tila and other sites in Uttar Pradesh have produced iron objects and slag with radiocarbon dates in the first half of the second millennium BCE, which, if confirmed, would make Indian iron-working broadly contemporary with the earliest iron-working elsewhere (Tewari 2003).

In the Ṛgveda the word ayas means metal, probably copper or bronze. Later Vedic texts distinguish “dark metal” (śyāma ayas, kṛṣṇāyasa), that is iron, from “red metal” (lohita ayas), copper; the Chāndogya Upaniṣad uses “everything made of iron” (kārṣṇāyasa) as one of its examples of a single substance known through its products (6.1.6). The Arthaśāstra places mines and metal workshops under a superintendent of mines and a superintendent of metals, who is to run workshops for copper, lead, tin, brass, bronze and other metals (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 3.2.2 Smelting
docs.text: Before modern blast furnaces, iron was smelted in small clay furnaces fed with ore and charcoal and blown with bellows. The product was a spongy bloom of iron and slag, which was hammered repeatedly to expel the slag and consolidate the metal. Such furnaces were operated in the nineteenth century across central and eastern India by specialist communities such as the Agaria of the Maikal hills, whose techniques, myths and worship of Lohāsur, the iron demon who dwells in the furnace, were described by Verrier Elwin (Elwin 1942). Most of these furnaces closed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when cheap imported and factory iron undercut them.

docs.title: 3.2.3 Forging Large Iron: The Delhi Pillar
docs.text:
The most famous product of Indian blacksmiths is the iron pillar in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi (Figure 3.3): about 7.2 m long and more than six tonnes in weight, set up as a standard (dhvaja) of Viṣṇu by a king Candra who is generally identified with Candragupta II (c. 375–415 CE), and probably brought to Delhi from elsewhere centuries later. From the craftsman’s point of view its interest lies in how it was made. It was built up by forge-welding: lumps of bloomery iron, each the product of a small furnace, were heated and hammered on to the growing mass, a task that demanded many furnaces, a large team and great control of heat (Balasubramaniam 2002). A still larger forge-welded pillar, now broken, lies at Dhar in Madhya Pradesh, and forge-welded iron beams support stone members in the temples of Puri and Konarak. The pillar’s slow corrosion, explained by R. Balasubramaniam through its high phosphorus content and the protective film that forms in Delhi’s climate, was not designed by its makers; the inscription, the metallurgy and the other large iron objects are discussed in Volume 14, Chapter 4 (Balasubramaniam 2000).

Figure 3.3. The forge-welded iron pillar of king Candra (generally identified with Candragupta II, c. 375–415 CE) in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi, seen through an arch of the stone screen of the later mosque. The visitors at the railing give the scale. Photo: Aiwok, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.3 Crucible Steel
docs.text:
South India and Sri Lanka were the home of a high-carbon steel made in sealed crucibles, known in English as “wootz”, a corruption of the Kannada and Telugu word ukku, steel. Pieces of iron, with wood, leaves or other carbon-rich material, were sealed in small clay crucibles and heated in a furnace for many hours (Figure 3.4a); the iron absorbed carbon and melted, and on slow cooling formed a small cake of steel with about 1–2% carbon. Ingots of this steel were traded to Persia and Syria, where smiths forged them at low temperatures into blades with the swirling “watered” pattern later admired in Europe as “Damascus steel” (Bronson 1986; Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004).

Archaeological evidence for crucible steel production in South India goes back to the late centuries BCE at sites such as Kodumanal and Mel-siruvalur in Tamil Nadu, and to the first millennium CE in Sri Lanka, where Gillian Juleff also discovered wind-powered iron-smelting furnaces on hill slopes (Srinivasan 1994; Juleff 1996). The Periplus (mid-first century CE) lists “Indian iron and steel” among the goods shipped from western India to the Red Sea (Casson 1989). Indian steel and Indian swords were well known in the Islamic world: Arabic and Persian writers on swords and minerals, from al-Kindī in the ninth century to al-Bīrūnī in the eleventh, distinguished Indian blades and Indian steel among the varieties they described. European travellers and officials of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries described crucible steel production at several places in Mysore, Salem and Hyderabad, and their reports stimulated scientific interest in Britain.

The watered pattern of Damascus blades comes from bands of iron carbide in a softer steel matrix. Its dependence on trace impurities in the Indian ingots and on forging at moderate temperatures was shown by J. D. Verhoeven and the bladesmith A. H. Pendray, who reproduced genuine watered blades (Verhoeven et al. 1998); reports of carbon nanotubes in a seventeenth-century sabre (Reibold et al. 2006) describe its microstructure and do not mean that the smiths were consciously making “nanomaterials”. The science of wootz is treated in Volume 14, Chapter 5. For the craft historian the decline matters most: crucible steel making died out in the nineteenth century not because a “secret” was lost but because its markets and fuel supplies disappeared.

docs.title: 3.4 Zinc
docs.text:
Zinc boils at about 907°C, below the temperature needed to reduce its ore, so in an ordinary furnace it escapes as vapour. At Zawar near Udaipur in Rajasthan, smelters solved the problem by downward distillation in clay retorts set upside down in a furnace above condensing vessels (Figure 3.4b); the huge heaps of discarded retorts were excavated by P. T. Craddock, L. K. Gurjar and K. T. M. Hegde (Craddock et al. 1983). Zinc was distilled there from about the ninth or tenth century CE, and on a very large scale from about the fourteenth (Craddock 2017); in Europe industrial production began only after William Champion’s patent of 1738. For the craftsman, metallic zinc mattered because it made possible high-zinc brass and the zinc alloy of Bidrī ware (below). The process and the rasaśāstra descriptions of it are treated in Volume 14, Chapter 6.

Figure 3.4. Two products of controlled heat. (a) In crucible steel, iron and carbon-rich plant matter sealed in a small clay crucible were heated until the iron took up carbon and melted. (b) At Zawar, zinc was distilled downwards: retorts filled with roasted ore and charcoal stood mouth downward in a perforated plate, so that the zinc vapour escaped into a cooler chamber below and condensed there instead of burning away in the fire (simplified after the reconstruction by Craddock and his colleagues).

docs.title: 3.5 Gold and Silver
docs.text: Gold ornaments are known from the Indus cities, and gold has been worked continuously in the subcontinent ever since. The Arthaśāstra distinguishes several kinds of gold by origin, among them river gold, mine gold and gold obtained by “chemical” means, and describes the testing of gold on a touchstone and the duties of the state goldsmith, who was to work in a guarded workshop and was liable to heavy penalties for adulteration (2.13–14) (Kangle 1960–1965). Ancient workings at Kolar and Hutti in Karnataka show that gold was mined from hard rock in the first millennium CE; when British companies began mining at Kolar in the 1870s and 1880s they followed the old workings. Goldsmithing techniques, including filigree, granulation, kundan setting and enamelling, are discussed in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 3.6 Bidrī Ware
docs.text:
Bidrī ware, named after the city of Bidar in Karnataka, the capital of the Bahmanī sultans from 1429, is made of a cast alloy of zinc with a small amount of copper. The surface is engraved and inlaid with silver (sometimes gold or brass) wire or sheet, and the object is then coated with a paste of soil (traditionally taken from the old fort walls of Bidar) mixed with sal ammoniac. The paste turns the zinc alloy a deep, permanent matt black while leaving the silver bright. Bidrī ware flourished in the Deccan sultanates and under the Nizams of Hyderabad, and is still made in Bidar and Hyderabad; huqqa bases, boxes and trays are the classic forms (Figure 3.5). It is registered as a Geographical Indication.

Figure 3.5. A Bidrī huqqa base made at Hyderabad or Bidar, about 1750–1800. The zinc alloy has been blackened, leaving the inlaid silver flowering plants and borders bright (Los Angeles County Museum of Art). Photo: Los Angeles County Museum of Art; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Related inlay techniques include koftgarī, in which gold or silver wire is hammered into a cross-hatched iron or steel surface (Rajasthan, and formerly Sialkot and Gujarat), and tārkashī, the inlay of brass wire in wood (Mainpuri, Uttar Pradesh).

docs.title: 3.7 Coins, Copper Plates and Inscribed Metal
docs.text:
Some of the most abundant products of Indian metalworkers are coins. The earliest Indian coins, the silver “punch-marked” coins of the Ganga valley and the north-west (from about the fifth or fourth century BCE), were made by cutting pieces of silver of a standard weight and stamping them with a series of small symbols. Later dynasties issued cast copper coins, coins struck between engraved dies on the Greek model, and, under the Kuṣāṇas and Guptas, fine gold coins whose designs are among the masterpieces of Indian miniature sculpture. Making coins required the refining and assaying of metals, the engraving of dies and strict control of weight and fineness; mint-masters were important officials. In the early fourteenth century Ṭhakkura Pherū, a Jain official at the Delhi mint, wrote a treatise on coins (Dravyaparīkṣā) recording the weight and metal content of the coins that passed through his hands, together with his treatise on gems (Chapter 10).

Land grants and other important documents were engraved on copper plates (tāmraśāsana), strung together on a ring and sealed with the royal seal. Many thousands survive, most of them from the fourth and fifth centuries CE onwards, and they are a major source for Indian history. Their texts were composed by court poets and scribes, and the plates were often engraved by goldsmiths or other craftsmen, whose names are sometimes recorded at the end of the inscription.

docs.title: 3.8 Bells, Lamps and Ritual Metalwork
