docs.title: 5.5.3 The Calico Craze
docs.text:
Between the 1660s and the 1690s Indian cottons became a craze in England and the Netherlands. The English Company’s imports of Indian piece-goods rose steeply, and in some years of the 1680s exceeded a million pieces (Chaudhuri 1978). Beverly Lemire has shown what made the cloth attractive to English buyers (Lemire 1991). It was light, washable and colour-fast, so that it could be laundered without losing its pattern, as most European printed and dyed cloth could not. It was also cheap enough to reach far beyond the rich. Calicoes and chintzes went into bed-hangings and quilts, linings, aprons, handkerchiefs and petticoats, and then into gowns. The loose morning-gown called a “banyan”, after the Gujarati merchant (vāṇiyā), was a fashion among English gentlemen. Through pedlars, shopkeepers and the second-hand trade, printed cotton reached servants and the families of tradesmen. Lemire argues that it accustomed a wide public to fashions that changed from season to season, and so helped to create the consumer market that the later English cotton industry served.

The craze provoked a reaction from those whose livelihoods it threatened. In London in the summer of 1719 silk-weavers from Spitalfields attacked women wearing calico in the streets and tore their gowns, and a pamphlet war set the “calico madams” against the honest wool and silk manufacturers of England. The legislation that followed is described below. Its gaps mattered as much as its prohibitions. Fustian, with a linen warp and a cotton weft, was not covered by the ban on printed cottons, and an Act of 1736 confirmed that printed linen-and-cotton cloth was lawful. English printers therefore learned their trade on mixed fabrics for the home market and on Indian calicoes for re-export, and English spinners and weavers began to produce the cotton yarn and cloth that the printers needed (Lemire 1991; Riello 2013). In France, where the ban of 1686 was enforced with severe penalties, Indian and imitation indiennes were nevertheless smuggled and worn throughout the period of prohibition. When it ended in 1759, printworks such as that founded by Christophe-Philippe Oberkampf at Jouy-en-Josas in 1760 quickly took up the trade.

docs.title: 5.5.4 Protection and Imitation
docs.text:
The popularity of Indian cottons provoked protests from wool and silk manufacturers. France prohibited the import, manufacture and wearing of printed cottons in 1686, a ban that lasted until 1759. In England, an Act of 1700 prohibited the import of printed and painted calicoes from Asia for domestic use, and the Calico Act of 1721 prohibited the wearing and use of most printed cottons altogether. These measures did not stop the trade; Indian cloth continued to be imported and re-exported to Africa and the Americas, where it was a staple of the Atlantic trade, including the trade in enslaved Africans (Riello 2013).

Giorgio Riello and Prasannan Parthasarathi have argued that the competition of Indian cottons was a major stimulus to the European cotton industry: Europeans set out to imitate Indian products, learned mordant dyeing and printing from Indian methods, and mechanised spinning and weaving in order to compete with Indian cloth on price and quality (Riello 2013; Parthasarathi 2011). This is an important argument about the origins of the Industrial Revolution, though other historians give more weight to factors within Europe; it should be presented as a thesis of current scholarship rather than an established fact.

docs.title: 5.5.5 The Paisley Motif
docs.text: The teardrop or cone-shaped motif known in Persian as boteh and in Hindi and Urdu as būṭā or kairī (“mango”) became, on Kashmir shawls, one of the most influential designs in the history of textiles. When European manufacturers imitated Kashmir shawls in the early nineteenth century, the town of Paisley in Scotland became so important a centre of production that the motif came to be known in English as “paisley” (Ames 1986).

docs.title: 5.6 Indian Cloth in Africa and the Atlantic World
docs.text:
Europe was neither the oldest nor the most demanding overseas market for Indian cloth. Africa, on both its coasts, bought Indian textiles for centuries, and African buyers had firm and changing preferences that Indian weavers and dyers learned to meet. The commercial history of these trades, with their ports, merchants and companies, is told in Volume 19. This section looks at them from the side of the makers: what was made, for whom, and how distant tastes reached the loom and the dye-vat. Table 5.1 lists some of the cloths made for particular markets.

docs.title: 5.6.1 East Africa
docs.text:
Gujarati cottons reached the Swahili towns of the East African coast long before the Portuguese entered the Indian Ocean (Volume 19). For the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, Pedro Machado has reconstructed the trade in detail (Machado 2014). Vāṇiyā merchants of Diu and Daman supplied most of the cloth sold at Mozambique Island, and they financed weavers in Jambusar and other towns of Gujarat to produce it. On the African side, cloth was the main currency in which ivory was bought from the traders of the interior. The cloths were cheap, mostly white, blue-dyed and checked cottons, but they had to be exactly right. African buyers knew the qualities and patterns they wanted, rejected bales that did not match the current fashion, and changed their preferences from one season to the next. The merchants therefore sent precise instructions about colour, width, length and pattern back to Gujarat, and the weavers’ work was shaped by the taste of consumers they never saw.

Dark indigo-dyed cotton, known on the Swahili coast as kaniki, was the staple of this trade. In the nineteenth century Indian cloth met new competitors: unbleached American sheeting, called merikani on the coast, and British printed and dyed goods. Jeremy Prestholdt has shown how East African consumers, through their choices among these cloths, shaped what Indian, American and British manufacturers made for them (Prestholdt 2008).

docs.title: 5.6.2 West Africa and the Atlantic
docs.text:
From the seventeenth century, Dutch, English, French and Portuguese traders carried Indian cloth to West Africa. Much of it passed through European ports for re-export. Cotton cloth from Coromandel, Gujarat and Bengal was among the most important goods in the assortments that European ships took to the African coast, and on many English and French slaving voyages of the eighteenth century it was the largest single category of goods exchanged for enslaved people (Riello and Parthasarathi 2009; Riello 2013). The weavers and dyers of Coromandel and Gujarat can have known little of this. It is nonetheless part of the history of their cloth.

Company lists name many cloths made for this trade. “Guinea cloth” was a plain cotton, usually dyed deep blue with indigo, sometimes striped. Romāls (from rūmāl, “handkerchief”) were squares woven in checks. Other names, such as “niccanees”, “chelloes” and “tapseels”, covered striped and checked cloths. West Africa had its own long traditions of cotton weaving, on narrow strip looms, and of indigo dyeing. Indian cloth therefore did not fill an empty market. It succeeded by matching and extending local tastes, above all for deep blues and for red and blue checks, and each stretch of the coast had its own preferences, which a ship’s assortment had to meet if it was to sell.

In the nineteenth century two Indian cloths held special places in West African markets. On the Senegal river, blue cotton guinées from French Pondicherry served as a currency in the trade in gum arabic. Richard Roberts has traced how the fortunes of Pondicherry’s weavers and dyers came to depend on this trade and on French tariff policy, until cheaper machine-made imitations displaced them (Roberts 1992). In the eastern Niger Delta, a checked cotton woven in the Madras region and sold as “real Madras handkerchief” became a cloth of prestige among the Kalabari Ijo. They call it injiri, and wear it and display it at funerals. Kalabari women make a cloth of their own from it, pelete bite (“cut-thread cloth”), by cutting and pulling out threads to create new patterns, a process that Tonye Erekosima and Joanne Eicher have called the “cultural authentication” of an imported cloth (Erekosima and Eicher 1981). Handloom weavers in coastal Andhra and Tamil Nadu continued to make madras checks for this market through the twentieth century.

docs.title: 5.6.3 Made to Order
docs.text:
In all these markets Indian textile workers made cloth to order for customers they never met. A weaver in Jambusar or a dyer near Pulicat produced for buyers whose taste reached him only through samples, merchants’ instructions and the occasional rejected bale. The success of Indian cloth in Africa, Southeast Asia and Europe rested on this responsiveness, and on the ability of weavers and dyers to change their products (Chapter 13). When European manufacturers set out to capture these markets, they copied the products that Indian makers had developed for them. In the nineteenth century British mills made imitation “Guinea cloth” and madras checks for Africa, as French and English printers had made imitation chintz for Europe.

The name of one such cloth outlived the trade that made it. “Madras”, the checked cotton of the Coromandel coast, travelled with the Atlantic trade to the Caribbean as well as to West Africa. In the French Antilles, madras head-ties and skirts became part of the dress of Creole women, and they remain an emblem of Martinican and Guadeloupean identity. In the twentieth century, handwoven madras from the same coastal region was sold in North America as a summer fabric, and its tendency to run when washed was turned into a selling point. Through such names, cloth designed by Indian weavers for distant customers became part of the dress and the vocabulary of places that knew little of where it came from.

docs.title: 5.7 The Dyers and Printers
docs.text: Dyeing and printing were, like other crafts, hereditary occupations. In north and west India the main communities include the Raṅgrez (Muslim dyers), the Chhīpā or Chhīmpā (printers, both Hindu and Muslim), the Nīlgar (indigo-dyers) and the Khatrī of Gujarat and Sindh. Some Chhīpā communities claim the Marathi poet-saint Nāmdev, a calico-printer and tailor by birth, as one of their own. In south India, dyeing and painting of cloth were often done by specialists attached to weaving communities. Because dyeing involved foul-smelling vats and the handling of urine, dung and animal products, some dyeing operations were considered polluting, and dyers’ quarters were often placed at the edges of towns, near water.

docs.title: 5.8 Synthetic Dyes and the Decline of Natural Dyeing
docs.text:
The discovery of synthetic dyes in Europe transformed dyeing worldwide. W. H. Perkin’s mauve (1856) was followed by synthetic alizarin, made from coal-tar anthracene by Graebe and Liebermann in 1868–69 and manufactured from the early 1870s, and by synthetic indigo, marketed by BASF in 1897. Synthetic alizarin ruined the cultivation of madder in Europe and the market for Indian dye-roots; synthetic indigo brought about the collapse of Indian indigo exports in the early twentieth century (Watt 1908). Indian dyers and printers turned to cheaper synthetic dyes, and many natural-dye techniques survived only in a few places.

Modern Relevance: Natural Dyes and Pollution

Interest in natural dyeing revived from the 1970s, through the work of craft organisations, designers and dyers in Kutch, Rajasthan, Andhra and elsewhere, and natural-dyed textiles now command a premium market. At the same time the modern textile industry, which uses synthetic dyes on a vast scale, has caused severe water pollution in textile towns; the bleaching and dyeing units of Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu, for example, were the subject of prolonged litigation over the pollution of the Noyyal river. Natural dyeing is not automatically “clean”: mordants and iron solutions must also be handled and disposed of carefully.

docs.text: For technique and trade, Gittinger (1982); for the Indian process as recorded by eighteenth-century Europeans, Irwin and Brett (1970); for the textiles of the Calico Museum, Irwin and Hall (1971); for chintz in Europe, Crill (2008); for the Egyptian finds, Barnes (1997); for Indian textiles in the Indian Ocean world, Barnes (2005); for the calico craze in England, Lemire (1991); for East Africa, Machado (2014).

docs.title: Chapter 6: Kumbhakāra: Pottery and Terracotta
docs.text: Pottery is the most abundant evidence of the human past in South Asia, and the potter is the most widespread of Indian artisans. Every village needed water-pots, cooking pots, storage jars and lamps, and every household ritual required new earthen vessels. Archaeologists use the changing forms and wares of pottery to define cultures and periods; anthropologists find in the potter’s caste and craft a key to the village economy. This chapter surveys the archaeological wares, the potter’s techniques, the terracotta traditions and the glazed and studio pottery of recent centuries.

docs.title: 6.1.1 From Mehrgarh to the Indus Cities
docs.text: Pottery appears at Mehrgarh in Baluchistan in the sixth millennium BCE, and wheel-thrown pottery by the fourth millennium. The mature Harappan cities (c. 2600–1900 BCE) produced a remarkably standardised range of wheel-made red ware, often painted in black with geometric designs, intersecting circles, fish-scales and pipal leaves; large storage jars, dish-on-stand forms and perforated jars are characteristic (Figure 6.1a). Potters’ kilns have been found in several Indus cities. Besides pottery, Indus craftsmen made glazed faience and a very hard fired stoneware used for bangles, both of which required careful control of firing (Kenoyer 1998).

docs.title: 6.1.2 Later Wares
docs.text:
After the decline of the Indus cities, regional cultures of the second and early first millennia BCE are known by their pottery: the Ochre Coloured Pottery of the Ganga–Yamuna Doab, the Black-and-Red Ware widespread across India, and the Painted Grey Ware (c. 1200–600 BCE; Figure 6.1b) associated with early iron-using communities of the western Ganga plain. Northern Black Polished Ware (c. 700–200 BCE), a thin, wheel-made ware with a lustrous black surface, is the hallmark of the cities of the Ganga valley in the age of the Buddha and the Mauryas (Allchin and Allchin 1982). How its glossy surface was produced is still debated; it seems to have involved a very fine slip and firing in a reducing atmosphere. In the early centuries CE, Rouletted Ware and other fine wares found at Arikamedu and other coastal sites show links with Indian Ocean trade.

Figure 6.1. (a) A storage jar of the mature Harappan period (c. 2600–1900 BCE) from Chanhudaro, painted in black on red with interlocking leaves and circles (National Museum, New Delhi). (b) Sherds of Painted Grey Ware, about 1000 BCE, from Hastinapura and other sites in Uttar Pradesh and Haryana, with black designs on a grey ground (British Museum). Photo: Ismoon, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 6.1.3 What Potsherds Tell
docs.text: Archaeologists rely on pottery because it is abundant, durable and sensitive to change. The shapes, fabrics, surface treatments and decoration of pots change over time and differ between regions and communities, so that sherds can be used to date layers, define cultures and trace contacts. Scientific methods add further information: thin sections examined under the microscope (petrography) and chemical analysis can identify the clays and tempers used and so the place where a pot was made; residues absorbed into the walls of pots can reveal what was cooked or stored in them, such as dairy products, meat or plant oils. Ethnographic study of living potters, who often make pots in ways similar to those of the past, helps archaeologists to interpret their finds, while reminding them that the same form can be made in very different ways.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Clay and Its Preparation
docs.text: Potters select clays from river beds, tanks and fields, often mixing two or more clays and adding temper such as sand, ash or dung to reduce shrinkage and cracking. The clay is dried, broken up, soaked, sieved or allowed to settle to remove coarse particles, and kneaded by hand and foot. Different clays and tempers are used for cooking pots, which must resist sudden heating, and for water-pots, which must be porous enough to cool their contents by evaporation.

docs.title: 6.2.2 Forming
docs.text:
Indian potters use several methods, often in combination (Figure 6.2):

  • The wheel. In north India the wheel is usually a heavy stone or wooden disc spun with a stick and running freely for some time; in parts of the south and east a kick-wheel or a wheel turned by an assistant is used.

  • Paddle and anvil. Wheel-thrown forms are thinned and shaped by beating the outside with a wooden paddle against a stone or clay anvil held inside. Large round-bottomed water-pots are made in this way.

  • Moulds. Lamps, toys, figurines and plaques are often pressed in moulds.

  • Hand-building. Coiling and pinching are used for large storage jars and for many tribal pottery traditions.

docs.title: 6.2.3 Firing
docs.text:
Most village pottery is fired in open bonfires or in simple pit kilns, covered with dung cakes, straw and potsherds; some regions use updraught kilns. Black pottery is produced by smothering the fire at the end of firing, so that carbon is deposited in the surface; red pottery by allowing air to reach the pots. The best-known black wares today are those of Nizamabad in Azamgarh district, Uttar Pradesh, with incised patterns filled with a silvery pigment after firing, and of Longpi in Manipur.

Figure 6.2. Three stages of village pottery (schematic). (a) The north Indian wheel is a heavy disc on a pivot, spun with a stick and left to run while the potter throws. (b) Round-bottomed pots are thinned and shaped by beating the outside with a wooden paddle against an anvil held inside. (c) Most village pottery is fired in the open or in pits under a covering of fuel and sherds; letting air reach the pots gives red ware, smothering the fire at the end deposits carbon and gives black ware.

docs.title: 6.3 Potters in Society
docs.text:
Potters (Kumhār in the north, Kumbhār in the west, Kumbāra in Karnataka, Kuyavar in Tamil Nadu, Kumor in Bengal and Assam) form a distinct jāti or set of jātis in every region of India, usually ranked in the middle or lower-middle of local hierarchies. In north India many potters call themselves Prajāpati, after the creator god, a self-description that asserts the dignity of a craft that makes forms out of clay. In the village economy potters supplied pots to households in return for grain under customary arrangements (Chapter 13), and they provided the new vessels needed for life-cycle rites, marriages and funerals. In many potter communities only men use the wheel, while women prepare clay, paint, burnish and sell pots.

Some Vedic ritual vessels were not made by potters at all. The fire-pan (ukhā) built for the great fire altar of the agnicayana and the mahāvīra pot of the Pravargya rite were shaped by the priests themselves, by hand and without a wheel, as part of the ritual. Brahmanical ritual thus valued the earthen vessel while keeping its making in priestly hands.

The pot is a powerful image in Indian thought. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.1.4) argues that “by one lump of clay everything made of clay is known” (Chapter 1); in later philosophy the pot (ghaṭa) and the potter’s lump became the standard examples of cause and effect, and the space inside a pot an image of the self limited by the body. Such images reflect the familiarity of philosophers with the craft, not the social standing of potters.

The Kalaśa

The water-filled pot (kalaśa, pūrṇa-ghaṭa), crowned with mango leaves and often a coconut, is one of the most widespread auspicious symbols of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain art and ritual. It is carved on gateways and pillars from the Sanchi stūpa onwards, set up at weddings and house-warmings, and used in the consecration of temples, when water from pots is poured over the image and the finial (kumbhābhiṣeka). In most of these uses the pot may be of metal as well as clay.

docs.title: 6.4.1 Figurines and Plaques
docs.text:
Terracotta figurines were made in the Indus cities and in great numbers in the early historic period. Mould-made plaques of the Mauryan, Śuṅga and Kuṣāṇa periods from sites such as Chandraketugarh, Kauśāmbī and Mathurā show richly ornamented female figures, couples and narrative scenes. Terracotta panels decorated brick temples and monasteries, as at Paharpur in Bangladesh (8th–9th centuries) and in Gupta-period temples such as Bhitargaon.

The Indus cities have produced large numbers of hand-modelled terracotta figurines of women, men and animals, as well as toy carts with wheels, whistles, rattles and models of bullocks with movable heads. Their purposes, whether religious, magical or playful, are debated, but the toy carts are among the earliest evidence for wheeled vehicles in South Asia and closely resemble the bullock-carts still used in the region. In later periods, mould-made terracotta toys and figurines were produced on a large scale for markets and festivals, and the making of clay toys for fairs remains a seasonal occupation of potters in many parts of India, as at Krishnanagar in Bengal, famous for its finely modelled and painted clay figures of people of every occupation.

docs.title: 6.4.2 The Temples of Bengal
docs.text:
In the delta of Bengal, where building stone is scarce, brick temples of the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries were faced with moulded and carved terracotta panels showing scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa, the life of Kṛṣṇa, battles, hunts, processions and daily life. The temples built under the Malla kings at Bishnupur, among them the Śyāma Rāya (1643; Figure 6.3), the Jor-Bangla or Keṣṭa Rāya (1655) and the Madana Mohana (1694), are the best known. David McCutchion’s surveys documented hundreds of these temples and classified their forms (McCutchion 1972).

Figure 6.3. Terracotta panels on the Śyāma Rāya temple at Bishnupur, built under the Malla kings in 1643. The larger panels show crowned figures playing the flute, the familiar image of Kṛṣṇa, framed by friezes of smaller figures. Photo: Amitabha Gupta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 6.4.3 Votive Horses and Figures
docs.text:
Terracotta animals are offered to village and local deities throughout India. The long-necked horses of Panchmura and other villages of Bankura district in West Bengal, made by potters for offering to local deities, have become a symbol of Bengali craft (Figure 6.4). In Tamil Nadu, potters make huge terracotta horses, sometimes several metres high, for the shrines of the guardian deity Aiyaṉār, built in sections and fired in place. In many villages of Tamil Nadu the potters (Vēḷār or Kuyavar) who make these horses and the images of village deities are reported also to serve as priests (pūcāri) in the shrines of those deities, so that the maker of the image is also its ritual servant, outside the Brahmanical temple system; the practice varies from place to place. At Molela in Rajasthan, potters make painted terracotta plaques of the folk deity Devnārāyaṇ, worshipped especially by the Gujars, and of other deities, which pilgrims carry home to install in village shrines. Kramrisch’s Unknown India (1968) brought these village and tribal traditions to international attention as art in their own right (Kramrisch 1968).

Figure 6.4. Long-necked terracotta horses of the Bankura type, with two elephants, outside a craft shop in West Bengal. Photo: Footlooseinme, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

docs.title: 6.5 Bricks and Tiles
docs.text: Fired brick was used on a large scale in the Indus cities, whose bricks were made in standard proportions of 1:2:4, and again in the cities, stūpas and temples of the Ganga plain and the delta from the late centuries BCE. Brick-making was often done by specialised groups and by seasonal labourers. Roof tiles were used in many regions, especially in the wet south-west; in 1865 the Basel Mission established a tile factory at Mangalore, whose interlocking “Mangalore tiles” were soon made by many firms and spread across India and beyond. Today India has a very large brick industry, using clamp and kiln firing, in which many workers, including whole families, are seasonal migrants, often bound by advances to kiln owners; the industry is also a major source of air pollution. The humble brick thus raises the same questions of labour and environment as the finer crafts.

docs.title: 6.6 Clay Images
docs.text: Potters and specialist image-makers make clay images of deities for festivals, which are worshipped for a few days and then immersed in rivers, tanks or the sea. The most famous are the images of Durgā and her family made for the autumn festival of Durgā Pūjā in Bengal. In the Kumartuli quarter of Kolkata, generations of image-makers (kumor, pāl) build the images on frames of bamboo and straw, coat them in layers of river clay mixed with straw and husk, and paint and dress them; similar workshops exist in towns across eastern India. In Maharashtra, the images of Gaṇeśa for the Gaṇeśa festival, which became a public festival in the 1890s under the influence of Bal Gangadhar Tilak, are made in many towns, among them Pen in Raigad district. The use of plaster of Paris and synthetic paints in place of clay and natural colours has caused pollution of water bodies, and courts and pollution-control authorities have issued guidelines encouraging a return to clay.

docs.title: 6.7 Glazed Pottery
docs.text:
Glazed pottery was made in the Indus cities in the form of faience, but glazed earthenware vessels became common in India only after the twelfth century, under the influence of Persian and Central Asian traditions, and chiefly for tiles and fine wares. Glazed tiles decorate Sultanate and Mughal buildings in Multan, Lahore and Delhi. The tomb of Shāh Rukn-i ʿĀlam at Multan (early fourteenth century) is covered with glazed tiles and carved brick, and the tile mosaics of the Lahore Fort and of the mosque of Wazir Khan at Lahore (1630s) are among the finest examples of the art in South Asia. The tile-makers (kāshīgar, from Kāshān in Iran, a famous centre of the craft) of Sindh, Multan and Lahore continued the tradition into modern times.

The “blue pottery” of Jaipur is not made of clay but of a frit body of ground quartz, powdered glass, fuller’s earth (multānī miṭṭī), borax and gum, shaped in moulds and painted in cobalt blue and other colours under a clear glaze. The technique is related to Persian fritware and is said to have reached Jaipur from Delhi in the nineteenth century under the patronage of Sawai Ram Singh II. It almost died out in the mid-twentieth century and was revived from the 1950s through the efforts of the painter Kripal Singh Shekhawat (1922–2008) and craft promoters such as Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay. Khurja in Uttar Pradesh, by contrast, is a centre of glazed earthenware and modern ceramics, producing both traditional blue-and-white wares and goods for the industrial market.

docs.title: 6.8 Pottery in the North-East and Tribal India
docs.text: At Longpi in Ukhrul district, Manipur, potters of the Tangkhul Naga community make cooking and serving vessels by hand, without a wheel, from a mixture of ground black serpentinite rock and a special clay. The vessels are shaped with simple tools, fired in an open fire and rubbed while hot with the leaves of a local plant, which gives them their dark sheen. Many Ādivāsī communities in central and eastern India also make their own pottery by hand, sometimes as a task of women; these traditions are surveyed in Volume 23 of this series.

docs.title: 6.9 Regional Pottery Traditions
docs.text: Every region has its own pottery forms and techniques; a few examples illustrate the range. In Kutch, the potters of Khavda make thin red pots painted with geometric designs in white and black before firing, a style admired for its resemblance to ancient painted wares. In Assam, potters of the Kumar and Hira communities make vessels by different methods; the Hira potters, among whom women make pots by hand without a wheel, are a well-known example of a hand-building tradition. In Manipur, besides Longpi, there are coiled and paddled traditions in the Imphal valley. In Tamil Nadu, potters make the great Aiyaṉār horses as well as everyday wares; in Kerala, potters produce the large cooking pots used in temple kitchens. In Rajasthan, Alwar was known for paper-thin pottery (kāgzī), and Pokaran and Bikaner for painted wares. The potters of Delhi, Khurja and Gurgaon produce garden pots and decorative ware for the urban market. Many of these local forms are now made only for ritual use or for collectors, as plastic and metal vessels replace clay in daily life (Ranjan and Ranjan 2007).

docs.title: 6.10 Studio Pottery
docs.text:
Studio pottery, in which an individual artist designs and makes his or her own work, came to India in the twentieth century. Gurcharan Singh (1896–1995), who learned pottery in Japan as a young man, founded the Delhi Blue Pottery Trust in the 1950s, and with his son Mansimran Singh established the pottery at Andretta in Himachal Pradesh. Ray Meeker and Deborah Smith founded the Golden Bridge Pottery at Pondicherry in 1971, which became an important centre for high-fired stoneware and the training of potters. Studio potters have often worked with traditional potters, sometimes in mutually fruitful collaboration and sometimes in relationships marked by inequalities of education and access to markets.

Modern Relevance: The Village Potter Today

Traditional pottery faces strong competition from metal, plastic and factory-made ceramics. Water-pots and cooking pots have been widely replaced, though earthen pots remain popular for cooling water in summer, for curd, and for festivals such as Dīpāvalī, when millions of clay lamps are made. Potters have adapted by making garden pots, decorative terracotta and tiles, and government schemes have distributed electric wheels. The potters who prosper are usually those near cities and tourist routes; in remote villages many potters’ sons have left the wheel for wage work.

docs.title: 6.11 Pottery and Sustainability
docs.text: Earthen pots have attracted renewed interest as alternatives to plastic: clay cups (kulhaṛ) for tea, once standard at railway stations in north India, have been promoted again in recent years, and clay water-coolers and cooking pots are sold in cities as healthy and “natural”. Such revivals can help potters, but they also raise practical problems: the supply of suitable clay from village commons and tanks, which are increasingly enclosed or polluted; the fuel needed for firing; and the low prices that make it hard for potters to earn a living. Some potters now use electric kilns and improved fuel-efficient kilns developed with the help of government and voluntary agencies.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For archaeological pottery, Allchin and Allchin (1982) and Kenoyer (1998); for Bengal temples, McCutchion (1972); for village terracotta and ritual art, Kramrisch (1968); for regional pottery traditions today, Ranjan and Ranjan (2007).

docs.title: Chapter 7: Dāru, Danta and Śilā: Wood, Ivory and Stone
docs.text: Wood was the first building material of India and remained the material of most houses, of much temple architecture in the Himalaya and Kerala, and of furniture, carts, boats, tools, toys and images. Because it decays, little old woodwork survives, but the earliest Indian stone architecture, in the rock-cut halls of the western Deccan and the gateways of Sanchi, faithfully copies wooden forms, beams and joints. This chapter is about the crafts of cutting, joining and carving hard materials. It surveys the carpenter and his regional traditions, furniture and boats, the makers of musical instruments, sandalwood and the lac-turned and painted wooden toys of several regions, and then ivory and stone, which were carved with related tools and often by related communities. Bamboo, cane and the softer plant fibres, worked by different methods and usually by different people, have a chapter of their own (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.1 The Carpenter
docs.text: The carpenter (takṣan, later vardhaki, Hindi Baṛhaī, Tamil Taccaṉ, Malayalam Āśāri) appears in the earliest Vedic texts, where the poet’s hymn is compared to a chariot built by a skilled craftsman. In the village economy of later centuries the carpenter made and repaired ploughs, carts and doors, and was paid in grain (Chapter 13). In south India carpenters form one of the five Viśvakarma crafts (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 7.1.1 Selecting Timber
docs.text: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century) devotes a chapter to the selection of wood for images. The craftsman enters the forest on an auspicious day, chooses a suitable tree, worships it the night before and asks the beings who live in it to move elsewhere; the manner and direction of the tree’s fall are read as omens (Bhat 1981–1982). The architectural treatises classify timbers by suitability and list trees to be avoided, such as those struck by lightning or growing in cremation grounds. The woods most prized for building and carving include teak (śāka), sal, deodar (devadāru) in the Himalaya, jackfruit and rosewood in the south, and for fine work, sandalwood and ebony.

docs.title: 7.2.1 The Himalaya
docs.text: In the hills of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, houses and temples are built in the kāṭh-kuṇī technique, with alternating courses of dry stone and long horizontal timbers interlocked at the corners. The timber cage gives the walls flexibility in earthquakes. The temples of the Kullu, Mandi and Chamba regions, such as the Hiḍimbā Devī temple at Manali (1553) and the older Lakṣaṇā Devī temple at Bharmaur, have carved wooden doorways, pillars and brackets. Kashmir has a separate tradition of fine carving in walnut wood and of khatambandh ceilings, made of small pieces of wood fitted into geometric patterns, and of pinjrakārī, lattice-work screens of small turned or cut pieces of wood joined without glue. The wooden mosques and shrines of Srinagar, such as the Shāh-i Hamadān shrine, with their tiered pyramidal roofs, are the finest monuments of Kashmiri carpentry, and the houseboats of the Dal and Nagin lakes, built from the late nineteenth century for European visitors, display the same skills of panelling and carving.

docs.title: 7.2.2 Gujarat and Rajasthan
docs.text: The towns of Gujarat, such as Ahmedabad, Patan, Vadnagar and Surat, preserve carved wooden house facades (havelīs) and the elaborately carved wooden shrines of Jain households and temples. Carved brackets with figures of musicians, dancers and animals, balconies and doors are characteristic. In Rajasthan, the carved and painted doors and furniture of Shekhawati and the carved wood of Jodhpur and Barmer continue as industries, now largely for export.

docs.title: 7.2.3 Kerala and the South
docs.text: Kerala’s temples, palaces and large houses (nālukeṭṭu, “four blocks” around a courtyard) are built with stone or laterite bases and walls and elaborate timber superstructures and roofs. Their carved ceilings, brackets and doorways, and the temple theatres (kūttampalam) built for the performance of Kūṭiyāṭṭam, show the art of the Kerala carpenter at its finest. The Padmanabhapuram palace (16th–18th centuries) is the best preserved example. Carved wooden processional chariots (ratha, tēr) for temple festivals are made throughout south India, some of them several storeys high.

docs.title: 7.2.4 Saharanpur and Other Centres
docs.text: Saharanpur in Uttar Pradesh developed in the nineteenth century as a major centre of carved furniture and decorative woodwork, with inlay in brass and bone. Hoshiarpur in Punjab was known for wood inlaid with ivory (now bone or plastic), and Mainpuri for tārkashī, brass-wire inlay in wood (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 7.3 Furniture
docs.text: Traditional Indian interiors had little furniture by European standards: people sat and slept on mats, carpets, cushions and low stools, and the most widespread piece of furniture was the cot (chārpāī), a wooden frame strung with rope or tape. Courts used thrones, low platforms, chests, palanquins and canopied beds. From the seventeenth century, Europeans in India commissioned furniture in European forms from Indian craftsmen, who adapted it with Indian materials and ornament: cabinets and desks from Gujarat and Sindh inlaid with ivory and ebony, furniture veneered with engraved ivory from Vizagapatam (Visakhapatnam) in the eighteenth century, and the heavily carved “blackwood” (rosewood) furniture of Bombay in the nineteenth. Such “Anglo-Indian” furniture was later adopted by Indian households as well, and carved furniture remains a major craft industry, now largely for export.

docs.title: 7.4 Boats and Ships
docs.text: Some of the most skilful Indian woodworkers were boat- and ship-builders. Indian Ocean ships were traditionally built with planks sewn together with coir rope rather than nailed, a technique well suited to beaching on sandy coasts. At Beypore in Kerala, carpenters still build large wooden sailing ships of the dhow type (uru), mainly for owners in the Persian Gulf, without written plans, from teak and other hardwoods. The river boats of Bengal and Assam, the snake-boats (cuṇṭan vaḷḷam) used in the boat races of the Kerala backwaters, and the fishing craft of every coast are products of distinct regional traditions. In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, Parsi master-builders of the Wadia family at the Bombay dockyard built teak warships and merchant ships for the East India Company and the Royal Navy, some of which remained in service for many decades (Wadia 1955). Indian shipbuilding is discussed further in Volume 19.

docs.title: 7.5 Musical Instruments
docs.text: Instrument-making is a specialised branch of woodwork. It also draws on the skills of the turner, the inlayer, the metalworker and the leather-worker, and above all on acoustic judgement. Many instrument-makers come from carpenters’ communities, but the trade has recruited from many others. The history of the instruments as music, their classification and their acoustics are treated in Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya; this section is concerned with the makers, their materials and their workshops (Deva 1978).

docs.title: 7.5.1 The Vīṇā of Thanjavur
docs.text: The Sarasvatī vīṇā of south India is made above all at Thanjavur, where it took its modern form under the Nāyaka and Maratha courts. Its large resonating bowl is carved from a block of seasoned jackwood (Artocarpus heterophyllus). In the most prized form, the ekāṇḍa (“single-piece”) vīṇā, the bowl, the neck and the dragon-like yāḷi head are carved from one log; in others the parts are carved separately and joined. The bowl is hollowed to a thin, even wall and closed with a soundboard of the same wood. The hollow neck carries twenty-four brass frets set in a ridge of black wax, so that the maker, and later the player, can shift each fret slightly to correct its pitch by ear. A second resonator, traditionally a gourd, is fixed under the upper end of the neck. Inlaid decoration of ivory or deer horn has largely given way to bone and plastic since the ivory trade was banned. The work is done in small family workshops, in which the carving of the bowl, the fitting of neck and frets and the final adjustment may be divided among different hands. The Thanjavur vīṇā is a registered Geographical Indication.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Sitār and Tānpurā
docs.text:
The sitār and the tānpurā combine a resonator made from a dried gourd (tumbā, Lagenaria siceraria) with a neck and soundboard of wood, usually tun (Toona ciliata) or teak. The gourds are grown for the purpose, dried for months, cut, cleaned and strengthened inside before the soundboard is fitted; the neck is hollowed and fitted with pegs and, on the sitār, with frets, and the whole is polished and decorated with inlay or carving. The most delicate operation is the shaping of the broad bridges of bone (formerly ivory or stag horn). Their slightly curved upper surfaces, together with the threads (jīvā) placed under the strings of the tānpurā, produce the buzzing resonance called jawārī (Volume 9). Because the strings wear grooves in the bridge, the jawārī must be “opened” again from time to time, so musicians keep returning to the maker, and the relationship between player and maker lasts as long as the instrument is played. The sitār itself reached its modern form only over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, as players and makers together added strings and frets and enlarged the instrument (Miner 1993).

Miraj, in southern Maharashtra, is the best-known centre of sitār and tānpurā making. Family tradition traces the craft to the mid-nineteenth century. Metalworkers of the Muslim Shikalgar community, whose name comes from the Persian for a polisher of weapons, began then to repair the instruments of musicians at the court of the Patwardhan chiefs of Miraj. Their descendants turned to making instruments and now supply musicians across India. The town’s association with the singer Abdul Karim Khan of the Kirana tradition, who lived there, added to its reputation among vocalists. Kolkata, Varanasi and Delhi have other important workshops. In Kolkata the makers Hiren Roy and the firm of Kanailal are commonly associated with the instruments, and the different sound ideals, of Vilayat Khan and Ravi Shankar respectively: an instance of the close collaboration between performer and maker in fixing the form of an instrument.

docs.title: 7.5.3 Drums and Their Makers
docs.text:
Drums bring the woodworker and the leather-worker together. The shells of the mṛdaṅgam and the pakhāvaj are carved or turned from jackwood or other hardwoods, and the right-hand drum of the tablā from a block of dense wood; the left-hand drum is of copper, brass or clay. The heads are of goatskin or calfskin, laid in several layers and laced with braces of hide. The black loading paste is built up on the head in thin layers and rubbed down with a stone until the drum gives a clear pitch (Volume 9). The maker must judge the thickness and quality of each skin, the tension of the lacing and the composition and weight of the paste, and the player depends on him for repairs and new heads. Laws protecting wild animals have also changed the craft: the small south Indian frame drum kañjira was traditionally headed with the skin of the monitor lizard, and since the animal was protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972, makers have turned to goatskin and synthetic heads.

Because they handle skins, drum-makers have often come from castes treated as untouchable, even when their instruments were played by high-caste musicians in temple and concert music. T. M. Krishna’s history of the makers of the mṛdaṅgam in Tamil Nadu, most of them Dalits and many of them Christians, traces the families who made instruments for the leading performers of the twentieth century, among them the family of Sebastian that gives the book its title. It shows that the makers’ knowledge of hides, pastes and tuning shaped the sound of Karnatak percussion. The makers themselves, however, were kept at a social distance by the Brahmin musicians who relied on them and were scarcely acknowledged in the histories of the music (Krishna 2020). Similar questions arise for the makers of tablā and pakhāvaj in the north, and for village drum-makers, whose drums are often played by the same communities at festivals and funerals. Leather-work in general is discussed in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 7.5.4 Wind Instruments
docs.text: Bamboo flutes are made in many places, but the town of Pilibhit in Uttar Pradesh has become the main centre of their manufacture, working thin-walled bamboo much of which is brought from the North-East. The maker burns the finger-holes with heated iron rods and tunes the flute by adjusting their size and position. The nāgasvaram, the double-reed instrument of south Indian temple music, is made by turners at Narasingapettai near Kumbakonam, traditionally from the dense wood of the ācā tree (Hardwickia binata), with a separate flared bell and a reed cut from a dried marsh grass.

docs.title: 7.6 Sandalwood
docs.text:
Sandalwood (candana, Santalum album) is prized for its close grain and its fragrance, and is used for images, boxes, fans and small carvings; its oil is a basis of Indian perfumery (Chapter 10). The finest sandalwood came from the forests of Mysore and the Western Ghats. The Gudigār community of the coastal and Malnad districts of Karnataka (Sagar, Sirsi, Kumta) are the best-known sandalwood carvers.

Sandalwood has long been a state monopoly in Karnataka; Tipu Sultan is said to have declared it a royal tree in the late eighteenth century, and for most of the twentieth century every sandalwood tree, even on private land, was the property of the state. Laws were liberalised in the early twenty-first century. Over-exploitation, smuggling (the brigand Veerappan, killed in 2004, was its most notorious figure) and disease have drastically reduced the wild population, and Santalum album is classed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Carvers increasingly use other woods.

docs.title: 7.7 Lacquered and Painted Wooden Toys
docs.text:
India has many traditions of wooden toys, often made by communities who also make ritual objects and furniture (Ranjan and Ranjan 2007). They fall into two broad families. The first is turned and lacquered. At Channapatna in Karnataka, toys are turned from the light, fine-grained wood of aale mara (Wrightia tinctoria) and coloured by pressing a stick of coloured lac against the object as it spins on the lathe, so that the lac melts with the heat of friction and coats the surface; local tradition credits Tipu Sultan with encouraging the craft, and Channapatna toys are a registered Geographical Indication. Etikoppaka in Andhra Pradesh uses a similar technique, now with vegetable colours, and Varanasi has its own lacquered toys and small objects. In Kutch the Vāḍhā community turns and lacquers wood on the bow-lathe.

The second family is carved and painted. At Kondapalli in Andhra Pradesh, figures and groups are carved from the soft wood of tella poniki (Givotia), joined with a paste of tamarind seed and sawdust, and painted with village scenes, bullock-carts, animals and deities. The craftsmen of Nirmal in Telangana have made carved and painted figures, toys, furniture and paintings in a style of their own since the time of the Nizams. At Sawantwadi in Maharashtra, lacquered and painted toys, fruits and furniture are made alongside the circular playing cards of the gañjīfā game (Chapter 11).

Modern Relevance: Wood, Forests and Craft

Woodcraft depends on access to forests, and modern forest law has often worked against artisans. Restrictions on felling, introduced to protect forests, have made traditional timbers scarce and expensive for carvers and toy-makers, while large-scale commercial felling continued for much of the twentieth century. Many communities now use plantation woods such as mango, acacia and rubber-wood; the challenge is to secure legal and sustainable supplies of timber for the craftsmen who depend on it.

docs.title: 7.8 Woodworkers Today
docs.text: The village carpenter remains an essential figure in rural India, making and repairing doors, windows, furniture, ploughs and carts, though steel, plastic and factory-made goods have replaced many of his products. Urban carpenters, many of them migrants, build and fit furniture in the cities. Carving and inlay survive mainly where they have found tourist, export or temple markets, as in Saharanpur, Hoshiarpur, Kashmir, Mysore and the temple towns of the south. Machine tools such as electric saws, lathes and routers have been widely adopted, and computer-controlled carving machines now reproduce traditional designs; the hand-carver competes with them on quality and individuality rather than on price. Training programmes and design interventions have tried to help carvers find new products and markets, with uneven success.

docs.title: 7.9 Ivory
docs.text:
Ivory carving is one of the oldest luxury crafts of the subcontinent. Ivory combs, pins and dice are found in the Indus cities. One of the gateways of the great stūpa at Sanchi (late first century BCE or early first century CE) bears an inscription recording that a carving on it was made by the ivory-workers (dantakāra) of Vidiśā, a precious reference to a craft group as donor and maker. An Indian ivory statuette of a woman, perhaps a yakṣī or the goddess Śrī, was found at Pompeii, buried in 79 CE, and a hoard of carved ivories of the first or second century CE, mostly Indian in style, was excavated at Begram in Afghanistan.

In later centuries ivory was carved in many courts and cities: in Orissa, in Mysore and Travancore, in Delhi, and in Murshidabad, where under the Nawabs of Bengal carvers made boats, figures and caskets. A throne of carved ivory, sent by the Maharaja of Travancore, was among the most admired Indian exhibits at the Great Exhibition in London in 1851.

Scholarly Note: The End of Ivory Carving

The international trade in ivory was banned under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) from 1990, and India’s Wildlife (Protection) Act, as amended in the early 1990s, banned trade in both Indian and imported ivory. The ban was necessary to protect elephants, whose populations had been devastated by poaching. Former ivory carvers turned to bone (mostly camel bone), horn, wood and resin. The craft as such has effectively come to an end, and surviving historical ivories are now museum objects.

docs.title: 7.10 Stone
docs.text: Stone sculpture and architecture are treated as arts in Volume 16 of this series; here we consider stone-working as a craft. Quarrying, splitting, dressing, carving and polishing stone were the work of specialised communities of masons and sculptors, whose skills are visible in monuments from the polished Mauryan pillars of the third century BCE to the temples of the present day.

docs.title: 7.10.1 Techniques
docs.text: Stone was split from the quarry by cutting rows of wedge-holes and driving in wooden or iron wedges, a method whose marks can still be seen at ancient quarries and on unfinished monuments. Carving proceeded from rough blocking-out with heavy chisels to fine work with small chisels, drills and abrasives; the final surface could be left textured or polished with fine sand and leather. The high polish of Mauryan pillars and of some later sculptures was obtained by long abrasion. Different stones demanded different techniques: the soft sandstones of central India and the schists of Gandhāra and of the Hoysaḷa temples (the chloritic schist often called soapstone) allowed deep and intricate carving, while the granite of Tamil Nadu required great labour for every detail.

docs.title: 7.10.2 Living Traditions
docs.text: Hereditary stone-carvers still work in many parts of India. At Mamallapuram, near the seventh- and eighth-century Pallava monuments, granite carvers make images for temples and for sale. In Odisha, the stone-carvers of Puri and Bhubaneswar carve sandstone, chlorite and soapstone in the style of the medieval temples, and some families have preserved palm-leaf manuscripts of śilpa texts (Chapter 2). In Rajasthan, the white marble of Makrana, used for the Taj Mahal, and the stones of Jaisalmer, Dholpur and other quarries are carved into screens, images and architectural elements; the marble temples of the Jains at Mount Abu (11th–13th centuries) show the extraordinary delicacy that marble carving can achieve.

docs.title: 7.10.3 Screens and Inlay
docs.text:
Two specialities of Indo-Islamic architecture deserve mention. Pierced stone screens (jālī), cut from a single slab in geometric or floral patterns, admitted light and air while giving privacy; the screens of the Sidi Saiyyed mosque at Ahmedabad (1573; Figure 7.1) and of Mughal tombs and palaces are famous examples. Inlay of coloured stones in marble (Persian parchīnkārī, often called by the Italian name pietra dura) reached its height in seventeenth-century Mughal buildings such as the tomb of Iʿtimād al-Daula at Agra and the Taj Mahal. Whether the Mughal technique derived from Florentine work brought by European craftsmen or developed from earlier Indian and Persian inlay is debated. Craftsmen in Agra continue to make inlaid marble objects today, largely for tourists.

Figure 7.1. Pierced stone screens (jālī) filling an arched window of the Sidi Saiyyed mosque, Ahmedabad (1573). Each square panel carries a different geometric or floral pattern. Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 7.10.4 Hazards
docs.text: Stone-carving and quarrying expose workers to silica dust. Silicosis, an incurable lung disease, is widespread among quarry workers and stone-carvers in Rajasthan and elsewhere, and has become a major issue for labour and health campaigners. In 2019 the government of Rajasthan announced a policy on compensation and rehabilitation for workers affected by the disease.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For a regional encyclopaedia of contemporary crafts including woodwork, toys and stone-carving, Ranjan and Ranjan (2007); for the Bṛhatsaṃhitā on the selection of wood, Bhat (1981–1982); for musical instruments, Deva (1978), and for the makers of the mṛdaṅgam, Krishna (2020); for the Bombay shipbuilders, Wadia (1955).

docs.title: Chapter 8: Veṇu and Tṛṇa: Bamboo, Cane and Plant Fibres
docs.text: Mats, baskets, ropes, fans, umbrellas and containers made from bamboo, cane, grasses, reeds, palm leaves and other plant fibres are among the most widespread and least studied of Indian crafts. They are cheap, perishable and usually made for daily use, often by women and by communities of low status, and they rarely appear in museums or texts. Yet they are technically sophisticated, closely adapted to local environments and essential to rural life. This chapter surveys the materials, the main products (mats, baskets, rope, coir and jute, leaf and pith work, fans and umbrellas) and the people who make them. The spinning and weaving of fibres into cloth are treated in Chapter 4, and the palm leaves, barks and papers used for writing in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 8.1 Bamboo and Cane
docs.text:
Bamboo (veṇu, vaṃśa) and cane (rattan) are the most versatile plant materials of India, especially in the North-East and the forested regions of central and southern India. They are used for houses, bridges, fences and furniture, for baskets, mats, fish-traps and storage containers, for musical instruments such as flutes and the plucked zither, and for tools and utensils, including water-carriers made from bamboo internodes. Basket-makers form distinct, often low-ranked, castes in many regions (Basor, Dom, Medara, Kaikāḍī), and Manu lists the basket-maker among those whose food a Brahmin should not eat (Chapter 1).

The skills begin with the material. Bamboo is cut in the dry season, when it is least attacked by borers, and is often soaked in water for weeks, or stored above the hearth where smoke and heat season it and keep insects away. A culm is split with a heavy knife into strips and then into thin, flexible splints, which are scraped to an even thickness; the hard, glossy outer layer is used for fine and durable work, the softer inner layers for coarser things. Cane, the stem of climbing palms of the genus Calamus, is stripped of its spiny sheath and either used whole, for frames and bindings, or split into strands for weaving. From these materials makers produce plain, twilled and open hexagonal weaves, coiled work and lashed frames, choosing the weave for strength, flexibility or ventilation: open weaves for fish-traps and poultry cages, tight twills for grain baskets that are sometimes plastered with mud or dung.

In the North-East, bamboo and cane work reaches great refinement: the finely woven cane baskets and hats of the Nagas, the Adis and other peoples of Arunachal Pradesh, the cane furniture of Tripura and Assam, and the Assamese jāpi, a conical sun- and rain-hat of split bamboo and palm leaves, which has become a symbol of Assamese identity (Chapter 12 and Volume 23). In the hills, bamboo and cane are also materials of construction. Houses on bamboo stilts, with floors and walls of split and woven bamboo, are general, and the Adi and other peoples of Arunachal Pradesh built suspension bridges of cane across the rivers of the eastern Himalaya, with a walkway hung from cane cables and enclosed in a tube of cane hoops. Such bridges, and the village houses, were built and repaired by collective labour, and the knowledge of where to find suitable canes, when to cut them and how to join them was held by the community rather than by a caste of specialists. In this the North-East differs from much of India, where basket-making was the hereditary work of particular, often low-ranked, castes.

docs.title: 8.2 Grasses, Palms and Bast Fibres
docs.text:
The raw materials of the fibre crafts are as varied as India’s environments:

  • Grasses and sedges, such as muñja and kāśa (species of Saccharum), kuśa (Desmostachya bipinnata), the korai sedge of Tamil Nadu, sabai grass of eastern India, sikkī grass of Bihar, and reeds of many kinds.

  • Palm leaves and fibres, from the palmyra, date, coconut and other palms, used for mats, baskets, fans, umbrellas, thatch and writing material.

  • Bast fibres, from the stems of jute, hemp, flax, ramie and other plants, used for rope, sacking and coarse cloth.

  • Coir, the fibre of the coconut husk, used for rope, matting and brushes.

  • Leaves and sheaths, such as the leaves of the sal and palāśa trees, stitched into plates and cups, and banana fibre and sheath.

Many of these plants have ritual as well as practical uses. Kuśa grass is spread around the Vedic fire and used to make purificatory rings; the sacred thread of the twice-born and the girdle of the Vedic student were made of specified grasses and fibres, such as muñja. Leaf plates made of sal or palāśa leaves are used at feasts and in rituals because they are new and are thrown away after use.

docs.title: 8.3 Mats
docs.text:
Mats were the basic furniture of most Indian homes, used for sitting, sleeping, drying grain and praying, and several regional traditions are renowned for their fineness. The most celebrated are the mats of Pattamadai in Tirunelveli district of Tamil Nadu, woven by Labbai Muslim families from split and dyed korai sedge; the finest are soft enough to be folded like cloth. Soumhya Venkatesan’s study of the Pattamadai weavers shows how state training schemes and the language of national heritage have reshaped what counts as skill in the craft and who is recognised as holding it (Venkatesan 2009) (Chapter 13).

In Bengal, the madur reed of Medinipur is woven into madurkāṭhi mats on a simple loom with a warp of cotton or jute. The “cool mats” (śītalpāṭī) of Cooch Behar, Assam and the Sylhet region are woven from split strips of the stem of a marsh plant (Schumannianthus dichotomus); they are smooth and cool to sleep on, and their weaving in Sylhet has been inscribed by UNESCO (Chapter 12). In Manipur the water reed called kauna is made into mats, cushions and baskets, and in coastal regions throughout the south and east palm-leaf mats are woven, often by women. Mats were also made in prisons and by refugees, and many mat-weaving traditions were adapted for urban and export markets in the twentieth century; several have been registered as Geographical Indications.

docs.title: 8.4 Baskets and Coiled Work
docs.text: Baskets are made by plaiting, twining, wickerwork and coiling. Plaited baskets of bamboo and palm leaf are the most common in India. Coiled basketry, in which a bundle of grass is wound round with a binding strip and stitched into a spiral, is used for fine containers and decorative objects. In the wet lands of north Bihar, women of the Mithilā region dye the golden sikkī grass in bright colours and coil it into boxes, baskets, toys and figures, which were traditionally part of a bride’s dowry. In Odisha, Jharkhand and West Bengal, and especially in Mayurbhanj, Ādivāsī and other communities twist sabai grass into rope and coil it into baskets, mats and bags. Around Prayagraj (Allahabad), women make coiled baskets with a core of kāśa grass bound with strips of muñja (moonj).

docs.title: 8.5 Rope and Cordage
docs.text: Rope was needed everywhere: for wells, carts, boats, buildings, beds (the woven cot, chārpāī, has a frame strung with rope or tape) and animals. The rope-maker (rajjusarja) appears in the Yajurveda’s list of occupations (Chapter 1). Ropes were made from muñja and other grasses, hemp, jute, coir and the fibres of trees and creepers, by twisting yarns into strands and strands into rope, often with simple wheels or hooks. The sewn boats of the Indian Ocean depended on coir cordage (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 8.6 Coir
docs.text:
Coir is the coarse, water-resistant fibre of the husk of the coconut. In Kerala, coconut husks were traditionally soaked (“retted”) for months in the backwaters and lagoons until the fibre could be beaten out by hand with wooden mallets, a task done mainly by women of the Īḻava and other communities. The fibre was spun by hand into yarn on simple wheels, and the yarn woven into mats and matting or twisted into rope. Coir has been exported since at least the medieval period, when Arab writers noted its use for sewing ships, and in the nineteenth century European firms established coir factories at Alappuzha (Alleppey), which became the centre of the industry. The Coir Board was established under the Coir Industry Act of 1953.

The coir industry has long been associated with poor working conditions, especially for the women who ret and beat the husks, and it was one of the bases of the labour movement in Kerala. The retting of husks in backwaters also pollutes the water. Mechanisation of defibring and spinning has reduced the drudgery of the work but also the number of jobs.

docs.title: 8.7 Jute
docs.text: Jute, a bast fibre from plants of the genus Corchorus, was grown in Bengal and spun and woven by hand into coarse cloth, sacking and rope for local use. In the nineteenth century, after the fibre was successfully spun by machine in Dundee in Scotland, jute became a great industrial commodity. The first jute mill near Calcutta was set up at Rishra in 1855, and by the early twentieth century the mills along the Hughli were the largest jute industry in the world, producing sacking for the world’s grain, cotton and sugar trade. The cultivation of jute by peasants in eastern Bengal, and its processing in Calcutta’s mills, belong to the history of colonial industry rather than of crafts. Since the late twentieth century, however, hand-made jute bags, mats and decorative goods have been revived as crafts in Bengal as an alternative to plastic.

docs.title: 8.8 Leaf, Sheath and Pith
docs.text:
Other plant materials are used for specialised crafts:

  • Leaf plates and cups (pattal, dona) of sal, palāśa, banana or areca sheath, stitched with thin twigs or pressed in moulds; their production employs many forest-dwelling women and is promoted as an alternative to disposable plastic.

  • Sola pith (śolā), the light white pith of a marsh plant (Aeschynomene), carved by the Mālākār community of Bengal into the elaborate crowns worn by brides and grooms, the decorations of the images of Durgā, and models of temples and figures. Sola pith was also used for the sun-helmets (“sola topi”) of the colonial period.

  • Palm-leaf craft, from fans and umbrellas to toys and boxes; the preparation of palm leaves for writing is described in Chapter 11.

  • Banana fibre, extracted from the stem and used for rope, mats and, in recent years, for fabrics and paper.

docs.title: 8.9 Fans and Umbrellas
docs.text: Hand-fans (pankhā) of palm leaf, bamboo, grass, cloth and peacock feathers were essential in the Indian heat, from the simple palm-leaf fan of the village to the embroidered and beaded fans of courts and the large ceremonial fans and fly-whisks (cāmara) that were emblems of royalty and divinity, carried beside kings and images of gods. The large cloth fan suspended from the ceiling and pulled by a servant, the pankhā of colonial bungalows, required the constant labour of “punkah-wallahs”. Umbrellas of palm leaf, bamboo and cloth were made in many regions; the parasol (chatra) was a symbol of sovereignty in Indian kingship and Buddhist art, and ceremonial umbrellas are still made for temple processions, as in the appliqué umbrellas of Pipli in Odisha (Chapter 12) and the decorated umbrellas displayed on elephants at the Pūram festival of Thrissur in Kerala.

docs.title: 8.10 The Makers of Fibre Crafts
docs.text: The fibre crafts are mostly practised by women and by communities of low status or Ādivāsī origin: basket-makers such as the Basor, Turi, Dom and Medara, mat-weavers, rope-makers and leaf-plate makers. Their products are cheap, their incomes low, and their skills seldom recognised as “craft” by buyers or officials. Many depend on access to common lands, wetlands and forests for their raw materials, and have suffered as these lands have been enclosed, drained or protected. The same fibre crafts are now promoted as sustainable alternatives to plastic, and a few, such as sikkī work and Pattamadai mats, have found high-value urban markets. Whether the makers gain from that interest depends less on the materials than on who controls the trade (Chapter 15).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For a regional encyclopaedia of contemporary crafts, including bamboo, cane, grass and fibre work, Ranjan and Ranjan (2007); for a classic survey, Chattopadhyay (1975); for the Pattamadai mat-weavers, Venkatesan (2009); for the commercial products of plant fibres in the early twentieth century, Watt (1908).

docs.title: Chapter 9: Carman: Leather and Leather-Workers
docs.text: Leather was indispensable to the agrarian and military economy of India. It lifted water from wells, held the plough-bullocks to the yoke, carried oil, ghee and water, blew the smith’s fire, sounded in the drum, protected the soldier and the horse, bound books and, above all, covered feet. Yet the people who made it were placed at the very bottom of the social order. Because their work began with the skins of dead animals, the castes who removed carcasses, tanned hides and made leather goods were treated as untouchable across most of India. Leather is therefore the clearest case of the paradox that runs through this volume: a craft on which everyone depended, practised by people whom the dominant texts and customs despised. This chapter describes the materials and processes of the tanner, the uses of leather in the village and the town, footwear and the leather arts, the colonial and modern leather industry, and the long struggle of leather-working communities against the stigma attached to their work.

docs.title: 9.1 Hide and Leather in Early Sources
docs.text:
Skin as such was not regarded as impure in early Indian ritual. In the Vedic soma sacrifice the stalks were pressed with stones on a bull’s hide (adhiṣavaṇa-carman), and the skin of the black antelope (kṛṣṇājina) was the seat and garment of the consecrated sacrificer and of the Vedic student. What came to be stigmatised was not the hide but the handling of carcasses and the work of turning raw skins into leather. The law-books place the leather-worker (carmakāra) among the lowest of the “mixed” castes and among those whose food a Brahmin should refuse (Chapter 1) (Olivelle 2005). Wooden sandals (pādukā), which avoid leather altogether, became the footwear of ascetics and the form in which the feet of gods and teachers were worshipped.

Other sources show leather in everyday use. The Arthaśāstra’s list of goods to be received into the treasury includes several kinds of animal skins, with notes on their regions of origin and their colours (2.11) (Kangle 1960–1965). The Buddhist monastic code devotes a whole section of the Mahāvagga, the “Section on Skins” (Cammakkhandhaka), to leather. It tells how the monk Soṇa Koḷivisa, who had been brought up in luxury, walked up and down in meditation until his feet bled, and how the Buddha then allowed monks to wear sandals with a single lining. It goes on to forbid sandals with many linings, sandals of particular colours and ornaments, and the skins of certain animals (Horner 1951). The rules assume a trade in leather goods of many grades, from plain sandals to ornamented footwear for the rich.

docs.title: 9.2 From Hide to Leather
docs.text:
The village leather-worker’s first task was the removal of dead cattle. In much of India the carcasses of animals that died in the village were the customary perquisite of the leather-working families, who were also obliged to remove them. They flayed the animal, sold or used the meat according to local custom, and took the hide. A raw hide decays within days. It was preserved (“cured”) by salting or by drying it in the sun, and could then be stored or sold to tanners in the towns.

Tanning turns the perishable protein of the skin into a stable material by combining it with tannins. The Indian tanner used vegetable tannins, and the sequence of operations, which varied in detail from place to place, followed the general pattern shown in Figure 9.1. The cured hide was soaked in water to soften and clean it. It was then laid in a pit or a large earthen vessel of lime and water for several days, which loosened the hair and the outer layer of the skin. The tanner scraped off the hair and the flesh on a sloping wooden beam with a blunt knife, and washed the hide to remove as much lime as possible. The tanning itself was done in pits or pots filled with a liquor of crushed bark and fruit. In the north the usual material was the bark of babūl (Acacia nilotica); in the south it was the bark of avaram (Senna auriculata, formerly Cassia auriculata). Myrobalan fruit, the same tannin that the dyer used (Chapter 5), was widely added. Light skins of goats and sheep needed some weeks; the heavy hides of buffalo used for well-buckets and sandal soles needed months, with the liquor renewed and strengthened from time to time. The tanned leather was dried, rubbed with oil or tallow while still damp to make it supple (“currying”), and stretched, beaten, coloured and finished according to its use.

Figure 9.1. The main stages of vegetable tanning as practised by Indian village and town tanners. Details varied by region and by the kind of skin; heavy buffalo hides for buckets and soles spent months in the tan-pits, light goat-skins only weeks.

Tanning was slow, wet, heavy and foul-smelling work. Tan-yards stood at the edges of villages and towns, near water and away from the houses of higher castes, and the smell of the pits clung to the workers, a fact that was used to justify their exclusion. The skill lay in judging the condition of the hide at each stage: how long to lime, how strong to make the liquor, when the tan had “struck through” the thickness of the hide, and how much oil the leather would take. In the nineteenth century the tanners of the Madras Presidency became known for half-tanned goat- and calf-skins, tanned with avaram bark and exported to Britain for finishing. The trade called them “East India tanned” skins, and they were one of the largest Indian leather exports before chrome tanning replaced the vegetable process (Roy 1999).

docs.title: 9.3 Leather in Field, Well and Workshop
docs.text:
Before the electric pump, the most important single use of leather in rural India was the lifting of water. In the well-irrigated plains of the north and the Deccan a pair of bullocks walking down a ramp drew a large leather bucket up from the well on a rope running over a pulley, and a man tipped its contents into the channel at the top. The bucket was called mot in Marathi and charsā or pur in parts of north India. It was made of thick buffalo leather and needed constant repair, as did the harness and the straps that bound the bullocks to yoke and plough. In the Maharashtrian village the Chāmbhār was one of the hereditary village servants (balutedār) who received a share of the harvest in return for making and mending the well-bucket, the sandals, the whips and the leather parts of the harness, while the Mahār removed dead cattle (Chapter 13). Irfan Habib’s survey of medieval technology places the bucket-and-pulley lift beside the Persian wheel as one of the two main ways of raising well-water for irrigation (Habib 2008).

Leather served many other needs. The water-carrier (bhishtī), usually Muslim, carried water through the streets of towns in a goatskin bag (mashak) slung over his back. Large jars of raw hide (kuppā) stored and carried oil and ghee. Bellows of goatskin blew the fires of smiths and founders (Chapter 3), and the drums of temple, court and village were headed and laced with hide (Chapter 7). Soldiers carried shields of thick buffalo or rhinoceros hide, often lacquered and fitted with bosses of metal, and cavalry depended on saddles, bridles and girths. In the towns, leather was used for boxes, trunks, belts, the bindings of books (Chapter 11) and the covers of instruments.

docs.title: 9.4 Footwear
docs.text:
Every region had its own footwear. In Rajasthan and Punjab the closed slipper called jūtī or mojaṛī, with a pointed or upturned toe, was made of vegetable-tanned leather and, for festive wear, embroidered with silk, metal thread and beads; Jodhpur, Jaipur, Patiala and Amritsar are well-known centres. In the Deccan the open sandal (chappal) took many local forms. The most famous is the Kolhapuri sandal (Figure 9.2), of heavy buffalo leather, with plaited straps and a loop for the big toe, made by Chāmbhār and Dhor families in the districts around Kolhapur and across the border in northern Karnataka. A good Kolhapuri is stitched entirely by hand and softens and darkens with wear.

Figure 9.2. Kolhapuri sandals of buffalo leather, with plaited straps and toe-loops, on sale in Kolhapur. Photo: Subodh Kulkarni, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Kolhapuri shows how the old structures of the trade persist. The sandal was registered as a Geographical Indication in 2019, covering districts of Maharashtra and Karnataka, with the leather development corporations of the two states among the registered proprietors. In June 2025 an Italian fashion house showed sandals closely resembling Kolhapuris in a Milan collection without naming their source. After protests from artisans’ groups and Indian commentators it acknowledged the Indian inspiration, and talks followed about collaboration with the makers. The episode drew wide attention to the limits of what a GI can protect. It protects the name, not the design, and a design can travel freely while the makers who developed it over generations remain among the poorest workers in the trade (Chapter 15).

In the cities, footwear became an industry. Agra developed from the nineteenth century into one of India’s largest centres of hand-made shoes, made in small workshops by families of the Jāṭav community, who had long been classed as Chamārs. Owen Lynch’s study of the Jāṭavs of Agra in the 1960s showed how shoe-making families used the urban market, education, conversion to Buddhism and electoral politics to contest the status that caste assigned them, while the trade itself remained controlled largely by merchants of other communities (Lynch 1969).

docs.title: 9.5 Leather as an Art
docs.text:
Some of the most remarkable Indian leather-work was made for performance. In the shadow theatre of Andhra Pradesh (tolu bommalāṭa) and Karnataka (togalu gombeyāṭa), large, jointed puppets of goat or deer skin are scraped until they are translucent, perforated, and painted in strong colours, so that the light of a lamp behind the screen throws coloured shadows (Figure 9.3). Itinerant families perform the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata with them through the night. In Kerala the smaller puppets of tōlpāvakkūttu are used in temple performances of the Rāmāyaṇa in the Palakkad region, and in Odisha the rāvaṇachāyā uses opaque, unpainted figures. The puppet-makers of Andhra, among them those of Nimmalakunta in Anantapur district, now also make painted leather lampshades, wall-hangings and bags for urban buyers.

Figure 9.3. Detail of a painted leather shadow puppet from Karnataka, attributed to the eighteenth century (Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum, Pune). The hide is scraped thin, painted and perforated so that lamplight passes through it. Photo: Sharvarism, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Leather and embroidery met in the work of the Mochīs of Kutch. Members of this cobbler and leather-working community developed a fine chain-stitch embroidery worked with a hooked awl (ārī), the same tool they used for stitching leather, and made embroidered garments and hangings for the courts and merchants of Kutch and Saurashtra. Their work, now in museum collections, shows a stigmatised community creating a courtly art (Irwin and Hall 1973). In Bikaner, the Usta painters decorate vessels and lamps of camel hide with raised and gilded designs, a technique also applied to other surfaces. Tooled and gilded leather covered the finest Indo-Islamic books (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 9.6 Tanneries and the Colonial Economy
docs.text:
In the nineteenth century leather became an industry in the modern sense. Raw hides and skins were exported from Calcutta and Madras in large quantities, and the half-tanned skins of Madras found a market in Britain. The army created a new demand for boots, saddlery, harness and belts. The Government Harness and Saddlery Factory at Cawnpore (Kanpur), set up in the 1860s, and private firms that followed it made the city the centre of military leather goods, and Kanpur’s tanneries along the Ganga grew with them. In Calcutta, Chinese immigrants established tanneries in the eastern suburb of Tangra; in the North Arcot district of Madras, Muslim merchant families of Vaniyambadi and Ambur built up the tanning trade. Chrome tanning, in which the hide is treated with salts of chromium, was introduced in the early twentieth century. It takes days rather than weeks and gives a lighter, more water-resistant leather, and it gradually displaced vegetable tanning for most purposes.

Tirthankar Roy’s study of the leather industry in the late colonial period shows how this growth changed the organisation of the work (Roy 1999). Ownership of the larger tanneries and the trade in hides passed largely to merchants and firms from outside the leather-working castes, while the wet and dirty work of the yards continued to be done by Dalit and, in some regions, Muslim labourers. The village leather-worker, meanwhile, lost much of his customary work as factory footwear spread and, later in the twentieth century, as the electric pump replaced the leather bucket.
