After independence the Central Leather Research Institute was founded at Madras in 1948, and leather became one of India’s major export industries, concentrated in the Vellore–Ambur region of Tamil Nadu, Kanpur and Unnao, Agra and Kolkata.

The industry’s waste has been a heavy burden on the rivers beside which it grew. Lime, sulphides, decaying flesh and, above all, chromium from the tan-yards polluted the Ganga at Kanpur and the Palar in Tamil Nadu. In 1987 the Supreme Court of India ordered tanneries at Kanpur that had not installed treatment plants to close, and in 1996, in a case brought by the Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum, it applied the principle that the polluter must pay to the tanneries of Tamil Nadu. Common effluent treatment plants and the relocation of the Kolkata tanneries to a leather complex at Bantala followed, but pollution and the exposure of workers to chemicals remain serious problems.

docs.title: 9.7 Caste, Stigma and Resistance
docs.text:
Because leather-work involved the skins of dead animals, the communities who removed carcasses, tanned hides and made leather goods, such as the Chamār, Mochī, Mādiga, Cakkiliyar, Dhor and Chāmbhār, were treated as untouchable (Chapters 1 and 13). The irony that the high-caste user of a well-bucket, a drum or a pair of sandals depended daily on the work of people whose touch he regarded as polluting was not lost on critics of caste. The poet-saint Raidās (Ravidās), a leather-worker of Banaras, became the focus of a religious movement among Chamārs in north India and the Punjab, and his poems speak of his trade without shame (Hawley and Juergensmeyer 1988). The makers of drums, many of whom came from leather-working castes, are discussed in Chapter 7.

Historians have also questioned the label itself. Ramnarayan Rawat has shown that in the United Provinces most Chamārs were agricultural labourers and cultivators rather than leather-workers, and that the identification of the whole caste with leather owed much to Brahmanical ideas of pollution and to colonial ethnography (Rawat 2011). Works such as G. W. Briggs’s The Chamārs (1920), written by a missionary, and the caste entries of the census and the gazetteers fixed a “traditional occupation” on a large and varied population (Briggs 1920). Chamār activists of the early twentieth century answered with histories of their own, tracing their descent from ancient rulers or from Raidās, and in the Punjab the Ad Dharm movement of the 1920s claimed a separate religion for the Dalits of the province (Omvedt 2008). In Maharashtra, B. R. Ambedkar’s movement of the 1920s and after urged the Mahārs and other Dalits to refuse the customary duties of removing dead cattle and eating carrion, which it treated as marks of servitude (Zelliot 1992).

The structures he attacked have not disappeared. In July 2016 Dalit men skinning a dead cow at Una in Gujarat were publicly flogged by men who accused them of killing it. The attack set off a wave of Dalit protest in which many leather-working families refused to remove carcasses at all, a public withdrawal of the very service that caste had imposed on them. In the village as in the factory, the leather trade still carries the history described in this chapter. Respect for the craft must include respect for the freedom of those born into it to leave it, and for the dignity of those who choose to stay (Chapter 15).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the leather industry in the colonial period, Roy (1999); for the Chamārs and the critique of the “leather-worker” stereotype, Rawat (2011), with Briggs (1920) as an example of the older ethnography; for the shoe-makers of Agra, Lynch (1969); for the monastic rules on footwear, Horner (1951); for anti-caste movements, Omvedt (2008).

docs.title: Chapter 10: Ābharaṇa: Jewellery, Gems, Glass, Lac and Perfume
docs.text: Jewellery in India has never been only adornment. It is a store of wealth, especially for women, for whom it has often been the most secure form of property; a marker of status, caste, region and marriage; an offering to deities; and a vehicle of belief about protection and good fortune. India was also, for two thousand years, a major source of precious stones, above all diamonds, and its lapidaries and gem-merchants developed a specialised literature on the testing of gems. This chapter is about the crafts of adornment. It surveys the history of ornament, the goldsmith’s techniques, the regional traditions, and the gem trade and its literature, and then the humbler materials from which most Indians’ ornaments were made: beads of stone, shell and glass, and bangles of glass and lac. It ends with perfume, which the texts treat, like jewellery, as part of the adornment of the person. Glass, lac and perfume also demanded a practical knowledge of materials transformed by heat, solution and distillation; the chemical tradition of rasaśāstra that theorised such transformations is treated in Volume 14.

docs.title: 10.1 Ornament from the Indus to the Mughals
docs.text:
The Indus cities produced gold and silver ornaments, bangles of shell, faience and stoneware, and beads of carnelian, agate, lapis lazuli and steatite; the long, perfectly drilled carnelian beads of Harappa and Chanhudaro are among the most skilful stone work of the ancient world (Kenoyer 1998). Early historic sculpture, from Bharhut and Sanchi to Mathurā and Amarāvatī, shows men and women wearing heavy necklaces, ear ornaments, armlets, girdles and anklets, many of which can be matched with surviving pieces, such as the gold jewellery with granulation and inset stones excavated at Taxila (Marshall 1951).

Sanskrit literature has a rich vocabulary of ornaments, which lexicons such as the Amarakośa list in detail: the necklace (hāra, of many strings and types), the armlet (keyūra, aṅgada), the bracelet (valaya, kaṅkaṇa), the ear-ring (kuṇḍala, karṇikā), the crown or diadem (kirīṭa, mukuṭa), the girdle with tinkling bells (mekhalā, kāñcī, raśanā), and the anklet (nūpura, mañjīra). Poets describe the sound of anklets and girdle-bells as part of a woman’s beauty, and sculptors carved these ornaments in great detail on images of gods, goddesses and yakṣīs. Iconographic texts prescribe the ornaments of each deity, and temple images are dressed and adorned with real jewellery for worship and festivals.

Under the Mughals and the Rajput courts, jewellery became an art of extraordinary richness, combining Indian forms and gem-setting with Persian and Central Asian taste: jewelled turban ornaments (sarpech), pendants, rings and daggers set with diamonds, rubies, emeralds and spinels, often with enamel on the reverse. Jewels were exchanged as gifts and tribute and were a central part of royal treasuries.

docs.title: 10.2 The Goldsmith
docs.text: The goldsmith (suvarṇakāra, Hindi Sunār, Tamil Taṭṭāṉ) appears in the Arthaśāstra as a figure the state must watch closely: the state goldsmith works in a guarded workshop, receives gold by weight, and is fined heavily for substitution or adulteration (2.13–14) (Kangle 1960–1965). The goldsmith was ranked low in the Dharmaśāstras, in part, perhaps, because of this association with deceit. In south India goldsmiths are one of the five Viśvakarma crafts (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 10.2.1 Techniques
docs.text: Filigree Fine twisted wire bent into patterns and soldered into openwork. Cuttack in Odisha (tārakasī) and Karimnagar in Telangana are known for silver filigree. Granulation Tiny spheres of gold fused to a surface; known from Taxila and from early historic south India. Repoussé and chasing Sheet metal shaped by hammering from behind and refined from the front, the main technique of temple jewellery and of much tribal silver. Kundan The setting of stones in a bed of lac within a gold frame, using strips of highly refined gold foil (kundan) pressed and burnished around each stone. The technique allows irregular, uncut or flat stones to be set closely together. Mīnākārī Enamelling (from Persian mīnā): coloured glass powders fused into recesses engraved in gold or silver. Jaipur is famous for enamel on gold, often on the backs of kundan pieces; Varanasi for pink enamel (gulābī mīnākārī); Lucknow, Delhi and Nathdwara for other styles. The Jaipur tradition is said to have been introduced by craftsmen brought from Lahore in the late sixteenth century. Thewā A speciality of Pratapgarh in Rajasthan, in which a sheet of gold, cut and engraved with fine figurative scenes, is fused onto coloured glass.

docs.title: 10.2.2 Gold and Silver Thread
docs.text: Gold and silver thread (zarī, kalābattū) for weaving and embroidery is itself the product of a specialised metal craft. Silver is drawn through a series of progressively smaller holes in a draw-plate to make very fine wire, which is flattened between rollers and wound round a core of silk or cotton thread; for gold thread the silver wire is gilded. Surat in Gujarat has long been the main centre of the industry, with Varanasi, Agra and other weaving towns. Flattened wire (bādlā) and sequins are also used in embroidery. Since the twentieth century, much “zarī” has been made from copper or from metallised plastic film rather than silver.

docs.title: 10.2.3 Temple Jewellery
docs.text: In south India heavy gold jewellery is made for temple images, and in the twentieth century this “temple jewellery” style, in gilt silver or imitation materials, was adopted for the costumes of Bharatanāṭyam and other classical dancers. Nagercoil in Kanyakumari district is a well-known centre of temple-style jewellery. The jewels of major temples, given by kings and devotees over centuries, form some of the largest collections of historic jewellery in India.

docs.title: 10.2.4 Assaying and Hallmarking
docs.text: Goldsmiths and their customers have always needed ways to judge the purity of gold. The touchstone, on which the streak left by a gold object is compared with the streaks of test-needles of known fineness, is described in the Arthaśāstra and was used by Indian goldsmiths and money-changers until modern times (Chapter 3). Gold was refined by cementation and cupellation, and its fineness expressed in units of varṇa or, later, in carats. Since 2021 hallmarking by assaying centres recognised by the Bureau of Indian Standards has been compulsory for most gold jewellery sold in India, replacing the customer’s trust in the individual goldsmith with a system of public certification.

docs.title: 10.2.5 Goldsmiths in Modern India
docs.text:
The modern state has shaped the goldsmith’s trade as directly as the Arthaśāstra’s superintendent once did. To curb gold smuggling and reduce private demand for gold, the Gold Control Rules of 1963 at first prohibited the making of new ornaments in gold finer than 14 carats. Customers were used to jewellery of about 22 carats and would not buy the lower standard, and the rule caused severe distress among goldsmiths, many of whom lost their work. It was soon relaxed. The Gold (Control) Act of 1968 then required goldsmiths and dealers to be licensed and to keep accounts of the gold they held. The Act was repealed in 1990, and the import and trade of gold were liberalised in the following years.

The organisation of the craft has also changed. In the cities the old relation between a family goldsmith and his clients has largely given way to retail jewellers, from small shops to national chains, who sell finished jewellery and employ or subcontract the craftsmen who make it. Much of the hand work in the jewellery workshops of Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai and other cities is done by migrant artisans (kārīgar) from West Bengal. They work in small rented rooms for piece rates, often far from their families. Machines now make chains, and many standard pieces are cast in multiples from wax models produced in rubber moulds or designed on computer and printed. Mandatory hallmarking has further moved the guarantee of quality from the goldsmith to the institution. The goldsmith’s skill remains essential for setting, enamelling, filigree and repair, but the craftsman is often hidden behind the shop.

docs.title: 10.3 Regional and Tribal Jewellery
docs.text:
Every region and community has its own ornaments, and many ornaments mark marital status. In much of north India married women wear toe-rings (bichhiyā), glass or lac bangles and vermilion in the parting of the hair; in Maharashtra the black-beaded maṅgalsūtra; in Tamil Nadu and Kerala the tāli tied at marriage; in Bengal the conch-shell and red lac bangles (śaṅkhā and palā). The “sixteen adornments” (solah śṛṅgār) of a bride are a conventional north Indian list.

Pastoral and Ādivāsī communities wear heavy silver ornaments, which serve as savings and as markers of identity: the necklaces, anklets and armlets of Rabārī and other pastoral women in Gujarat and Rajasthan, the silver of the Lambāṇī (Banjārā), and the bead, brass and shell ornaments of the Naga peoples, among whom ornaments once signified rank and achievements in war and feasting. Dhokra brass ornaments are cast by the lost-wax method in central and eastern India.

Under classical Hindu law, a woman’s own property (strīdhana) included the gifts she received at marriage, especially ornaments; in a society in which women rarely inherited land, jewellery was often the main property a woman could call her own.

docs.title: 10.3.1 Ornament and the Life-Cycle
docs.text:
Ornaments follow a person through life, and their making is tied to the household rites that mark its stages. The piercing of a child’s ears (karṇavedha) is counted among the life-cycle rites (saṃskāra) in several lists, and small children are given anklets with bells, black threads and amulets against the evil eye. At marriage a bride receives ornaments from both families, and in many communities the set she wears identifies her region, caste and religion as clearly as her dress. Widowhood was marked by their removal. In many Hindu communities a widow’s bangles were broken and her nose- and toe-rings taken off, a practice that expressed in metal and glass the loss of status that the law-books and custom imposed on widows. Some ornaments have their own history: the nose-ring, for example, is rarely if ever shown in early Indian sculpture and became common only in the medieval period, after which it was adopted so widely that it came to be thought of as an ancient Indian ornament.

Village and small-town jewellery is also money. Silver anklets, necklaces and armlets are valued largely by weight; they are pawned with moneylenders in bad years, and melted and remade by the goldsmith when fashions change or a daughter must be provided for. The customer pays for the metal, and separately for the workmanship and for the metal lost in working, and disputes over weight and purity were a constant feature of the relation between goldsmith and client, the background to the suspicion of goldsmiths in the Arthaśāstra and the law-books. Because old pieces were so often melted down, few village ornaments survive from before the nineteenth century, and their history must be reconstructed from sculpture, painting and the forms still made. Oppi Untracht’s survey, based on years of fieldwork, records the forms, names and techniques of the jewellery of hundreds of communities, much of it made by village smiths with simple tools (Untracht 1997).

docs.title: 10.4.1 The Sources
docs.text: Ancient and medieval India was a major source of precious stones. Diamonds came from the alluvial deposits of the Krishna and Godavari valleys, from the Golconda region, and from Panna in central India; pearls from the Gulf of Mannar between India and Sri Lanka; beryl and other gems from south India. Rubies, sapphires and spinels were imported from Sri Lanka, Burma and Badakhshan, and emeralds, in the Mughal period, from Colombia via Europe. The Periplus lists pearls, transparent stones, diamonds and sapphires among the exports of south Indian ports (Casson 1989).

docs.title: 10.4.2 Texts on Gems
docs.text:
The testing of gems (ratnaparīkṣā) was a recognised field of knowledge; “the testing of silver” and “knowledge of the colouring of gems and of their mines” are among the sixty-four arts of the Kāmasūtra (1.3.15; Chapter 1). The Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the examination of precious articles for the treasury (2.11) describes pearls, gems, diamonds and coral, their sources, and the qualities of good and faulty stones: a good gem, it says, should be well formed, clear, smooth, heavy and lustrous, with radiance within (Kangle 1960–1965). The Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century) has chapters on the testing of gems, including diamonds, pearls, rubies and emeralds (Bhat 1981–1982). Separate lapidary treatises, such as the Ratnaparīkṣā attributed to Buddhabhaṭṭa and the Agastimata, were edited and translated into French by Louis Finot (Finot 1896); the Garuḍa Purāṇa includes a series of chapters on gems drawn from this literature. The Ratnaparīkṣā of Ṭhakkura Pherū (1315), a Jain official at the court of the Delhi sultan ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī, describes the gems he saw in the royal treasury, with their weights and prices, from the point of view of a working assayer.

These texts combine practical observation (colour, transparency, hardness, weight, flaws) with beliefs about the good and bad fortune brought by particular stones. They should be read as records of medieval connoisseurship and belief, not as gemmology in the modern sense.

docs.title: 10.4.3 The Nine Gems
docs.text:
In later astrological tradition, each of the nine “planets” (navagraha) was associated with a gem: the Sun with ruby, the Moon with pearl, Mars with coral, Mercury with emerald, Jupiter with yellow sapphire or topaz, Venus with diamond, Saturn with blue sapphire, and the lunar nodes Rāhu and Ketu with hessonite (gomeda) and cat’s-eye (vaiḍūrya). A ring or pendant with all nine stones (navaratna) became a popular auspicious ornament.

A Note on Gem “Therapy”

The belief that wearing particular gems can change a person’s fortune or health is a matter of faith and astrological tradition. There is no scientific evidence that gems have such effects, and they should never be used in place of medical treatment. Preparations of gems and metals taken internally as medicines can be harmful (see Chapter 3).

docs.title: 10.5 Diamonds
docs.text:
Until diamonds were found in Brazil in the 1720s, India was the principal source of diamonds known to Europe and western Asia. The French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, who visited the diamond mines of the Golconda kingdom, including Kollur on the Krishna, in the mid-seventeenth century, described thousands of labourers digging and washing the gravels, the merchants who bought the stones, and the Indian method of polishing diamonds on wheels with diamond powder and oil. He noted that Indian cutters preferred to preserve weight rather than maximise brilliance (Tavernier 1889).

Many famous diamonds came from India. The Koh-i-Noor, whose early history is largely legend, passed through Mughal, Persian, Afghan and Sikh hands before it was taken by the East India Company after the annexation of the Punjab in 1849 and presented to Queen Victoria; it was recut in London in 1852 and is now in the British Crown Jewels (Dalrymple and Anand 2017). The large blue diamond that Tavernier sold to Louis XIV is the ancestor of the Hope diamond, now in the Smithsonian Institution. The Regent diamond, found in the Golconda region about 1698, is in the Louvre, and the Daryā-i Nūr, taken from Delhi by Nadir Shah in 1739, is among the Iranian crown jewels.

Diamond cutting today is concentrated in Surat in Gujarat, where an industry that grew from the 1960s and 1970s cuts and polishes a large share of the world’s smaller diamonds. It employs hundreds of thousands of workers, many of them migrants from Saurashtra, in conditions that range from modern factories to small workshops.

docs.title: 10.6.1 Stone Beads of Khambhat
docs.text: The cutting and drilling of hard stones such as carnelian, agate and jasper into beads is one of the oldest continuous crafts of western India. The Indus bead-makers worked carnelian from the Rajpipla hills of Gujarat; in the medieval and early modern periods, Khambhat (Cambay) on the Gulf of Khambhat became the great centre of agate and carnelian working, exporting beads across the Indian Ocean to East Africa, Arabia and Southeast Asia. The stones are heated to deepen their colour, chipped into shape, ground, drilled and polished. Studies of present-day bead-makers at Khambhat have helped archaeologists understand ancient techniques (Kenoyer 1998). The work is dangerous: workers who breathe the fine dust produced by grinding are at high risk of silicosis.

docs.title: 10.6.2 Conch Shell
docs.text: The conch shell (śaṅkha), sacred to Viṣṇu and blown in temples, was cut into bangles and ornaments from Indus times onwards. In Bengal, the white shell bangles (śāṅkhā) worn by married Hindu women, together with red lac or coral bangles, are made by the Śāṅkhārī community, especially in Bishnupur and Dhaka, from shells of Turbinella pyrum fished in the Gulf of Mannar.

docs.title: 10.6.3 Pearls
docs.text: The pearl fisheries of the Gulf of Mannar, between south India and Sri Lanka, were famous in antiquity; the Periplus and Tamil literature mention them, and the Pāṇḍya kings controlled them. Divers of the Paravar community dived for oysters in the seasonal fisheries, under the control first of local rulers and then of the Portuguese, the Dutch and the British. Pearls were also brought from the Persian Gulf. The Paravars converted to Catholicism in the sixteenth century, partly to gain Portuguese protection; in their history craft, caste, religion and empire on the Indian coast cannot be separated.

docs.title: 10.7.1 Beginnings
docs.text: The Indus craftsmen made faience and a glassy stoneware, but true glass appears in South Asia only in the first millennium BCE. Glass beads and bangles are found at sites of the Painted Grey Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware cultures in the Ganga valley, and become common in the early historic period. Claims for glass in Harappan contexts are uncertain and most refer to faience. The Sanskrit word for glass is kāca; “glass gems” (kācamaṇi) were a byword for the imitation of the precious.

docs.title: 10.7.2 Beads and Bangles
docs.text:
From the late centuries BCE, South Indian sites such as Arikamedu near Pondicherry produced small drawn glass beads in great quantities. These “Indo-Pacific” beads, made by drawing a tube of glass and cutting it into short lengths, were traded around the Indian Ocean from East Africa to Southeast Asia for some two thousand years (Francis 2002). Alok Kanungo’s ethnoarchaeological study of present-day glass-bead makers in India illustrates techniques that help archaeologists interpret ancient workshops (Kanungo 2004). Excavations at Taxila produced glass beads and bangles, and imported Roman glass vessels (Marshall 1951).

Glass bangles are worn by married women across much of north and central India. Their manufacture is concentrated today at Firozabad in Uttar Pradesh. Glass is melted in furnaces, gathered and drawn onto a rotating cylinder to form a continuous coil; the coil is cut into rings, whose ends are then joined in a flame, often by home-based workers, before the bangles are decorated. The industry has a long record of hazardous working conditions and child labour, which reforms and enforcement have reduced but not eliminated.

Firozabad’s industry grew in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries (Chapter 14). It replaced imported glass bangles, and it was helped in the Svadeśī years by the call to buy Indian goods. Its furnaces burned coal for most of the twentieth century. Firozabad lies within the Taj Trapezium Zone, the area around the Taj Mahal in which the Supreme Court of India, from the mid-1990s, ordered polluting industries to switch to cleaner fuels in order to protect the monument. The glass furnaces were therefore required to move to natural gas, which changed their technology and costs and drove some small units out of business. Bangles are not only made but also sold by specialists. In north India the Manihār or Cūṛīhār communities, mostly Muslim, have traditionally sold glass and lac bangles and fitted them on customers’ wrists, a service of some intimacy that brought men of these communities into the women’s quarters of households of every caste and religion.

docs.title: 10.7.3 Glass Vessels
docs.text: Glass vessels were less common in India than in western Asia, and much fine glass was imported, from the Roman world in antiquity and from Iran, Venice and later Bohemia and Britain in the early modern period. Indian glassmakers did, however, make bottles, flasks, bowls, lamps and huqqa bases, some decorated with enamel and gilding, in the Mughal and later periods; Gujarat and the courts of north India were among the centres. Glass was also used for inlay in palace walls, for bangles and beads, and, from the nineteenth century, for the reverse paintings on glass made in Thanjavur, Gujarat and elsewhere.

docs.title: 10.7.4 Mirrors
docs.text: At Āṟanmuḷa in Kerala, a few families of craftsmen make metal mirrors (āṟanmuḷa kaṇṇāṭi) from a high-tin bronze, cast and then polished to a reflective surface. The mirror is one of the eight auspicious objects of Kerala ritual and is a registered Geographical Indication. Mughal and Rajput palaces used small pieces of convex mirror glass in plaster for the decoration of “mirror halls” (śīśmahal), and small mirrors are sewn into the embroidery of Gujarat and Rajasthan.

docs.title: 10.8.1 The Material
docs.text:
Lac (lākṣā) is a resin secreted by the lac insect, Kerria lacca, which lives on the branches of trees such as palāśa (Butea monosperma), kusum (Schleichera oleosa) and ber (Ziziphus). The encrusted twigs (“stick-lac”) are harvested, crushed and washed to give “seed-lac”, which is melted and stretched into thin sheets that break into flakes: shellac. The red dye washed out of the raw lac was used for dyeing silk and wool and as a cosmetic. Lac softens with heat and hardens on cooling, and it is used as an adhesive, a varnish, a sealing wax and a moulding material. The word “lac” comes through Persian from Sanskrit lākṣā; “shellac” refers to the thin flakes.

India has long been one of the world’s main producers of lac. Much of it is cultivated, by inoculating host trees with brood-lac, by Ādivāsī communities in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and neighbouring states. The Indian Lac Research Institute was founded at Namkum near Ranchi in 1924, and its successor institution continues research on lac and other natural resins. Shellac had a large industrial market in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, as a varnish, as an electrical insulator and as the material of gramophone records, until it was replaced by synthetic plastics; it is still used as a food glaze and a coating for tablets.

The Mahābhārata tells how Duryodhana tried to burn the Pāṇḍavas in a house of lac (lākṣāgṛha) built to catch fire easily; they escaped through a tunnel.

docs.title: 10.8.2 Lac Crafts
docs.text: Lac is used for bangles, especially in Rajasthan, Hyderabad and Bihar, made by the Lakherā and Maṇihār communities: coloured lac is softened over a fire, rolled round a core, shaped to the size of the wearer’s wrist and decorated with glass stones, mirror pieces and foil. Lac is also used to colour turned wooden toys and objects (Chapter 7), to fill the backs of hollow gold ornaments and as the bed in which kundan stones are set (Section 10.2), and as sealing wax.

docs.title: 10.9 Perfume
docs.text:
Scent completed the adornment of the body. Perfumery (gandhayukti, “the combination of scents”) was one of the arts of the cultivated person and the subject of chapters in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā and other texts (Bhat 1981–1982). Indian perfumes were made from sandalwood, aloeswood (agaru), musk, camphor, saffron, vetiver, flowers and resins, and used in worship, in the bath and on the body. James McHugh’s study of smell in Indian religion and culture surveys this literature (McHugh 2012). F. R. Allchin argued that terracotta apparatus from early historic sites in Gandhāra and the Ganga valley may have been used for distillation, perhaps of alcoholic spirits (Allchin 1979); the interpretation is debated.

The perfumers (gandhī, aṭṭār) of Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh continue to make ittar by a distillation method known as deg-bhapkā. Flowers or other materials are heated with water in a copper still (deg); the vapour passes through a bamboo pipe into a copper receiver (bhapkā) standing in cold water and containing sandalwood oil, which absorbs the fragrance. Kannauj attars include rose (gulāb), jasmine, screwpine (keoṛā), vetiver (khas), henna blossom (hinā) and miṭṭī, made by distilling baked earth to capture the smell of the first rain. Kannauj perfume is a registered Geographical Indication, but the industry has declined under competition from synthetic fragrances and the scarcity of sandalwood oil.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the lapidary texts, Finot (1896); for Tavernier’s account of the mines and diamond trade, Tavernier (1889); for the Koh-i-Noor, Dalrymple and Anand (2017); for regional jewellery, Untracht (1997) and Ranjan and Ranjan (2007); for the 1956 exhibition of Indian textiles and ornaments, Jayakar and Irwin (1956); for beads, Francis (2002) and Kanungo (2004); for perfume and smell, McHugh (2012); for natural products of commercial importance in the early twentieth century, including lac, Watt (1908).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Citra and Utsava: Painting, the Book, Festival Crafts and Games
docs.text: Painting in India was practised on many surfaces: the walls of caves, temples, palaces and houses; palm leaves and paper; cloth, wood, leather and the human body. Histories of Indian art usually treat painting as a fine art, and focus on the great cycles of Ajanta and the miniatures of the Mughal and Rajput courts. This chapter looks at painting as a craft: at the organisation of painters’ workshops and families, at their materials, pigments and methods, at the making of books, which joined painters to scribes, paper-makers and binders, and at the wide range of painted things, from scrolls carried by storytellers to pictures sold to pilgrims. It then turns to the crafts of celebration and play. Festivals require images, lamps, decorations and effigies; games require boards, pieces and cards; children’s play requires toys; and performance requires masks, puppets and costumes. Many of these things are ephemeral, made to be used for a season and then immersed, burned or discarded, and they are made by a wide range of people, from hereditary potters and painters to householders and children. Painted and printed textiles are described in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 11.1 Painters and Their Workshops
docs.text:
Painting (citra, ālekhya) is one of the sixty-four arts of the Kāmasūtra, and courtly literature often shows princes and princesses painting portraits of absent lovers. Its learned theory, set out in the Citrasūtra of the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa (Kramrisch 1928) and in the six limbs of painting (Chapter 1), and the history of the great mural, manuscript and court traditions, from Ajanta to the Mughal, Deccani, Rajput and Pahāṛī schools, are treated in Volume 16 of this series. The texts were written for connoisseurs and patrons as much as for painters. The painters themselves appear in other sources as hereditary craftsmen, usually of modest rank, working in families and workshops.

The best-documented workshop is the imperial library-workshop (kitābkhāna) of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605), which employed scores of painters, calligraphers, gilders and binders. Persian masters trained Indian painters, many of them from Hindu artisan families. Paintings were often the work of several hands: one artist designed the composition, another painted it, another did the faces. Abu’l Fazl names many of the painters, among them Daswanth and Basawan, and inscriptions on the paintings record their names (Abu’l Fazl 1873; Beach 1992).

At the Rajput and hill courts painting was a family occupation. B. N. Goswamy’s study of Nainsukh of Guler (c. 1710–1778) and his family showed how a lineage of painters, the descendants of Paṇḍit Seu, moved between the small hill courts of the western Himalaya, transmitting styles, drawings and techniques from father to son and between brothers (Goswamy 1997). Painters kept stocks of drawings and tracings (charbā) made by pouncing, through which compositions passed from generation to generation. Their names were seldom recorded on the paintings themselves; genealogical records kept by priests at pilgrimage centres such as Haridwar have helped to identify them.

In the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Indian painters at Patna, Murshidabad, Lucknow, Delhi, Thanjavur and other cities worked for British patrons, producing paintings of Indian trades, castes, festivals and costumes in a style adapted to European taste, known as “Company painting”. Sets of paintings of artisans at work, made for European buyers, are themselves a valuable source for the history of crafts, though they present crafts through the categories of the colonial observer.

docs.title: 11.2 The Painter’s Materials and Methods
docs.text:
Painters of manuscripts and miniatures worked on sheets of paper made thick and smooth by pasting several layers together and burnishing them with a stone. They drew first with a brush in a light colour, corrected the drawing, and then laid on a thin white priming. Colours, ground on a stone slab and mixed with gum, were applied in successive layers, each burnished from the back to make the surface smooth and brilliant. Gold was applied as shell gold (gold leaf ground with gum) and burnished to a shine; beetle-wing cases were sometimes used for the green of jewels. Brushes were made of squirrel or kitten hair set in quills, the finest having only a few hairs. Painters learned to make their own colours and brushes as part of their apprenticeship.

Painting on cloth required a different preparation: the cloth was sized with starch or gum, often coated with chalk and burnished, as in Odisha paṭṭacitra, while the large paṛ scrolls of Rajasthan were painted on starched coarse cotton with mineral colours. Murals required the preparation of plaster and, in some traditions, painting on wet lime.

docs.title: 11.2.1 Pigments
docs.text:
Whether they worked on palm leaf, paper, cloth or walls, Indian painters used mineral and organic pigments bound with gum or glue. The common palette included:

  • black from lamp-soot (kajjala);

  • white from chalk, kaolin or lead white;

  • red ochre, vermilion (hiṅgula, mercury sulphide, natural or made by combining mercury and sulphur) and red lead;

  • yellow ochre and orpiment (haritāla, arsenic sulphide);

  • green from terre verte or from mixing orpiment and indigo;

  • blue from indigo and from ultramarine made from lapis lazuli, imported from Badakhshan;

  • gold and silver applied as leaf or ground into paint.

“Indian yellow” (peorī), a bright yellow used in Mughal and Rajput painting, was reported in 1883 by T. N. Mukharji to be made at Monghyr in Bihar from the urine of cows fed on mango leaves (Mukharji 1883). The report was long doubted, but the main colouring matter of the pigment, a salt of euxanthic acid, is an animal metabolite consistent with his account; the practice has long since ceased.

Health and Safety Note

Several traditional pigments are poisonous. Orpiment contains arsenic; vermilion contains mercury; red lead and lead white contain lead. Grinding, mixing and using them without precautions can cause serious poisoning, and they should never be ingested or applied to the skin. Vermilion and sindūr powders sold today may also be contaminated with lead.

docs.title: 11.3 The Arts of the Book
docs.text: Painters shared the making of books with scribes, paper-makers, illuminators and binders. The book was itself a craft object, and its materials changed over time from leaf and bark to paper.

docs.title: 11.3.1 Palm Leaf and Birch Bark
docs.text: Before paper, the main writing materials of India were palm leaf and, in the north-west, birch bark. Palm leaves (of the talipot or palmyra palm) were cut to size, boiled or soaked, dried and polished. In the north they were written on with ink and a reed pen; in the south and Odisha the letters were incised with a metal stylus and then rubbed with lamp-black mixed with oil, which filled the incisions and was wiped from the surface. The leaves were pierced with one or two holes, strung on cords and protected between wooden boards, which were often painted. Birch bark (bhūrjapatra) was split into thin sheets and written on with ink; many of the oldest surviving Indian manuscripts, including Buddhist texts from Gandhāra, are on birch bark. In Assam the Vaiṣṇava monasteries wrote on the prepared bark of the agaru tree (Chapter 12). Writing ink (masī) was usually made from lamp-black or charcoal with gum and water. Carbon inks are very stable, which is one reason why so many Indian manuscripts remain legible. Manuscripts were protected by wrapping in cloth and with insect-repellent substances, but they were usually recopied every few generations, and the survival of a text depended on the continuous work of scribes.

docs.title: 11.3.2 Paper
docs.text:
Paper was invented in China and reached India through the Islamic world. It came into use in India in the early second millennium CE, and Irfan Habib’s survey of medieval technology connects its spread with the Delhi Sultanate (Habib 2008). In Gujarat and western India, Jain manuscripts on paper become common from the thirteenth century, gradually replacing palm leaf, which remained the usual writing material in the south until the nineteenth century. Paper was made from rags and fibres, beaten to a pulp, lifted on a screen of fine bamboo strips, pressed and dried, and burnished with a stone to give a smooth writing surface. Important centres included Sialkot, Kalpi, Daulatabad, Ahmedabad and Sanganer.

The papermakers (kāghazī) of Sanganer near Jaipur, who are said to have settled there under the patronage of the Jaipur court, still make handmade paper, now mainly from cotton rags and for export and stationery. Hand-made paper was promoted by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission after independence, and the Kalpi papermakers continue as a cluster. In Arunachal Pradesh the Monpa people make paper from the bark of a local shrub (Daphne), used for Buddhist texts.

docs.title: 11.3.3 Calligraphy, Illumination and Binding
docs.text:
With paper came the Persian-style codex and a cluster of crafts that the Indo-Islamic courts held in very high esteem. In the Islamic tradition the copying of the Qurʾān was a pious act, and calligraphy (khushnavīsī) was ranked above painting. The Sultanate period developed a distinctive Indian script for the Qurʾān, known as bihārī, with heavy, flat letter-forms; under the Mughals the flowing nastaʿlīq became the favoured hand for Persian poetry and history. Abu’l Fazl’s account of Akbar’s library-workshop treats calligraphy before painting, names the leading scribes, and records that Akbar honoured Muḥammad Ḥusain of Kashmir with the title zarrīn qalam, “golden pen” (Abu’l Fazl 1873). Calligraphers were often men of learning and good family, and many signed their work; the painters who illustrated the same manuscripts were usually of humbler origin and signed only occasionally.

A fine manuscript passed through many hands (Losty 1982). Paper-makers supplied sheets that were dyed, sized with starch and burnished with an agate or a smooth stone until the pen glided over them; the scribe ruled the page with a frame of strings pressed into the paper (misṭar) and wrote with a reed pen cut to a slant; the illuminator (muzahhib) painted the headpieces, rulings and floral borders in gold and colours; the margins (ḥāshiya) of albums were sometimes of separately coloured, gold-sprinkled or marbled paper (abrī), a technique practised especially in the Deccan; and the binder (ṣaḥḥāf) sewed the gatherings and made covers of stamped, tooled and gilded leather (Chapter 9) or, from the eighteenth century, of painted and lacquered pasteboard. The lacquered pen-boxes (qalamdān) and book-covers made for scribes gave Kashmiri papier-mâché its old name, kār-i qalamdānī, “pen-box work”.

The same period saw a great expansion of Jain manuscript production in western India. Jain merchants and monks commissioned copies of the Kalpasūtra and other canonical texts, first on palm leaf and then, increasingly from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, on paper, illustrated in the western Indian style with gold and lapis blue; the temple libraries (bhaṇḍāra) of Patan, Jaisalmer and Cambay preserved them in large numbers. Hindu households and temples, too, kept illustrated manuscripts of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the Gītagovinda and devotional texts. Behind all these books stood scribes, paper-makers, illuminators and binders, most of them anonymous. Printing, which spread in India in the nineteenth century, brought most of their crafts to an end, though calligraphers continued to write lithographed Urdu books and newspapers into the late twentieth century.

docs.title: 11.4 Painted Scrolls and Storytelling
docs.text:
Some of the most remarkable Indian paintings were made to be used in performance. Itinerant painter-storytellers unrolled painted scrolls while singing the stories depicted on them, and performers carried painted boxes and cloths from village to village. In Rajasthan the Joshī families of Shahpura and Bhilwara paint the paṛ, a horizontal cloth several metres long, with the epics of the folk deities Pābūjī and Devnārāyaṇ; the Bhopā priest-singer and his wife perform the epic at night in front of the unrolled cloth, which serves as a portable temple. The carpenters of Bassi near Chittorgarh make the kāvaḍ, a portable wooden shrine with hinged painted panels, which the storyteller opens one by one as he narrates.

In Bengal the Paṭuā or Citrakar painters make vertical scrolls (paṭ) and sing the stories as they unroll them: episodes from the epics and the Kṛṣṇa legend, the goddess Manasā, the Muslim saint Satya Pīr, and in recent decades contemporary themes such as floods, epidemics, the tsunami of 2004 and social campaigns. Many Paṭuās are Muslims who paint and sing Hindu stories, and they have long lived between the two communities. In Telangana the Nakāśī family of Cheriyal paints long cloth scrolls for the genealogists and storytellers of particular castes, narrating the mythical origins of those castes. The leather shadow puppets of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala belong to the same world of travelling performance (Chapter 9).

These traditions joined painting to song and made it a form of public knowledge and memory. Their audiences were often villagers, pastoralists and lower-caste communities, for whom the painted cloth brought the god and the story to the village. They were not, however, an art only of those excluded from texts and temples: the same painters worked for landholders and patrons of high rank, and the temple painting described next served pilgrims of every class.

docs.title: 11.5 Painting for Temples and Pilgrims
docs.text: Temples and pilgrimage centres sustained large communities of painters. At Nathdwara in Rajasthan, the seat of the Puṣṭimārga image of Śrīnāthjī, painters make the large painted cloth hangings (picchavāī) hung behind the image according to the festival calendar, as well as small paintings and prints for pilgrims. At Puri, the Citrakāra painters of Raghurajpur and other villages paint the images of Jagannātha, Balabhadra and Subhadrā and the paṭṭacitra pictures sold to pilgrims (Chapter 12). At the Kālīghāṭ temple in Calcutta, Paṭuā painters in the nineteenth century developed a new style of quick watercolour paintings on mill-made paper, with bold outlines and broad washes, depicting deities, scenes from the epics, and satirical images of the new urban society of Calcutta: the dandy, the courtesan, the hypocritical priest. Kalighat paintings were cheap souvenirs; they are now valued as one of the sources of modern Indian art (Jain 1999). Popular prints made with lithographic and oleographic presses, such as those of the Ravi Varma Press founded in 1894, eventually displaced much of this hand-painted production.

docs.title: 11.6 Painting on the Wall and the Floor
docs.text: Much Indian painting is done by women on the walls and floors of houses, for festivals, marriages and rituals, and is renewed again and again. The Mithilā paintings of Bihar, the Warli paintings of Maharashtra, the sohrāy and khovar paintings of Jharkhand, the māṇḍaṇā of Rajasthan, the ālpanā of Bengal and the kōlam of the south (Chapter 12) belong to this category. These are not “folk” versions of a higher art, but distinct traditions with their own techniques, meanings and transmission from mother to daughter. Many of them have been transferred to paper and canvas for sale since the 1960s and 1970s, and some of their practitioners have become known as individual artists. Kramrisch’s Unknown India was one of the first exhibitions to present such work as art (Kramrisch 1968).

docs.title: 11.7 Painters in Society
docs.text:
Painters in India were generally members of hereditary communities: the Citrakāras of Odisha and Bengal, the Joshīs and Cītārās of Rajasthan and Gujarat, the Nakāśīs of the Deccan, the Muslim and Hindu painters of the Mughal and Rajput courts, the Paṭuās of Bengal. Painters were usually of modest standing, though a successful court painter could become wealthy and respected. Many painting communities included both Hindus and Muslims, or Muslims who painted Hindu subjects; the boundaries between religions were less important in the workshop than in later communal politics.

In the colonial period, art schools trained a new kind of artist, educated in European academic methods, and the distinction between the “artist” and the hereditary painter-craftsman hardened. Partha Mitter has traced how Indian artists and critics in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries negotiated between academic naturalism, nationalist revival of “Indian” styles, and the traditions of the bazaar painters (Mitter 1994). The modern recognition of Mithilā, Warli, Gond and Paṭuā painters as artists partly reverses this hierarchy, though questions of authorship, market and authenticity remain (Chapter 15).

docs.title: 11.8 Santiniketan and the Craft Revival
docs.text: In the early twentieth century, artists associated with the nationalist “Bengal school”, such as Abanindranath Tagore and Nandalal Bose, turned to Indian painting traditions, including Ajanta, Mughal and Rajput painting and folk art, for inspiration. At Santiniketan, where Rabindranath Tagore founded the art school Kala Bhavana in 1919, which became part of the university of Visva-Bharati when that was constituted in 1921, students learned painting alongside crafts such as batik, leatherwork, weaving and woodwork, and the nearby rural reconstruction centre of Sriniketan (1922) taught crafts to villagers as a means of livelihood. Nandalal Bose designed the posters for the Haripura session of the Indian National Congress in 1938 in a folk-inspired style and later illustrated the Constitution of India. These experiments helped to bridge the gap between “art” and “craft” that colonial institutions had opened, and they anticipated the post-independence craft revival (Mitter 1994).

docs.title: 11.9.1 Chess
docs.text: Indian craftsmen made the boards, pieces, dice and cards of many games, and the games themselves carried ideas across religions and continents (Topsfield 2006). The game of chess probably developed in India by about the sixth century CE, from a game called caturaṅga, “four-limbed”, after the four divisions of an ancient army: elephants, horses, chariots and foot-soldiers. The game travelled to Iran, where it was known as chatrang and later shaṭranj, and from the Islamic world to Europe (Murray 1913). Indian craftsmen made chessmen of ivory, wood, stone and metal, and chessboards, often embroidered or inlaid, were among the luxury goods of Indian courts. Chess sets carved for European buyers in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with the armies of the East India Company opposing those of Indian rulers, are among the curiosities of colonial craft.

docs.title: 11.9.2 Pachīsī and Caupaṛ
docs.text: The race games of pachīsī and caupaṛ, played on a cross-shaped board with pieces moved according to throws of cowrie shells or long dice, were popular across India. Their boards were usually made of cloth, embroidered or appliquéd, so that they could be folded and carried. A large pavement board for the game is laid out in the courtyard of Akbar’s palace at Fatehpur Sikri, where, according to tradition, the emperor played with living pieces. The game of dice is also central to the Mahābhārata, in which Yudhiṣṭhira loses his kingdom at dice.

docs.title: 11.9.3 Gañjīfā
docs.text:
Gañjīfā is a game of circular playing cards (Figure 11.1), introduced from Iran in the Mughal period. The Mughal pack had eight suits; Indian painters created new packs with ten suits based on the ten incarnations of Viṣṇu (daśāvatāra gañjīfā) and other themes. The cards were painted by hand on layers of paper or cloth stiffened with lac or gum, or on ivory or tortoise-shell for the rich. Sawantwadi in Maharashtra, Puri and other centres in Odisha, and Mysore were important centres; the craft survives in a few families, mainly for collectors.

Figure 11.1. Ten hand-painted gañjīfā cards from Rajasthan, nineteenth century, in opaque watercolour on card, each about 7 cm across (Los Angeles County Museum of Art). Photo: Los Angeles County Museum of Art; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 11.9.4 Gyān Caupaṛ: The Game of Knowledge
docs.text: The game known in Hindi as gyān caupaṛ and in other forms as mokṣapaṭ or paramapada sopānam, in which players move up ladders of virtue and down snakes of vice towards liberation, was played in many religious traditions, with Jain, Hindu, Sufi and other versions of the board. The boards were painted on cloth or paper, with numbered squares named after virtues, vices, states of being and heavens and hells, and were used as a form of moral instruction as well as entertainment. In the late nineteenth century the game was taken to Britain, where it was secularised and became “Snakes and Ladders”.

docs.title: 11.10 Toys and Dolls
docs.text:
Toys are made in every material: clay, wood, cloth, paper, palm leaf, lac, metal and pith. Some of the best-known wooden toy traditions are described in Chapter 7, clay toys and figures in Chapter 6. Several other traditions deserve mention:

Navarātri dolls In Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, households set up a display of dolls on stepped shelves during the autumn festival of Navarātri (kolu or golu, bombe habba), including deities, scenes from the epics, village life and new figures added each year. The display sustains a large seasonal industry of clay, papier-mâché and wooden dolls. The Thanjavur “dancing dolls” with nodding heads and the roly-poly dolls that right themselves when pushed are well-known types. Cloth dolls and puppets Women make cloth dolls for their children and for festivals in many regions. In Rajasthan, the string puppets (kaṭhputlī) of the Bhāṭ community, with carved and painted wooden heads and long cloth skirts, are used to perform the stories of heroes such as Amar Singh Rāṭhoṛ. Paper and papier-mâché Papier-mâché toys, masks and boxes are made in Kashmir, Rajasthan, Odisha and Bengal, from paper pulp or layers of pasted paper over moulds, and painted. Metal toys Small brass and bell-metal toys, such as miniature cooking sets, were made for children, especially girls, in many regions.

Toys are evidence of how societies imagined childhood and work: the miniature cooking sets given to girls, the carts, soldiers and animals given to boys, and the dolls used to rehearse weddings all teach social roles.

docs.title: 11.11 Kites
docs.text: Kite-flying is a popular pastime across much of India, and in Gujarat the festival of Uttarāyaṇ (Makar Saṅkrānti) in January is celebrated by kite-flying on a massive scale. Kites are made of thin paper on frames of split bamboo, and kite-makers in Ahmedabad, Khambhat, Jaipur, Lucknow and Bareilly produce them in huge numbers for the season. Kite-fighting, in which flyers try to cut each other’s strings, uses string coated with a paste of glue and powdered glass (māñjhā). Manufactured nylon and “Chinese” māñjhā, which does not break easily, has caused many injuries and deaths among people and birds, and its use has been banned by courts and authorities in several states and by the National Green Tribunal (2017).

docs.title: 11.12.1 Images Made to Be Immersed
docs.text: The clay images of Durgā in Bengal and of Gaṇeśa in Maharashtra and elsewhere, worshipped for some days and then immersed in water, are described in Chapter 6. Similar seasonal images are made for Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Kālī and Viśvakarma (Chapter 2) in eastern India, and for other deities elsewhere. The image-makers work for months before each festival, often on credit from the organising committees, and the decorations, crowns and ornaments of the images involve further crafts, such as the sola pith work of the Mālākārs (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 11.12.2 Effigies of Rāvaṇa
docs.text: For the festival of Daśaharā in north India, enormous effigies of Rāvaṇa and his brothers, built of bamboo and paper and filled with fireworks, are burned at the end of the Rāmlīlā performances. Their makers, in Delhi and other cities, include Hindu and Muslim craftsmen who work for weeks to prepare them.

docs.title: 11.12.3 Tāziya
docs.text: During Muharram, the Shia commemoration of the martyrdom of Ḥusain at Karbala, models of the tomb of Ḥusain called tāziya are carried in procession and then buried or immersed. They are made of bamboo, paper, tinsel, mica and cloth, sometimes on a very large scale, and in many towns of north India, such as Lucknow, their making is a craft of specialist families; in some places Hindus also make and carry tāziyas.

docs.title: 11.12.4 Lamps, Stars and Floor Designs
docs.text: Dīpāvalī is celebrated with clay lamps (Chapter 6) and, in many places, with paper lanterns; Christians in Kerala and Goa hang paper stars and build cribs at Christmas; in Kerala the harvest festival of Oṇam is celebrated with floral floor designs (pūkkaḷam); and women across India draw raṅgōlī, kōlam, ālpanā and māṇḍaṇā on floors and thresholds (above).

docs.title: 11.12.5 Fireworks
docs.text:
Fireworks are used at Dīpāvalī, weddings, temple festivals and many other celebrations. Their manufacture, once a small-scale craft, is now concentrated in Sivakasi in Tamil Nadu, which also produces matches and printed material. The industry has a long history of dangerous working conditions, fatal explosions and, in the past, extensive child labour, which have been the subject of court cases and regulation.

Health and Safety Note

Some festival materials are hazardous. Synthetic colours sold for Holī have been found to contain toxic dyes and heavy metals, and can cause skin, eye and respiratory injury; vermilion and other powders may contain lead. Plaster of Paris images and synthetic paints pollute rivers and lakes when immersed, and fireworks injure many people every year. Natural colours and clay images are safer alternatives.

docs.title: 11.13 Weddings
docs.text: Weddings are the largest single market for many Indian crafts. A wedding may require new saris and other clothes for the bride, groom and relatives, often of a regional type with particular colours and techniques (the red Banarasi sari of north India, the paiṭhaṇī of Maharashtra, the gharcoḷā and paṭolā of Gujarat, the Kāñcīpuram silk of Tamil Nadu); jewellery, much of it given to the bride as her own property; brass and copper vessels; decorated wedding chambers and pavilions; painted pots; sola-pith crowns in Bengal; and printed or painted invitation cards. Women decorate the bride’s hands and feet with henna (mehndī) in intricate patterns, an art practised both by family members and by professional henna artists. The wedding gifts of embroidery and quilts made by women of the bride’s family, such as the phulkārī of Punjab and the embroidered dowry textiles of Kutch, were once among the most important occasions for women’s craft (Chapter 12). Changes in wedding customs, such as the shift to machine-made saris and jewellery, therefore affect the livelihoods of many craftspeople.

docs.title: 11.14 Masks and Costumes
docs.text:
Masks are used in many Indian performance and ritual traditions, and their making is a specialised craft. The Chhau dance of Purulia in West Bengal uses large painted masks of papier-mâché and clay, with elaborate headdresses, made by craftsmen of the village of Charida and others, while Seraikela Chhau in Jharkhand uses smaller, more stylised masks; Chhau dance was inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010. In the Vaiṣṇava monasteries (satras) of Majuli in Assam, monks make masks of bamboo, clay and cloth for the dramatic performances (bhāonā) founded by the saint Śaṅkaradeva, including large masks of demons and the man-lion Narasiṃha. At the Samaguri satra, the best-known centre, a frame of split bamboo is covered with strips of cloth soaked in clay, smoothed, dried and painted. The masks range from face masks to figures large enough to cover the whole body of the performer, and some have movable jaws. In the Buddhist monasteries of Ladakh, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh, masks of papier-mâché and wood are kept for the masked dances (cham) performed at festivals.

Kerala’s performers wear costumes that are themselves assemblages of crafts. The headdresses, ornaments and skirts of Kathakaḷi dancers are made of carved light wood, cloth, glass, beetle-wings and paint by specialised craftsmen, and their make-up is applied by specialists in a process taking hours. The ritual performers of Theyyam in northern Kerala wear towering headdresses and costumes of palm leaves, areca sheath, cloth and metal, made anew for each performance.

docs.title: 11.15 Ephemeral Craft
docs.text:
Much of the festival craft described in this chapter is ephemeral: the image is immersed, the effigy burned, the kite lost, the floor-design swept away. Its value lies in the making and the use, not in the survival of the object. A history of Indian crafts written from museum collections, which preserve durable and precious objects, therefore leaves out much of what craftspeople made. Ephemeral crafts employ very large numbers of people, often seasonally, and they sustain skills, such as modelling, painting and the working of bamboo and paper, that are used in other crafts as well.

The seasonal rhythm of festival crafts also shapes the lives of their makers. Image-makers, kite-makers, lamp-makers and toy-makers work intensively for a few weeks or months, often on borrowed money, and depend on selling their whole stock before the festival; a rainy season, a change in fashion or a ban on a material can ruin them. Their skills are passed on within families, and many combine festival work with other crafts or with agricultural and wage labour for the rest of the year.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the Citrasūtra, Kramrisch (1928); for Mughal and Rajput painting, Beach (1992); for a family of hill painters, Goswamy (1997); for Kalighat, Jain (1999); for art in colonial India, Mitter (1994); for ritual and village painting, Kramrisch (1968); for regional toys, masks and festival crafts, Ranjan and Ranjan (2007); for the arts of the book, Losty (1982); for board and card games, Topsfield (2006), and for the history of chess, Murray (1913).

docs.title: Chapter 12: Deśa: A Regional Survey of Living Crafts
docs.text: Every region of India has its own crafts, shaped by local materials, by the needs and tastes of local patrons and markets, by the communities who practise them, and by long histories of contact. This chapter offers a brief regional survey of some of the best-known living traditions, complementing the material-based chapters that precede it. Table 12.1, at the end of the chapter, lists the principal crafts of each region with the chapters in which they are described, and can be used as a finding aid. It cannot be complete; a much fuller guide is the regional encyclopaedia edited by M. P. and Aditi Ranjan (Ranjan and Ranjan 2007). Ādivāsī and folk traditions are treated more fully in Volume 23. A final section looks briefly beyond India’s present borders, to Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

docs.title: 12.1.1 Kashmir: Shawls and Papier-Mâché
docs.text:
The Kashmir shawl is woven from pashm, the soft under-fleece of the Changthangi goat of Ladakh and the Tibetan plateau, collected by Changpa herders and traded to Srinagar. The fibre is very fine, about 12–16 microns in diameter, and must be cleaned and spun by hand; spinning was traditionally done by women at home, weaving by men in workshops. The most elaborate shawls were woven in the twill-tapestry technique known as kānī, in which the weft is wound on many small wooden bobbins (kānī) and interlocked around groups of warp threads, following a coded pattern-script, the tālīm, which the master reads aloud to the weavers (Figure 12.1). Embroidered shawls (amlīkār, sozanī) imitated the woven ones more cheaply.

Kashmir shawls were luxury goods at the Mughal court and in Iran and Central Asia, and from the late eighteenth century became a fashion in Europe, especially France. European imitations, woven on Jacquard looms in Lyon, Paisley and elsewhere, followed. The Kashmir industry collapsed in the 1870s, when the Franco-Prussian War and changing fashion destroyed the French market, and famine struck the valley (Irwin 1973; Ames 1986). Kānī weaving survives on a small scale in and around Kanihama, and Kashmir pashmina and the Kānī shawl are registered Geographical Indications.

Figure 12.1. The end border of a Kashmir shawl of about 1810, woven in the twill-tapestry technique with a row of cone-shaped būṭā motifs, the “paisley” of European imitations (Chapter 5) (Los Angeles County Museum of Art). Photo: Los Angeles County Museum of Art; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Shāhtūsh, an even finer wool from the Tibetan antelope (chiru), was the material of the shawl that “could pass through a ring”. Because the antelope must be killed to obtain it, trade in shāhtūsh is banned under CITES and Indian law.

Kashmiri craftsmen also make felted woollen rugs (namdā), embroidered with chain-stitch, and gabbā, rugs made of old woollen blankets dyed, cut and stitched together in appliqué and embroidered. Its carpets, introduced from Persia and Central Asia, are described in Chapter 4; three other crafts, papier-mâché, walnut carving and khatambandh ceilings, are described here.

Kashmiri papier-mâché (kār-i qalamdānī, “pen-box work”, Chapter 11) divides the work between two specialists. The sākhtsāz makes the object: paper pulp is pressed onto a mould, or layers of paper are pasted over it, and the dried shell is cut from the mould, joined and smoothed. The naqqāsh then grounds it with chalk and glue, burnishes it and paints it in watercolour and gold or silver leaf with flowers, birds, hunting scenes or the dense all-over floral pattern called gul-i hazāra (“a thousand flowers”), finally sealing the surface with varnish. The craft made pen-boxes, caskets and trays for courtly buyers, and from the nineteenth century vases, boxes and ornaments for European ones. The carvers of walnut wood (Juglans regia) work in several depths, from deep, undercut carving of chinar leaves, lotuses and vines to shallow relief, lattice and plain polished work. The khatambandh ceilings are assembled from small, thin panels of pine or deodar fitted together in geometric patterns.

Kashmir is also unusual in that its embroidery for the market has been largely men’s work. The fine needlework (sozanī) on pashmina shawls, the chain-stitch worked with a hook (ārī) on woollen rugs and furnishing fabrics, and crewel-work in wool on cotton are done mainly by men, in workshops and at home, while women’s part in the shawl economy was concentrated in spinning. The contrast with the household embroideries of Punjab, Bengal and Kutch (Chapter 4) suggests that the division of craft work between men and women was a matter of local custom and market organisation, not of the nature of the work.

docs.title: 12.1.2 Ladakh and the Buddhist Himalaya
docs.text: In Ladakh, Lahaul, Spiti and Sikkim, crafts were shaped by Tibetan Buddhism and by the trade routes across the Himalaya. Monasteries commissioned painted scrolls (thangka), wall paintings, clay and metal images, carved and painted wood, and ritual objects, often made by itinerant craftsmen from Tibet and Nepal as well as by local families. The coppersmiths of Chilling in Ladakh, who make tea-pots, ladles and ritual vessels of copper and brass, are said to descend from Newar craftsmen from Nepal. Women weave woollen cloth and make felt and carpets, and the pashmina trade linked the herders of the Changthang with the weavers of Kashmir.

docs.title: 12.1.3 Punjab and Himachal
docs.text:
The phulkārī and bāgh embroideries of Punjab are described in Chapter 4. The rumāls of Chamba in Himachal Pradesh are square covers embroidered in double-satin stitch, so that the image is the same on both sides, on designs drawn by the painters of the Pahāṛī courts, showing scenes of Kṛṣṇa, weddings and hunts. Kullu shawls, woven on handlooms with geometric borders, are another important craft of the hills.

Phulkārī was embroidered by the women of Hindu, Sikh and Muslim households across undivided Punjab, especially in the families of Jaṭ cultivators, and the same patterns crossed religious lines; it was the textile of the family and the village rather than of any one faith. The court of Ranjit Singh (r. 1799–1839) at Lahore was the last great indigenous patron of crafts in the north-west. It commissioned arms, jewellery, shawls and tents of Kashmir cloth, and under Ranjit Singh the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar was covered with gilded copper and inlaid marble, work that drew metalworkers, gilders and stone-inlayers to the city. Kashmir itself came under Sikh rule in 1819 and under the Dogra rulers of Jammu in 1846. Heavy taxation of the shawl trade and the famines of the period drove many Kashmiri weavers to the towns of Punjab, among them Amritsar, Ludhiana and Nurpur, where they wove shawls for the Indian and European markets until the trade collapsed in the 1870s (Ames 1986).

docs.title: 12.1.4 Uttar Pradesh
docs.text: Uttar Pradesh is one of the most important craft regions of India: the silk weaving of Banaras (Chapter 4); chikan embroidery and zardozī metal-thread embroidery of Lucknow; the brassware of Moradabad; the glass of Firozabad; the carpets of Bhadohi and Mirzapur, an industry that grew in the nineteenth century; the black pottery of Nizamabad; the perfumes of Kannauj; and the printed cottons of Farrukhabad and Pilkhuwa. Much of this work is done by Muslim artisans, a fact reflected in the Persian vocabulary of many crafts.

docs.title: 12.2.1 Gujarat and Kutch
docs.text:
Gujarat has been a centre of textile production and export for more than a thousand years: the printed cottons found in Egypt were mostly made there (Chapter 5), and its ports exported paṭolā and printed cloth to Southeast Asia. Today its crafts include the double-ikat paṭolā of Patan, the bāndhaṇī of Jamnagar and Bhuj, the ajrakh of Ajrakhpur and Dhamadka, the mashrū of Patan and Mandvi, the carved woodwork of the old towns, and the bead-work of Saurashtra.

Kutch, in particular, is home to many communities with distinctive embroidery: the Rabārīs, whose women embroider in chain stitch with small mirrors; the Ahīrs; the Mutvās; the Sodhā Rajputs and Meghvāls, who practise the counted-thread sūf work, in triangular satin stitches worked from the back of the cloth; and many others. Judy Frater’s study of Rabārī embroidery shows how these styles express identity, and how they change (Frater 1995). In the 1990s some Rabārī communities decided to restrict the elaborate embroidered dowries that had become a heavy burden on families; women responded with new, quicker styles using ready-made trims.

In Kutch, too, the weavers of Bhujodi and neighbouring villages, of the Vaṇkar community, weave woollen shawls and blankets from the wool of local sheep and camel-hair for the pastoral communities of the region, and have adapted their designs for urban buyers. In Saurashtra, women of the Kāṭhī and other communities made elaborate glass-bead work: door-hangings (toraṇ), coverings for the bride’s bullock-cart, and ornaments, in which thousands of small glass beads are strung into figurative and geometric designs.

Rogan painting is done on cloth with a thick paste made by boiling castor oil and mixing it with pigments, which is drawn out with a metal stylus. Once made in several places in Kutch and Sindh, by the late twentieth century it survived only in a single family of the Khatrī community at Nirona. It has been revived by that family, led by Abdul Gafur Khatri, who received the Padma Shri in 2019, and is now taught to younger members of the community, including women.

docs.title: 12.2.2 Rajasthan
docs.text:
Rajasthan’s crafts include block printing at Sanganer, Bagru and Barmer; tie-dye; blue pottery and lac bangles at Jaipur; thewā at Pratapgarh; koftgarī; the terracotta plaques of Molela (Chapter 6); and the painted scrolls (paṛ) used by the Bhopā priest-singers who perform the epics of the folk heroes Pābūjī and Devnārāyaṇ, made by the Joshī painters of Shahpura and Bhilwara. Jaipur, a planned city founded in 1727, became a great centre of crafts under its rulers, and was designated a UNESCO Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art in 2015.

Western Rajasthan has its own textile crafts: appliqué and patchwork made by women of Barmer and Jaisalmer, block-printed and resist-dyed cottons (including ajrakh) at Barmer and Balotra, and woollen weaving by the Meghvāl community. Jaipur is also one of the world’s great centres for the cutting and polishing of coloured gemstones, and for silver jewellery, enamel and kundan work (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 12.2.3 Maharashtra
docs.text: Maharashtra’s crafts include the paiṭhaṇī silk saris of Paithan and Yeola; the leather sandals of Kolhapur, made by the Chāmbhār and Dhor leather-working communities; the lacquered toys and gañjīfā cards of Sawantwadi; and the wall paintings of the Warli, an Ādivāsī community of the Thane and Palghar districts. Warli paintings, white figures on a mud wall, were made for marriages and rituals; from the 1970s, encouraged by the craft boards and by the artist Jivya Soma Mashe (1934–2018), they were made on paper and cloth for sale and became widely known.

docs.title: 12.3.1 Bihar: Mithilā Painting
docs.text: In the Mithilā region of north Bihar and southern Nepal, women painted the walls of houses, especially the marriage chamber (kohbar), with images of deities, auspicious symbols and the lotus pond. The British official W. G. Archer saw these paintings on the walls of houses damaged in the earthquake of 1934 and later wrote about them. During the drought of the mid-1960s, the All India Handicrafts Board encouraged women in the villages around Madhubani to paint on paper for sale, and Mithilā (Madhubani) painting became one of the best-known Indian folk arts. Distinct styles developed in different communities: the brightly coloured bharnī style associated with Brahmin women, the line-drawing kachnī style of Kāyastha women, and the godnā (tattoo) style developed by Dalit women of the Dusādh and Chamār communities. Among the artists who have received national recognition are Sita Devi, Ganga Devi, Mahasundari Devi and Dulari Devi, the last from the Mallāh (fishing) community. Madhubani painting is a registered Geographical Indication.

docs.title: 12.3.2 Bihar and Jharkhand: Other Traditions
docs.text: Bihar also has the sujanī, quilted and embroidered covers made by women from layers of old cloth, in which women of Bhusura and other villages, organised in collectives since the late twentieth century, now embroider narratives of their own lives, of social issues and of local events alongside traditional motifs. In the Hazaribagh region of Jharkhand, women of several Ādivāsī and other communities paint the walls of their houses with sohrāy paintings at the harvest festival and with khovar paintings, scratched through layers of coloured earth, for marriages; these too have been transferred to paper and cloth for sale. Tasar silk weaving is important around Bhagalpur in Bihar and in Jharkhand, using silk reared by forest communities (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 12.3.3 Odisha
docs.text: Pipli, near Puri, is known for appliqué: cut shapes of brightly coloured cloth, often animals, birds, flowers and deities, sewn onto a ground to make canopies, umbrellas and hangings used in the processions of the Jagannātha temple, and now lampshades, bags and wall-hangings for the market. The paṭṭacitra painters (Citrakāra) of Raghurajpur and other villages near Puri paint cloth prepared with chalk and gum with images of Jagannātha and of episodes from the epics and the Kṛṣṇa legend, in bright mineral and vegetable colours; they also make painted palm-leaf books with incised drawings, and paint the images of Jagannātha, Balabhadra and Subhadrā for the temple. Odisha’s other crafts include the ikats of Sambalpur and Nuapatna, the silver filigree of Cuttack, stone carving, and Dhokra casting.

docs.title: 12.3.4 Bengal
docs.text: Bengal’s crafts include the kānthā (Chapter 4); the terracotta temples and votive horses of Bankura (Chapter 6); the bālucharī silk saris of Bishnupur; the Dhokra casting of Bikna and Dariyapur; the painted scrolls (paṭ) of the Paṭuās (Chapter 11); the conch-shell work of Bishnupur; and, historically, the ivory carving of Murshidabad (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 12.4 The South
docs.text:
Tamil Nadu is known for the silk of Kāñcīpuram, the bronzes of Swamimalai, the stone carving of Mamallapuram, the painted glass and gilded Thanjavur paintings (panel paintings with raised gesso, gold foil and inset glass stones, developed under the Maratha rulers of Thanjavur in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries), the Aiyaṉār horses, and the houses of Chettinad, built by the Nāṭṭukkōṭṭai Cheṭṭiyār merchant community with Burmese teak, Italian marble and locally made cement tiles. Kerala has the mirrors of Āṟanmuḷa, bell metal, coir (coconut fibre) products and its carpentry traditions. Karnataka has the counted-thread embroidery called kasūti, worked by women of the Dharwad region in geometric and temple-like motifs on saris; the lacquered toys of Kinnal; the silks of Mysore and Ilkal, sandalwood carving, Bidrī ware, the Lambāṇī embroidery of Sandur and the toys of Channapatna. Andhra Pradesh and Telangana have kalamkārī, the ikats of Pochampally, the toys of Kondapalli, Etikoppaka and Nirmal, the silver filigree of Karimnagar and the leather shadow puppets (tolu bommalāṭa), and the painted narrative scrolls of Cheriyal (Chapter 11). In Thanjavur, metalworkers make “art plates” of brass with appliqué figures of deities in silver and copper, and Kumbakonam and Swamimalai are centres of bronze-casting (Chapter 3).

Kerala’s temple murals, painted in a distinctive palette of red and yellow ochre, green and black on the walls of temples and palaces from about the sixteenth century, such as those of the Mattancherry palace at Kochi, were revived in the twentieth century through training at the Guruvayur temple’s mural institute. In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, women draw kōlam and raṅgōli designs of rice flour on thresholds every morning, an ephemeral art that combines devotional, aesthetic and geometric traditions and is passed from mother to daughter.

docs.title: 12.5 The North-East
docs.text:
The North-East is a region of great craft diversity, with traditions shaped by its many peoples and by its forests of bamboo and cane.

In Assam the silks described in Chapter 4, golden mugā, warm erī and white pāṭ, are woven in homes and in the weaving town of Sualkuchi into the mekhelā-chādar worn by Assamese women; bell metal is worked at Sarthebari, bamboo and cane everywhere, and masks are made in the Vaiṣṇava monasteries of Majuli (Chapter 11). In Nagaland each Naga people has its own textile designs, woven on the back-strap loom by women. Shawls marked status, and some designs were reserved for men who had given feasts of merit or achieved distinction in war; the Ao warrior’s shawl, with a central white band painted with animals and other figures, is a well-known example. Manipur has fine cotton and silk weaving, including the phanek wrap-skirt, the Longpi stone-and-clay pottery of the Tangkhul Nagas (Chapter 6), and water-reed (kauna) basketry and mats (Chapter 8).

Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura are known for cane and bamboo work, for Khasi and Garo basketry and the weaving of erī silk, for the Mizo puan, a wrap-around cloth woven by women on the back-strap loom whose designs mark occasions and status, and for the Tripuri riśā, a narrow woven band worn by women as a breast-cloth or headdress and given at a girl’s coming of age, together with the wrap-skirt (rignāi). In Arunachal Pradesh the Apatani, Adi, Mishmi and other peoples weave cotton and other fibres on back-strap looms in designs that mark community identity. In the Buddhist areas of Arunachal and Sikkim, craftsmen make wooden masks and bowls, woollen carpets, painted scrolls (thangka) and wood carving in the Tibetan tradition, and the Monpa make paper from the bark of a shrub (Chapter 11).

Besides its looms and silks, two Assamese traditions deserve notice here. The Vaiṣṇava monasteries (satras) of the tradition founded by Śaṅkaradeva (by tradition 1449–1568) were, and on Majuli still are, centres of craft as well as of devotion. Monks and lay devotees made the masks, costumes and properties for the plays (Chapter 11). The satras also produced manuscripts on sāñcipāt, the inner bark of the agaru tree (Aquilaria), which was cut into strips, dried, rubbed smooth and coated before it was written and painted on. The illustrated manuscripts of the Bhāgavata and other works in a distinctive Assamese style are their finest products, together with the Hastividyārṇava, a treatise on elephants painted for the Ahom court in 1734 (Volume 20). In lower Assam, the bell-metal smiths of Sarthebari cast and beat plates, bowls and the footed offering tray (xorāi) that serves as an emblem of Assamese hospitality, presented with betel to honoured guests.

docs.title: 12.6 Central India
docs.text:
Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh are rich in Ādivāsī crafts. The Dhokra casters of Bastar, around Kondagaon, make brass figures of deities, animals and people by the lost-wax method with wax threads (Chapter 3). Wrought-iron figures and lamps are made by Bastar smiths.
