The Gond and Pardhān Gond communities painted their walls and floors with patterns and figures for festivals; in the early 1980s the young Pardhān artist Jangarh Singh Shyam (c. 1962–2001) was brought by the artist J. Swaminathan to the newly founded Bharat Bhavan arts centre in Bhopal, and his paintings, with their dense patterning of animals, trees and spirits, launched a school of “Gond art” that now includes many artists. The Pithorā paintings of the Rāṭhvā and Bhilālā communities of eastern Gujarat and western Madhya Pradesh are painted on house walls in fulfilment of vows to the god Pithorā, with processions of horses, riders and other figures, under the direction of the ritual specialist (baḍvā).

The weaving towns of Chanderi and Maheshwar make light saris and fabrics in silk and cotton; Chanderi’s fine fabrics with gold-thread motifs were known in the Mughal period, and Maheshwar’s weaving was revived in the eighteenth century under Ahilyābāī Holkar and again in the twentieth century. Bagh prints are described in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 12.7 Beyond the Present Borders
docs.text: The modern frontiers of India cut across older craft regions. The weavers of Dhaka, the printers of Sindh and the tile-makers of Multan belonged to the same networks of materials, markets and techniques as their neighbours in present-day India, and Sri Lanka and Nepal developed traditions closely related to those of the subcontinent. This section notes some of them briefly; it is not a survey.

docs.title: 12.7.1 Sri Lanka
docs.text: The classic study of Sri Lankan crafts is Ananda Coomaraswamy’s Mediaeval Sinhalese Art (1908), written after his years as director of the Mineralogical Survey of Ceylon (Coomaraswamy 1908). It describes the crafts of the Kandyan kingdom, which lasted until 1815, mainly as they survived in the eighteenth century. The royal craftsmen worked in workshops attached to the court and held land in return for service to the king (rājakāriya). Most of them belonged to the artisan caste of the Navandanna, which included smiths, carpenters, painters and other craftsmen; groups of lower rank wove mats, made pots or worked as drummers. Among the latter were the Kinnara of the Dumbara valley near Kandy, whose mats are woven with geometric and animal designs in dyed fibre. Coomaraswamy’s picture of craftsmen maintained by king and temple and sheltered from the market became the basis of his idealised account of the traditional craftsman (Chapter 14). Other Sri Lankan crafts include lacquer applied to turned wood and laid on in coloured threads, brass and silver work, and the carved and painted masks of Ambalangoda on the south-west coast. These are made for the kōlam folk drama and for the sanni healing rituals, in which dancers impersonate the demons held to cause disease.

docs.title: 12.7.2 Nepal
docs.text: In the Kathmandu valley, crafts were the hereditary work of Newar castes, both Buddhist and Hindu. Buddhist Śākya families of Patan cast and embossed images and ritual objects in copper and brass, and the Tāmrakār were coppersmiths. The Citrakār painted images, masks and the cloth paintings called paubhā. Carpenters and carvers (Śilpakār) made the carved struts, doorways and latticed windows of temples, monasteries and houses, and the Prajāpati potters of Bhaktapur and Thimi still dry their pots in the open squares of their quarters (Slusser 1982). Newar craftsmen worked far beyond the valley. In 1260 the young Newar Anige (Araniko, 1245–1306) led a team of craftsmen to Tibet to build a golden stūpa for the Sakya hierarch Phagpa. He went on to the court of Khubilai Khan, where he directed imperial workshops and designed the White Stūpa of the Miaoying temple in Beijing, completed in 1279. For centuries afterwards Newar metalworkers and painters worked in Lhasa and in Tibetan monasteries. In the hills, papermakers make a tough paper called lokta from the inner bark of Daphne shrubs, a material related to that of the Monpa paper of Arunachal Pradesh (Chapter 11). The metal techniques of the Newars are discussed in Volume 14 and their painting in Volume 16.

docs.title: 12.7.3 Bangladesh
docs.text: Bangladesh shares with West Bengal the traditions of jāmdānī, kānthā (Chapter 4), conch-shell work (Chapter 10) and terracotta temple decoration, of which the Kantajew temple at Kantanagar near Dinajpur, completed in the mid-eighteenth century, is among the richest examples. Two further crafts have received international recognition. The śītalpāṭi (“cool mats”) of Sylhet are woven from thin strips split from the stems of the murtā plant (Schumannianthus dichotomus); UNESCO inscribed their weaving on its list of intangible heritage in 2017. The painting of cycle-rickshaws in Dhaka, whose backboards, hoods and frames carry film stars, landscapes, animals and political images, is a twentieth-century urban craft practised by specialist painters and inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.

docs.title: 12.7.4 Pakistan
docs.text:
In Sindh, besides the ajrakh (Sindhi ajrak; Chapter 5), women make rallī quilts, pieced and appliquéd from cotton scraps in bold geometric patterns and given in dowries; the same craft is practised across the border in Rajasthan and Kutch. Hala in Sindh is known for lacquered turned woodwork and glazed tiles, and Multan for glazed pottery and tiles in blue and white (Chapter 6). Chiniot in Punjab is a centre of carved wooden doors and furniture. The most visible modern craft of Pakistan is the decoration of trucks and buses: workshops in Karachi, Rawalpindi and other cities cover them with painted panels, carved wood, mirror-work and embossed metal, combining the skills of painters, carpenters and metalworkers in a style that changes with fashion.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For a regional encyclopaedia, Ranjan and Ranjan (2007); for the Kashmir shawl, Irwin (1973) and Ames (1986); for Rabārī embroidery, Frater (1995); for village and tribal ritual art, Kramrisch (1968); for Sri Lanka, Coomaraswamy (1908); for the Newar crafts of Nepal, Slusser (1982).

docs.title: Chapter 13: Śreṇī and Jāti: Guilds, Caste and Craft Knowledge
docs.text: How was craft knowledge organised, protected and handed down in India? Two institutions stand out in the sources: the guild (śreṇī), an association of people following the same trade, which is prominent in texts and inscriptions of the early historic period; and the hereditary occupational community (jāti), within which, for most of the last two millennia, most crafts were learned and practised. This chapter takes these in turn. It then looks at the ways in which production was organised (in the household, under village patrons, in court and temple workshops and for merchants), at the kind of knowledge that craftspeople held and the means they devised to record and teach it, at the relation between that knowledge and science, and finally at the work of women and children.

docs.title: 13.1.1 The Evidence of the Texts
docs.text:
The word śreṇī (Pali seṇi) means a row or series, and hence a group of people of the same occupation. Pali texts speak of eighteen guilds as a conventional number, and the Jātaka stories mention heads of craft groups, such as the chief of the carpenters or of the smiths (jeṭṭhaka), and villages of potters, smiths and carpenters. The great merchants (seṭṭhi, Sanskrit śreṣṭhin) of the Buddhist texts, such as Anāthapiṇḍika of Sāvatthī, who bought the Jeta grove for the Buddha by covering its ground with coins (a scene carved at Bharhut), were wealthy householders and financiers rather than leaders of craft guilds (Chakravarti 2002).

The Dharmaśāstras recognise the customs of occupational groups as law for their members. Gautama allows farmers, traders, herdsmen, moneylenders and artisans to settle matters according to the rules of their own groups (Gautama 11.21); Manu (8.41) tells the king to establish the law after examining the laws of castes, regions, guilds (śreṇīdharma) and families (Olivelle 2005); and the Yājñavalkya and Nārada law-books deal with breaches of the agreements made by guilds and other corporate bodies. The Arthaśāstra lists “guild troops” (śreṇībala) among the kinds of armed forces available to a king (9.2), regulates the conduct of artisans and their dealings with customers (4.1), and treats guilds as bodies to be watched and taxed (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 13.1.2 The Evidence of Inscriptions
docs.text:
Inscriptions give a more concrete picture (Chakravarti 2002).

  • Sanchi (late 1st century BCE or early 1st century CE). The ivory-carvers of Vidiśā record a carving on the southern gateway of the great stūpa as their work (Chapter 7).

  • Nasik (1st or 2nd century CE). An inscription of Uṣavadāta, son-in-law of the Western Kṣatrapa ruler Nahapāna (whose date is disputed), records that he invested sums of money with two weavers’ guilds (kolika-nikāya) at Govardhana, at fixed monthly rates of interest, so that the interest would provide robes and other necessities for the monks of the cave monastery. Another Nasik inscription, probably of the third century, records similar deposits with guilds of potters, of oil-pressers and of makers of water-machines. Guilds thus acted as trustees and bankers for perpetual endowments.

  • Indor (465 CE). A copper-plate of the reign of Skandagupta records an endowment deposited with the guild of oil-men (tailika-śreṇī) of Indrapura, who undertook to supply oil for a lamp in a temple of the Sun in perpetuity (Fleet 1888).

  • Mandasor (436 and 473 CE). The best-known guild inscription, composed by the poet Vatsabhaṭṭi, tells how a guild of silk-weavers (paṭṭavāya) migrated from Lāṭa (southern Gujarat) to Daśapura (Mandasor), built a temple of the Sun in 436 CE and repaired it in 473 CE. It describes how some members of the guild took up other occupations, becoming archers, story-tellers, astrologers and men of religion, while remaining members of the group (Fleet 1888).

In south India, inscriptions of the Cola period and later record powerful merchant associations, such as the “Five Hundred” (Aiññūṟṟuvar), and associations of weavers and artisans that made donations to temples and negotiated privileges with kings and temples (Chakravarti 2002).

docs.title: 13.1.3 Artisans, Kings and Temples in the South
docs.text: Medieval south Indian inscriptions show artisans as taxpayers, donors and bargainers. Cola and later inscriptions mention taxes on looms and on other craft activities. Others record grants of honours to particular artisan groups, which could include the right to blow conches at weddings and funerals, to wear sandals, to plaster the walls of their houses or to build houses of more than one storey. Such privileges were symbols of status, and their grant or denial was a matter of intense concern. Vijaya Ramaswamy’s study of weavers in medieval south India traces how weaving communities such as the Kaikkōḷar and the Sāliyar became temple donors and trustees and, by the Vijayanagara period, acted as corporate bodies, migrating when conditions were unfavourable and negotiating terms with temples and rulers (Ramaswamy 1985; Mines 1984). The silk-weavers of Madurai and other Tamil towns known as Saurāṣṭras (Paṭṭunūlkārar) speak an Indo-Aryan language related to Gujarati and trace their origin to migrations from Gujarat, probably in the later medieval period. They too moved across India in search of patrons and markets, as the Mandasor silk-weavers had done a thousand years earlier.

docs.title: 13.1.4 What Guilds Did
docs.text: From these sources we can infer that guilds regulated the work and conduct of their members, settled disputes among them, accepted deposits and endowments, made donations as corporate bodies, and in some cases maintained armed men. It is not clear how far they controlled apprenticeship or standards of workmanship, and it would be misleading to equate them simply with the craft guilds of medieval Europe or with modern trade unions. D. D. Kosambi saw the guilds as an important feature of an economy based on commodity production and trade in the early historic period, and linked their decline in the post-Gupta centuries to the growth of a more localised, village-based economy (Kosambi 1956); the timing and extent of that decline are debated.

docs.title: 13.2.1 Hereditary Occupation
docs.text:
By the late first millennium CE most crafts were practised by hereditary jātis, and the relation between jāti and occupation became a central feature of Indian society. A child born into a potter’s or weaver’s family learned the craft at home, married within the community, and was expected to follow the family occupation. This system ensured the transmission of skills, and it gave each community a recognised place and, often, a monopoly of its trade in a locality. It also confined people to occupations by birth, and ranked those occupations in a hierarchy of purity and status.

The relationship between jāti and occupation was never complete or unchanging. Many members of artisan castes have always worked as cultivators or labourers; occupations changed with new technologies and markets; and some communities, such as the Mandasor silk-weavers or the Kaikkōḷar weavers of Tamil Nadu, combined weaving with trade, soldiering or other work (Mines 1984; Bayly 1999).

docs.title: 13.2.2 Purity, Pollution and Untouchability
docs.text:
Crafts were ranked in part by notions of purity and pollution. The Brahmanical law-books declared some artisans’ food unacceptable to Brahmins (Chapter 1), and treated contact with dead animals, blood, hair and excrement as polluting. Leather-working, skinning dead animals, scavenging and sweeping were assigned to the lowest groups, who were treated as untouchable. In many regions some weaving, basket-making and drumming castes were also untouchable.

Untouchability meant more than low status. Untouchable artisans were excluded from temples, wells and schools, forced to live apart, and subjected to humiliating rules and violence. The leather-working castes, whose history is the clearest example, are the subject of Chapter 9, which also discusses Ramnarayan Rawat’s critique of the “leather-worker” stereotype and the protests that followed the Una flogging of 2016.

Scholarly Note: Ambedkar on Caste and Occupation

B. R. Ambedkar argued in Annihilation of Caste (1936) that defenders of caste confused it with the division of labour. The caste system, he wrote, is not merely a division of labour but a division of labourers into watertight compartments, graded one above the other; it assigns occupations by birth rather than by capacity, prevents people from changing occupations when technology and markets change, and so produces unemployment and degrades work. He drew particular attention to the way caste made certain kinds of work, such as scavenging, degrading by association (Ambedkar 1936). Uma Chakravarti has shown how control of women’s sexuality and marriage was central to the reproduction of caste, and therefore of hereditary occupation (Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 13.2.3 Caste in the Colonial Archive
docs.text: From the mid-nineteenth century, British administrators set out to describe and classify the castes of India. District gazetteers, ethnographic surveys and the decennial censuses recorded each caste with a “traditional occupation”; the census of 1901, under H. H. Risley, attempted to rank castes in order of social precedence. These exercises turned fluid, locally variable relationships into fixed categories and encouraged castes to organise themselves to claim higher places, often by asserting a link with a prestigious occupation or origin (Bayly 1999). Artisan castes petitioned to be recorded as Brahmins (Viśvakarma), Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas, took new names (Prajāpati for potters, Anṣārī for Muslim weavers), and founded caste associations and journals. The colonial archive is therefore both a valuable source on crafts around 1900 and an active force that shaped the identities it recorded.

docs.title: 13.2.4 Artisan Voices and Movements
docs.text:
Artisans and other working people also produced their own critiques of caste and their own visions of dignity. The bhakti poet-saints from artisan and untouchable castes, Kabīr the Julāhā weaver, Raidās (Ravidās) the Chamār leather-worker, Nāmdev the tailor and calico-printer, Gorā the potter, Senā the barber and Cokhāmeḷā the Mahār, used the imagery of their crafts and insisted that devotion, not birth, made a person worthy (Hawley and Juergensmeyer 1988). Raidās’s vision of “Begumpura”, the city without sorrow, imagines a society without caste or tax.

Several religious movements drew their following largely from artisan and labouring castes. The followers of Kabīr formed the Kabīr Panth, with monastic centres in Banaras and Chhattisgarh; the devotees of Raidās built temples and communities in Punjab and Uttar Pradesh, and in the twentieth century the Ad Dharm and later Ravidassia movements asserted a separate religious identity for Punjabi Dalits. In Chhattisgarh, the Satnāmī movement founded by Guru Ghāsīdās in the early nineteenth century rejected caste and idol worship and attracted many Chamārs. In modern times anti-caste thinkers from Jotirao Phule to Ambedkar have drawn on these traditions (Omvedt 2008). The Viśvakarma communities, with their own monasteries (maṭhas), priests and claim to sacred descent (Chapter 2), represent another form of artisan self-assertion, made from within the caste order rather than against it.

Weaving communities show how far an occupation’s meaning could be contested. In Gujarat the Vaṇkars (formerly called Dheḍs) wove coarse cotton cloth for villages and were treated as untouchable; in Maharashtra many Mahārs did the same. As mill cloth undermined coarse weaving in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, many left the craft for labour in towns, the army and the mills. The Mahār community became the core of Ambedkar’s movement, and in 1956 many Mahārs converted with him to Buddhism, rejecting the caste order that had defined their occupations. The Muslim weavers of north India, by contrast, kept the loom but rejected the name: the Momin Anṣārī movement replaced the derogatory “Julāhā” with a claim of honourable descent (Chapter 4). Leaving a craft and staying in it on new terms were both ways of refusing the place that caste assigned.

docs.title: 13.3.1 The Household Workshop
docs.text: Most crafts were practised in the household. The family was the unit of production, and children learned by watching and helping: winding bobbins, preparing clay, grinding pigments, carrying materials. As they grew older they took on more demanding tasks under the eye of a parent or an older relative, and eventually worked independently. In some crafts, such as sculpture, bronze-casting and the finer kinds of weaving and painting, a skilled master might take pupils from outside the family; the relationship between master (ustād, guru) and pupil (shāgird, śiṣya) could be close and long. Families and communities also guarded their techniques. Recipes for dyes, alloys and glazes were treated as family property and disclosed reluctantly to outsiders. This secrecy protected livelihoods, but it also meant that knowledge died with families who abandoned the craft.

docs.title: 13.3.2 The Jajmānī System
docs.text:
In many villages of north India, craftsmen and service castes (carpenters, smiths, potters, barbers, washermen and others) served a set of landowning households in return for annual payments in grain at harvest and gifts on ceremonial occasions. In Maharashtra the comparable village servants were the balutedārs, among them the carpenter, the smith, the potter and the leather-worker (Chapter 9). The American missionary William Wiser, who studied a village near Mainpuri in the 1920s, described these relationships as the “Hindu jajmani system” (from yajamāna, the patron of a sacrifice), a system of mutual obligations that bound castes together in a hereditary and reciprocal division of labour (Wiser 1936).

Later anthropologists and historians have criticised this picture. They have pointed out that the relationships were highly unequal, that patrons could withhold payment and service castes had little recourse, that much village craft was in fact paid for in cash or kind by the piece, and that the “system” was neither as ancient, as uniform nor as harmonious as Wiser suggested. C. J. Fuller argued that the very idea of a jajmānī “system” was largely a construction of observers (Fuller 1989). What is clear is that in many villages artisans’ livelihoods depended on customary relationships with dominant landowners, and that these relationships declined in the twentieth century with the spread of markets, factory goods and new opportunities outside the village.

docs.title: 13.3.3 Courts, Temples and Workshops
docs.text: Alongside household production and guild organisation, kings, temples and great households maintained their own workshops. The Arthaśāstra’s state workshops for weaving, metals and gold (Chapter 1) represent an ideal of royal control. Medieval south Indian temples employed carpenters, smiths, goldsmiths and potters, paid with shares of land and produce (Chapter 2). The Mughal emperors maintained a large establishment of imperial workshops (kārkhānas), described in Abu’l Fazl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī, which produced textiles, carpets, arms, jewellery, books and paintings for the court and for gifts (Abu’l Fazl 1873). Bernier, who described their halls in the Delhi fort (Chapter 4), also thought that the craftsmen’s skill was wasted because they were poorly paid and had little security (Bernier 1891). Regional courts, from the Rajput states to Thanjavur and Mysore, had their own workshops, and the patronage of such courts shaped styles of painting, jewellery and textiles. Court workshops brought together craftsmen of different origins, including immigrants from Iran and Central Asia, and fostered exchanges of technique and design. When courts declined, as in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, their craftsmen lost their patrons and either dispersed to other courts or turned to the market.

docs.title: 13.3.4 The Mahājans of Gujarat
docs.text: In the towns of Gujarat, associations called mahājan survived into the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Each trade or craft, such as cloth merchants, potters, carpenters or weavers, might have its own mahājan, which met under elected or hereditary heads, regulated the conduct of members, fixed holidays on which work was forbidden, settled disputes, imposed fines and supported charities such as animal shelters (pāñjrāpoḷ). Associations of the great merchants, often Jain and Vaiṣṇava Baniyas, could close the whole market of a city to put pressure on the authorities. Observers around 1900 compared these bodies with the guilds of ancient India and medieval Europe. Whatever the justice of the comparison, they are evidence that corporate organisation among merchants and artisans continued in some regions long after the period of the ancient śreṇīs.

docs.title: 13.3.5 Merchants and Artisans
docs.text: From at least the early modern period, much craft production for markets was organised by merchants, who advanced money or raw materials to artisans and bought their products. This “putting-out” or advance system gave merchants great power over artisans, but it also allowed artisans to reach distant markets. Weavers in eighteenth-century south India and Bengal negotiated with merchants and with the European companies, and could, in favourable circumstances, refuse advances or move to another territory (Parthasarathi 2001). In north Indian towns, merchant and artisan communities formed associations and neighbourhood organisations that regulated trade and supported religious and charitable institutions (Bayly 1983). For the late colonial and early independent decades, Douglas Haynes has shown how the weavers and merchants of the small towns of western India built a dense world of workshops, credit and petty capital, the beginnings of what is now called the informal economy (Haynes 2012). The colonial transformation of these relationships is the subject of the next chapter.

docs.title: 13.4 Knowledge Without Books
docs.text:
Why did so few Indian craftsmen write about their crafts? Part of the answer lies in literacy: until the twentieth century most artisans could not read Sanskrit or Persian, the languages of learned writing, and many could not read at all. Part lies in the nature of craft knowledge, much of which is embodied and tacit, learned by doing rather than by reading. Part lies in the social order. Learned treatises were written by and for literate elites, who classified and regulated crafts but rarely practised them. Sheldon Pollock has argued that Sanskrit intellectual culture held that every practice (prayoga) should be governed by a prior body of theory (śāstra), so that theory was held to come first even in fields, such as erotics, where practice obviously did (Pollock 1985). In such a culture the knowledge of texts was readily ranked above the knowledge of hands. Where artisans had access to writing, as among the Odishan stone-carvers or the Kashmiri shawl-weavers with their coded tālīm, they used it for their own purposes.

The chemist and philosopher Michael Polanyi argued that much human knowledge, from riding a bicycle to recognising a face or judging the quality of a material, is tacit, held in the body and in trained perception rather than in explicit rules (Polanyi 1958). Craft knowledge is largely of this kind. A dyer judges the readiness of an indigo vat by its colour, smell and froth; a smith judges the temperature of iron by its colour in the forge; a potter knows by touch whether clay is ready to throw. Kramrisch emphasised the craftsman’s dependence on a tradition of forms received and re-made in each generation (Kramrisch 1958). Such knowledge is acquired through long practice under the guidance of someone who already has it, and it is easily lost when the chain of transmission is broken.

Tacit does not mean unsystematic. Craftspeople experiment, compare results, adjust recipes and pass on rules of thumb; they classify materials by their working properties and have names for qualities and defects that outsiders do not notice. The double-ikat paṭolā, whose pattern depends on the precise calculation of thousands of resist-tied sections of warp and weft, or the distillation of zinc at Zawar, which required the control of a process that cannot be observed directly, show that craft knowledge could be precise, cumulative and inventive. Most craft traditions, however, lacked two things: a body of theory linking their procedures to explanations of nature, and institutions such as printing, scientific societies and laboratories through which such explanations could be tested and communicated beyond the workshop. The chief exception was rasaśāstra, which joined laboratory practice in metals and minerals to an elaborate theory, though for medical and alchemical ends rather than for the crafts (Section 13.6 and Volume 14). The absence of craft texts is therefore better understood as a different way of holding knowledge than as a sign that Indian crafts were “unscientific”: knowledge was kept in workshop routines, family recipes, oral formulas, pattern-books and drawings, and the trained perceptions of experienced workers, and it was vulnerable because it depended on the continuity of families and markets.

docs.title: 13.5 Learning a Craft: Apprenticeship, Pattern and Notation
docs.text: Craft knowledge was not carried only in hands and memories. Artisans also devised their own means of storing and passing on designs: coded scripts, pattern harnesses, wooden blocks, pounced tracings, counted formulas and memorised verses. These devices, and the forms of apprenticeship in which they were used, organised craft knowledge beyond the single household.

docs.title: 13.5.1 Master and Apprentice
docs.text: In the urban workshop crafts of north India, many of them practised by Muslim artisans, the relation between master (ustād) and apprentice (shāgird) had a vocabulary and an etiquette shared with music and wrestling (Volumes 9 and 20). An apprentice was often a relative or a neighbour’s son, received little or no pay while learning, and rose over several years from preparatory work to the loom, the embroidery frame or the engraver’s bench. The master’s name served as a credential, and a craftsman might be known as the pupil of a named master long after he had left the workshop. Apprenticeship could shade into dependence: where a master-weaver or merchant had advanced money to a family, the boy who learned in his workshop might be bound to work there until the debt was cleared. The hereditary sthapati lineages of the south and the stone-carvers of Odisha (Chapter 2) could take pupils from outside the family into a line of instruction.

docs.title: 13.5.2 The Kashmir Tālīm
docs.text:
One of the most elaborate artisans’ notations in India is the tālīm of the Kashmir shawl and carpet. In the production of the woven kānī shawl (Chapter 12), the design was drawn by a pattern-drawer (naqqāsh), a colour specialist (tarah-guru) fixed its colours, and a writer (tālīm-guru) translated the drawing into a coded script. The script specified, for each line of weaving, the colours to be used and the number of warp threads over which each was to be woven. The weavers followed the tālīm rather than the drawing, and the master of the loom read it out to them as they worked. The system separated design from execution: a design could be copied, altered, sent from one workshop to another, and woven by men who had never seen the drawing. It also created a hierarchy within the craft, in which the designer and the writer of the tālīm were well paid and the weavers, many of them bound to their employers by debt and heavily taxed by the state, were poor (Irwin 1973; Ames 1986).

Kashmiri carpet-weavers use the same method. The carpet tālīm, written on strips of paper in symbols for colours and numbers of knots, is chanted line by line by the head weaver, and the weavers repeat their part as they tie the knots. A carpet of great complexity can thus be woven by people who never see its design as a picture. The tālīm is a notation devised and owned by artisans, outside the learned scripts of Sanskrit and Persian; like the syllables of the drummer (Volume 9), it is precise because the work required precision.

docs.title: 13.5.3 The Pattern Harness and the Punched Card
docs.text: On the drawloom (Section 4.4) the design was stored not on paper but in the loom itself. A pattern-maker (naqshaband) worked from a design drawn on squared paper, in which each square stood for a group of warp threads and a pick of weft, and tied the pattern into the harness of cords, a task that could take weeks for a complex border. The finished naqsha could be taken off one loom, stored, lent or sold, and tied onto another: it was an object that embodied a design. When the Jacquard mechanism was adopted in Banaras and other centres in the early twentieth century, the same squared designs were transferred to sets of punched cards cut by card-punchers. Since the 1990s, designs have increasingly been prepared on computers, which print the cards or drive electronic Jacquards directly. Each of these changes has moved control of the design further from the weaver at the loom, towards the pattern-maker, the card-puncher, the computer designer and the merchant who commissions the work.

docs.title: 13.5.4 Blocks, Tracings and Samples
docs.text: Other crafts stored designs in their tools. A printer’s blocks are the pattern-book of the workshop: the set of blocks for a design may be kept for generations, and a design can be reproduced as long as its blocks survive (Chapter 5). Painters kept pounced tracings (charbā), through which compositions passed from father to son (Chapter 11). Designs also arrived from outside. From the seventeenth century the European companies sent patterns and samples to the Coromandel painters and printers to copy, and the Indian workshops adapted them to their own techniques (Crill 2008). In the opposite direction, John Forbes Watson’s The Textile Manufactures and the Costumes of the People of India (1866) was accompanied by sets of bound volumes of actual Indian cloth samples, distributed in Britain and India so that manufacturers could study, and imitate, the cloths that Indian buyers wanted (Watson 1866).

docs.title: 13.5.5 Counting and Memory
docs.text:
In women’s counted-thread embroidery the pattern is held as a count, not as a drawing. The kasūti of the Dharwad region of Karnataka (Chapter 12) is worked in four stitches: the double running stitch gavanti, the zigzag running stitch murgi, the darning stitch negi and the cross-stitch menthi. Its motifs of temple towers, chariots, lamps and birds are built up by counting the threads of the ground cloth, so that the double running stitch looks the same on both sides. The sūf embroiderers of Kutch likewise compose each motif by counting, planning its geometry in their heads as they work from the back of the cloth (Frater 1995). Such patterns are learned by sitting beside an experienced embroiderer and by copying older pieces, and they are remembered as sequences of counts and movements rather than as pictures. The same is true of the kōlam designs drawn on thresholds in Tamil Nadu, which girls learn from their mothers as rules for drawing lines around a grid of dots.

Image-makers learned iconography from meditation verses (dhyāna), which describe the posture, attributes, ornaments and colour of each form of a deity, and from proportional rules counted in tāla units (Chapter 2). Measuring cords and sticks marked with the units carried the system from the text into the workshop. The verse was memorised, and the cord and stick did the counting, so that a sculptor could reproduce a canonical form without consulting a manuscript.

docs.title: 13.5.6 From Workshop to Institution
docs.text: Since independence, the state and voluntary bodies have tried to reproduce apprenticeship in institutional form. They have set up training centres attached to the handicrafts and handloom boards, schemes that pay master craftspeople to teach pupils from outside their families, and schools such as the college of sculpture at Mamallapuram (Chapter 2). Soumhya Venkatesan’s study of the Labbai Muslim mat-weavers of Pattamadai in Tamil Nadu (Chapter 8) shows how such programmes, and the language of national heritage that comes with them, change what counts as craft knowledge and who is recognised as holding it. The weavers had to meet the expectations of officials, designers and buyers as well as those of their own families (Venkatesan 2009). Opening a craft to learners outside the hereditary community also raises a further question, taken up in Chapter 15: whether skills once protected by birth can be taught to anyone without undermining the livelihoods of those who hold them.

docs.title: 13.6 Craft and Science
docs.text: Was Indian craft knowledge a form of science? Colonial writers sometimes contrasted the “empirical” skill of the Indian craftsman with the “scientific” knowledge of the European, as if the craftsman merely repeated what his ancestors had done. Some modern writers go to the opposite extreme, claiming that ancient Indian craftsmen possessed secret sciences that anticipated modern physics or nanotechnology. Neither view does justice to the evidence. Indian learned traditions had their own theories of matter, in Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Jain and Buddhist philosophy, in Āyurveda and in rasaśāstra (Volumes 3, 13 and 14), but these were developed largely by and for learned specialists, and their connection with the practical knowledge of dyers, smiths and potters was usually loose. The history of Indian metallurgy and chemistry is told in Volume 14; this section looks only at the meeting of crafts with mechanical learning, with European science and with modern archaeometry.

docs.title: 13.6.1 Machines in the Texts
docs.text: Sanskrit literature knows the skilled maker of mechanical devices (yantra). The eleventh-century architectural treatise Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, attributed to King Bhoja of Dhārā, has a chapter on yantras describing, in general terms, mechanical figures that move, birds that fly or sing, devices that pour water and fountains for pleasure gardens. Story literature tells of wonderful automata: in the Pañcatantra, a weaver in love with a princess has his friend, a carpenter, make him a wooden Garuḍa that can fly, and he visits her in the guise of Viṣṇu; in Buddhist and Jain stories, craftsmen make mechanical dolls and flying contraptions. Such descriptions show admiration for the ingenuity of craftsmen and a lively interest in mechanical marvels, especially for courtly entertainment. They are not technical specifications, and attempts to read them as evidence of ancient aircraft or advanced machinery misunderstand their genre (Chapter 2). The practical devices of the crafts and the fields are better documented: water-lifting wheels, including the geared “Persian wheel” with a chain of pots, which spread in north India from about the thirteenth century, oil presses, sugar-cane mills, cotton gins, spinning wheels, looms and lathes. Irfan Habib’s survey of the period from about 650 to 1750 brings the evidence for these together (Habib 2008).

docs.title: 13.6.2 European Observers
docs.text:
From the seventeenth century, Europeans in India observed and recorded Indian techniques that they wished to understand, imitate or exploit, and some of their accounts are among the best evidence we have for Indian crafts before the colonial transformation. The records of chintz-making at Pondicherry made for French readers by Beaulieu and Cœurdoux are described in Chapter 5; European printers learned mordant printing partly from such accounts and partly from Armenian and other intermediaries (Irwin and Brett 1970; Riello 2013).

In the 1790s, Helenus Scott, a physician in Bombay, sent samples of Indian “wootz” steel to Sir Joseph Banks, President of the Royal Society. The chemist George Pearson analysed them and reported to the Society in 1795 on this remarkable steel and its properties (Pearson 1795). Francis Buchanan, travelling through Mysore and Malabar for the East India Company in 1800–01, described iron smelting and crucible steel-making in detail (Buchanan 1807). In 1819–22 Michael Faraday, working with the cutler James Stodart at the Royal Institution, analysed wootz and experimented with alloys of steel in an attempt to reproduce its qualities; this work was a step towards the scientific study of alloy steels (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004).

In 1971 the Gandhian historian Dharampal published a collection of eighteenth-century European accounts of Indian science and technology, including descriptions of iron smelting, the manufacture of ice at Allahabad by evaporation on cold nights, the drill plough, and inoculation against smallpox in Bengal (Dharampal 1971). The collection did much to correct the colonial picture of Indian technical backwardness, though it should be read alongside the Indian sources and the critical scholarship of later historians. Kapil Raj has argued more generally that modern science was not simply carried from Europe to India, but was in important respects made through encounters in which Indian practitioners, informants and intermediaries took an active part (Raj 2007). The same is true of crafts: Europeans who wrote about Indian dyeing, steel or textiles depended on the craftsmen who showed them their work, and whose names they seldom recorded.

docs.title: 13.6.3 Modern Study and Its Uses
docs.text:
Since the mid-twentieth century, scientists in India and abroad have studied historical Indian materials with the methods of archaeometry: chemical and isotopic analysis, metallography, electron microscopy and radiocarbon dating. The results described in earlier chapters, from the dating of Indian textiles found in Egypt and Indonesia to the reconstruction of zinc distillation at Zawar and of crucible steel, have often been won with the help of craftspeople, as when bladesmiths, bead-makers or dyers have reproduced historical materials for scientists. Conservation science is another meeting-point: laboratories such as the National Research Laboratory for Conservation of Cultural Property, founded at Lucknow in 1976, study textiles, paintings, metals and manuscripts and often consult the people who still make such objects. The earlier, nationalist history of Indian science and chemistry, begun by P. C. Ray and Brajendranath Seal, is discussed in Volume 14.

Careful study of this kind is also the best answer to the myths that gather around Indian crafts: claims that the Delhi pillar is “rust-free” or that wootz was deliberate “nanotechnology” (Chapter 3), that Dhaka muslin had thread-counts beyond any modern cloth (Chapter 4), that vāstu encodes magnetic “energies” (Chapter 2), or that the British cut off the weavers’ thumbs (Chapter 14). The real achievements are remarkable enough, and exaggeration only obscures them. Craft knowledge also has present uses that deserve testing rather than assumption. Natural dyeing and handloom weaving are models of low-energy production, and building techniques such as kāṭh-kuṇī are studied for their behaviour in earthquakes; but traditional techniques have their own costs, from the pollution of dye-works and tanneries to the silicosis of stone-carvers. The relationship worth building is one in which craftspeople are treated as holders of knowledge and partners in research, not merely as informants, and share in its benefits.

docs.title: 13.7 Women’s and Children’s Work
docs.text:
Women’s labour has been essential to almost every Indian craft, but it has often been invisible. In many crafts work was divided by gender: men threw pots on the wheel, women prepared clay and painted; men wove, women spun, wound and sized the yarn; men worked the forge, women worked the bellows. Some crafts, such as embroidery, quilting, floor- and wall-painting, and many forms of basketry and weaving in the North-East, were largely women’s work, done for the household and for gifts and dowries before they entered the market. State employment of women spinners is as old as the Arthaśāstra (Chapter 4).

These divisions were customary, not natural. In much of India women were kept from particular tools, the potter’s wheel, the loom of the professional weaver, the smith’s anvil, the sculptor’s chisel, and the exclusion was often explained in terms of ritual purity or of the sacredness of the tool, which was worshipped at festivals such as Viśvakarma Pūjā (Chapter 2). Yet the same tasks were women’s work elsewhere: in Assam, Manipur and the hill societies of the North-East the loom belongs to women (Chapter 4), among the Hira of Assam women build pots by hand (Chapter 6), and in Kashmir it is men who embroider (Chapter 12). Within a single craft, too, the stages were divided. In bāndhaṇī, the thousands of tiny knots are tied by women and girls at home, and the dyeing is done by men in the workshop; in many weaving households women wound, sized and warped the yarn that men wove. The stages done by women were usually those done at home and paid by the piece, and they were the ones least often recorded, credited or named.

Women also carried much of the knowledge of transmission. Girls learned embroidery, floor-painting and household weaving from their mothers and grandmothers, often by working on the textiles of their own dowries, so that learning a craft and preparing for marriage were the same process. Such knowledge passed outside the guild, the workshop and the caste council, through which men’s craft knowledge was organised, and it left few written traces. It is known mostly from the objects themselves and from modern ethnography (Frater 1995). When women’s crafts became commercial, women were frequently paid least, as in the home-based chikan embroidery of Lucknow (Chapter 4). Organisations such as the Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA), founded in Ahmedabad in 1972, have organised home-based women workers, including embroiderers, to improve their bargaining position (Chapter 15).

In household production, children worked from an early age, and their labour was part of the way skills were transmitted. In the commercial craft industries of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, however, the employment of children often had little to do with learning a family craft. Children were employed in large numbers in carpet-weaving, where their small fingers were valued for knotting; in glass-bangle making at Firozabad; in match and firework factories; in gem-polishing and in brassware workshops, often in hazardous conditions and sometimes in bondage to employers who had advanced money to their parents. Campaigns by Indian and international organisations from the 1980s, laws such as the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act of 1986 and its later amendments, labelling schemes and the expansion of schooling have reduced child labour in these industries, but not eliminated it. Any account of Indian crafts that celebrates the skill of child artisans without considering their conditions repeats the romanticism this volume tries to avoid.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For guilds and traders, Chakravarti (2002); for the Gupta inscriptions, Fleet (1888); for weavers in medieval south India, Ramaswamy (1985); for caste in modern history, Bayly (1999); for Ambedkar’s critique, Ambedkar (1936); for anti-caste thought, Omvedt (2008); for the jajmānī debate, Wiser (1936) and Fuller (1989); for artisans and merchants in western India, Haynes (2012); on theory and practice in Sanskrit learning, Pollock (1985); on tacit knowledge, Polanyi (1958); on the Kashmir tālīm, Irwin (1973); on craft, training and development, Venkatesan (2009); on medieval technology, Habib (2008); on European accounts of Indian technology, Dharampal (1971); on the circulation of knowledge between India and Europe, Raj (2007).

docs.title: Chapter 14: Crafts in the Colonial Economy
docs.text: Between the mid-eighteenth and the mid-twentieth centuries, the Indian craft economy was transformed. The East India Company, from a trading company, became the ruler of Bengal and then of most of India; British factory goods, above all cotton cloth, flooded Indian markets; and many artisan industries declined, while others adapted and some new ones grew. Nationalists from the late nineteenth century onwards made the ruin of Indian crafts a central charge against British rule, and the spinning wheel became the symbol of the freedom movement. This chapter examines what happened, how historians have measured and debated it, and how a famous myth, that of the muslin weavers’ severed thumbs, arose.

docs.title: 14.1 India in the Eighteenth-Century World Economy
docs.text:
In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, South Asia was one of the world’s largest producers of manufactured goods, and its cotton textiles were exported in great quantities to Southeast Asia, West Asia, East Africa and, through the European companies, to Europe, West Africa and the Americas (Chaudhuri 1978; Riello and Roy 2009). Two sets of estimates are often quoted to show the scale of this economy:

  • Angus Maddison estimated that India accounted for about a quarter of world GDP around 1700, falling to about 16 per cent in 1820 and under 5 per cent by 1950 (Maddison 2001). These figures largely reflect the size of India’s population; they do not measure productivity or living standards.

  • Paul Bairoch estimated that the Indian subcontinent produced roughly a quarter of the world’s manufactures in 1750, falling to under 2 per cent by 1900, while Britain’s share rose from about 2 per cent to nearly a fifth (Bairoch 1982); his figures are given in Table 14.1.

Table 14.1. Bairoch’s estimates of shares of world manufacturing output (per cent) Year Indian subcontinent United Kingdom China 1750 24.5 1.9 32.8 1800 19.7 4.3 33.3 1830 17.6 9.5 29.8 1860 8.6 19.9 19.7 1880 2.8 22.9 12.5 1900 1.7 18.5 6.2

Source: Bairoch (1982). The figures for the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries are rough estimates, based largely on assumptions about population and per capita consumption of manufactures.

Both sets of figures are estimates, and economic historians use them with caution. They do show, however, that the relative position of Indian manufacturing changed dramatically in the nineteenth century, in part because Britain industrialised and in part because Indian handicraft industries declined.

docs.title: 14.2.1 From Trade to Rule
docs.text:
Until the mid-eighteenth century, the European companies bought Indian textiles in competition with Indian and other Asian merchants, through brokers who advanced money to weavers. After the battle of Plassey (1757) and the grant of the revenue administration (dīvānī) of Bengal in 1765, the English Company used its political power to secure cloth on its own terms. Its agents (gumāśtas) forced advances on weavers, bound them to deliver only to the Company, fixed low prices, and used peons to confine, fine and beat weavers who failed to deliver or tried to sell to others. Company regulations from the 1770s and 1780s gave legal backing to many of these practices (Hossain 1988). In south India, Prasannan Parthasarathi has shown how the Company’s new controls eroded the bargaining power that weavers had previously enjoyed (Parthasarathi 2001).

The great Bengal famine of 1769–70, which killed a large part of the population of the province in the first years of Company rule, fell heavily on weavers, spinners and other artisans, who depended on buying grain in the market. Famine and scarcity recurred throughout the colonial period, and artisans, who had no land to fall back on, were among the first to suffer.

These coercive practices were described at the time by critics of the Company, among them William Bolts, a former Company servant, whose Considerations on India Affairs (1772) is one of the most detailed contemporary accounts (Bolts 1772).

docs.title: 14.2.2 The Myth of the Severed Thumbs
docs.text:
A story widely repeated in India holds that the British cut off the thumbs of the muslin weavers of Dhaka to destroy their craft. The story is not supported by any documentary evidence. It appears to derive from a misreading of a passage in Bolts’s book, which describes the oppression of the winders of raw silk in Bengal (whom he calls “Nagaads”), and reports that some of them had cut off their own thumbs to escape being forced to wind silk for the Company (Bolts 1772). Over time, in nationalist writing and popular memory, this account of self-mutilation by silk-winders became a story of mutilation by the British of the weavers of Dhaka muslin.

The myth should be abandoned, not because the Company’s treatment of weavers was benign, but because the documented reality is serious enough. Weavers were coerced by advances, confined, fined and flogged; they lost the freedom to sell to the highest bidder; and their earnings fell (Hossain 1988; Parthasarathi 2001). The decline of the Dhaka muslin industry in the early nineteenth century had several causes: the loss of Mughal court patronage, the Company’s purchasing regime, British tariffs on Indian cloth, and above all the arrival of cheap machine-made cloth from Lancashire.

docs.title: 14.3 Tariffs and Machine-Made Cloth
docs.text:
By the late eighteenth century British manufacturers, having learned to print, dye and finally spin and weave cotton by machine, could compete with Indian cloth in Britain and in third markets. Indian cottons entering Britain had long faced heavy duties or prohibition. The historian H. H. Wilson, writing in the 1850s, remarked that in the early nineteenth century Indian cotton and silk goods could have been sold profitably in Britain at much lower prices than British goods, and that British manufactures had to be protected by duties of 70–80 per cent or by prohibition; Romesh Chunder Dutt, who quoted him, made the contrast between British protection at home and enforced free trade in India a central argument of his Economic History of India (1902) (Dutt 1902). British goods, by contrast, entered India at low duties after the end of the Company’s trading monopoly in 1813; the remaining cotton import duties were abolished in 1882, and when they were reimposed in the 1890s for revenue, an equivalent excise was levied on cloth from Indian mills.

Imports of British cotton cloth and yarn into India grew rapidly from the 1820s, and by the later nineteenth century Lancashire cloth dominated the market for ordinary cloth. Handloom weavers lost much of their market, especially for plain cloth; spinners, most of them women working at home, lost almost all of theirs as handloom weavers turned to cheap machine-spun yarn.

docs.title: 14.4 The Drain and the Weaver
docs.text: Nationalist economists connected the fate of Indian crafts with a broader critique of colonial rule. Dadabhai Naoroji argued that a large part of India’s revenue was transferred to Britain each year, without equivalent return, in the form of the salaries and pensions of officials, interest on debt, the costs of the army and the profits of British firms: the “drain” of wealth from India (Naoroji 1901). Romesh Chunder Dutt added a detailed history of land revenue, famine and the decline of manufactures. In their view, the ruin of the weaver was one part of a system that impoverished India for Britain’s benefit (Dutt 1902). Later economic historians have debated the size of the drain and its effects, but the critique shaped Indian economic thought and policy for decades, including the protection of handlooms and village industries after independence.

docs.title: 14.5 The Deindustrialisation Debate
docs.text:
The nationalist case, set out in Naoroji’s Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) and in Dutt’s histories, was that British rule had “deindustrialised” India, destroying its manufactures and forcing artisans back onto the land. Later historians have debated the extent and causes of this decline.

  • Amiya Kumar Bagchi, using the surveys of Francis Buchanan-Hamilton for Gangetic Bihar in the 1810s and the census of 1901, argued that the share of the population dependent on industry roughly halved over the nineteenth century, a clear case of deindustrialisation (Bagchi 1976).

  • Morris D. Morris and others questioned the reliability of such comparisons and argued that handloom weaving survived on a larger scale than nationalists assumed (Morris 1963).

  • Tirthankar Roy has shown that many “traditional” industries adapted rather than disappeared: handloom weavers specialised in products the mills could not make cheaply, such as saris with complex borders, used mill yarn, adopted improved looms, and in some regions expanded their output in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries (Roy 1993, 1999).

  • The Cambridge Economic History of India surveys the evidence for the period as a whole (Kumar 1983).

The picture that emerges is of severe and uneven decline. Cotton spinning by hand collapsed; plain cloth weaving lost much of its market; iron smelting, paper-making and many other crafts dwindled; luxury crafts lost their courtly patrons. At the same time some handicrafts adapted and some new industries, such as carpets for export, grew; and from the 1850s Indian entrepreneurs built cotton mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad, so that by the early twentieth century India had a substantial modern textile industry of its own. Artisans who could not adapt fell into poverty, and many joined the ranks of landless labourers.

docs.title: 14.6 Other Crafts under Colonial Rule
docs.text:
The fate of crafts other than cotton weaving varied.

Iron and steel Village iron smelting declined steeply in the second half of the nineteenth century, as cheap imported iron and steel, carried by the railways, reached rural markets, and as forest laws restricted access to charcoal. Crucible steel production also ended. The first large modern steelworks in India, the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur, began production in 1911–12. Paper Hand-made paper was displaced by machine-made paper, both imported and, from the later nineteenth century, made in Indian mills. Shipbuilding Indian shipwrights built large ships for the East India Company and for Indian merchants at Bombay, Surat and on the Hughli in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries; the Wadia master-builders of Bombay built ships for the Royal Navy (Wadia 1955). The coming of iron and steam ships in the mid-nineteenth century, and the preference for British yards, ended this industry. Luxury crafts The decline of Indian courts and aristocracies after the Company’s conquests deprived many craftsmen of patrons. At the same time, new markets appeared among Europeans in India and abroad, for whom craftsmen produced “art wares” adapted to European taste: carved furniture, ivory and metal souvenirs, embroidered goods and shawls. New industries Some crafts expanded: carpet-weaving for export, the Firozabad glass bangle industry, and the brass industry of Moradabad grew in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, often using imported materials such as sheet brass and glass.

Tirthankar Roy’s study of several craft industries in the late colonial period, among them handloom weaving, silk, wool and leather, shows a pattern of change rather than simple decline: some branches of each industry collapsed, others adapted to new markets and new materials, labour relations became more commercial, and workshops employing wage labour grew at the expense of independent artisans (Roy 1999).

docs.title: 14.7 The Indian Cotton Mills
docs.text: Indian entrepreneurs answered British competition by building their own mills. The first successful cotton-spinning mill in Bombay was founded by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar in 1854, and Ranchhodlal Chhotalal opened the first mill in Ahmedabad in 1861. By the early twentieth century Bombay and Ahmedabad were great textile cities, with mills owned largely by Parsi, Gujarati Hindu, Jain and Muslim entrepreneurs. Their workforce included many people from weaving and other artisan castes who had lost their livelihoods, as well as migrants from agricultural communities. The mills competed with the handloom weavers for the market in coarse cloth, but they also supplied the weavers with yarn. In Ahmedabad, a dispute between millworkers and owners in 1918, in which Gandhi intervened, led to the foundation of the Textile Labour Association, a union based on Gandhian principles of arbitration, in which Anasuya Sarabhai played a leading role. The history of Indian textiles thus continued into the industrial age, with many of the same communities.

docs.title: 14.8 The Princely States
docs.text: Some princely states pursued their own policies towards crafts and industry. In Mysore, the state promoted sericulture and silk weaving, establishing a government silk-weaving factory in 1912, and the Mysore government’s industrial programme under the engineer-administrator M. Visvesvaraya (Dewan 1912–1918) included support for traditional as well as modern industries. Baroda under Sayajirao Gaekwad III (r. 1875–1939) founded the Kala Bhavan technical institute (1890), which taught both modern technology and the arts. Travancore, Hyderabad, Jaipur and other states maintained schools of art and crafts, museums and emporia. The princely states were not immune from the pressures of the colonial economy, but under some of them crafts and industry were deliberately fostered rather than left to decline.

docs.title: 14.9 Indigo and Cotton
docs.text:
Colonial rule also turned some craft materials into plantation and export crops. Indigo was grown in Bengal and Bihar under the control of European planters, who forced peasants to cultivate it on unfavourable terms. In 1859–60 the cultivators of Bengal rose in the “Indigo Revolt”; Dinabandhu Mitra’s play Nīl Darpaṇ (1860) dramatised their sufferings. In Champaran in Bihar, Gandhi’s first satyagraha in India (1917) was against the system that compelled tenants to grow indigo on part of their land. Synthetic indigo, marketed from 1897, ended the plantation industry in the following decades.

During the American Civil War (1861–65), when supplies of American raw cotton to Lancashire were cut off, cotton cultivation expanded rapidly in western India, and Bombay experienced a speculative boom that collapsed in 1865. Sven Beckert’s global history of cotton places the episode in a longer story, in which British and other states pressed India, Egypt and other regions to grow raw cotton for the mills of Europe while buying their cloth (Beckert 2014). India’s place in the world economy had been reversed: from the great exporter of cotton cloth it had become a supplier of raw cotton and a market for Lancashire.

docs.title: 14.10 Exhibitions, Art Schools and the Idea of “Indian Art Manufactures”
docs.text:
Paradoxically, the colonial state also became a collector and promoter of Indian crafts. Indian textiles, metalwork, jewellery and carvings were displayed at the Great Exhibition of 1851 in London and at many later exhibitions, and were acquired for the South Kensington Museum (later the Victoria and Albert Museum). George Birdwood’s The Industrial Arts of India (1880) praised Indian “art manufactures” as the products of a timeless village craftsman and deplored their corruption by European taste (Birdwood 1880). Schools of art were founded at Madras, Calcutta, Bombay and Lahore in the 1850s–1870s, partly to improve Indian design for the market; John Lockwood Kipling at Lahore and others collected and documented crafts. Abigail McGowan has shown how these colonial projects shaped the very idea of “Indian crafts” as a national heritage, an idea that nationalists then took up (McGowan 2009).

The Delhi Durbar of 1903, held to celebrate the accession of Edward VII, included a large exhibition of Indian art industries, organised by the economic botanist George Watt, whose catalogue surveyed the crafts of every province and lamented their decline under the influence of European taste and cheap imports (Watt 1903). From 1884 to 1917 the Journal of Indian Art, published in London, documented Indian crafts in illustrated articles, and provincial governments commissioned monographs on particular industries, such as cotton fabrics, silk, brass and copper ware, pottery, and wood-carving, in each province around 1900. These works, often written by district officers with the help of local informants, remain important sources, though they share the assumption that Indian crafts were static traditions in decline.

Ananda Coomaraswamy’s The Indian Craftsman (1909) drew on the British Arts and Crafts movement of William Morris and on his own studies of Ceylonese and Indian crafts to argue that the Indian craftsman, working within a guild and a religious tradition, embodied a way of life superior to industrial labour (Coomaraswamy 1909). His idealised picture paid little attention to caste hierarchy, but it gave Indian craft a philosophical dignity that strongly influenced later revivalists.

docs.title: 14.11 Svadeśī and Khādī
docs.text:
The Svadeśī movement in Bengal (1903–1908), launched in protest against Lord Curzon’s partition of the province in 1905, called for the boycott of British goods and the use of Indian ones. It encouraged handloom weaving and Indian enterprise, and its leaders included Surendranath Banerjea, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghose in Bengal, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai elsewhere. Rabindranath Tagore composed songs for the movement and organised the tying of rākhīs as a symbol of unity on the day the partition took effect (Sarkar 1973).

Sumit Sarkar distinguished two strands in the movement: the boycott of foreign goods, and “constructive Svadeśī”, the effort to build Indian industries, crafts and institutions in their place (Sarkar 1973). Both touched the crafts directly. Manchester cloth was the main target of the boycott, and imports of British piece-goods into Bengal fell in the first years of the agitation. Volunteers picketed shops, and in some places women gave up imported glass bangles along with foreign cloth. Swadeshi stores opened in Calcutta and the district towns to sell Indian-made cloth, soap, matches, cutlery and other goods. Some of these, such as the store opened in Calcutta by Saraladevi Chaudhurani, sold goods made by women at home.

The movement raised the demand for Indian cloth, but its benefits were unevenly shared. Sarkar showed that much of the cloth sold as svadeśī came from the mills of Bombay and Ahmedabad, whose owners profited more from the boycott than Bengal’s handloom weavers did. Handloom weaving nonetheless revived in parts of Bengal, helped by the fly-shuttle (Section 4.4) and by weaving schools. New Bengali enterprises were also founded, among them the Banga Lakshmi Cotton Mills (1906). The National Council of Education and the Bengal Technical Institute, both founded in 1906 and merged in 1910, set out to train Indians in technology and the industrial crafts; together they were the forerunners of Jadavpur University. In the same years Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, with British admirers of Indian art, founded the Indian Society of Oriental Art (1907), which promoted an “Indian” art drawing on Mughal, Rajput and Ajanta painting and, later, on folk and craft traditions (Chapter 11).

The boycott also had a coercive side. Poor traders, many of them Muslim, who depended on selling cheap foreign cloth, were pressed or forced to give it up, and the burning of their goods caused bitterness. Rabindranath Tagore, who had at first composed songs for the movement, withdrew from it. In his novel Ghare Baire (The Home and the World, 1916) the forced burning of a poor trader’s foreign cloth is one of the episodes through which he criticised nationalist zeal (Volume 24). The arguments of the Svadeśī years about whether to boycott or to build, about mill and handloom, and about whom the movement served, were taken up again, on a much larger scale, in the Gandhian campaign for khādī.

M. K. Gandhi made hand-spinning and hand-woven cloth (khādī) the centre of the national movement from the early 1920s. In Hind Swaraj (1909) he had condemned machinery as a symbol of modern civilisation (Gandhi 1997); in practice he called for the boycott and burning of foreign cloth, spun daily himself, and founded the All India Spinners’ Association (1925) and the All India Village Industries Association (1934). For Gandhi, the spinning wheel offered rural people, especially women, supplementary income during the agricultural off-season, and it symbolised self-reliance and the dignity of manual labour. A spinning wheel was placed at the centre of the flag adopted by the Congress, and was replaced by the Aśokan wheel in the national flag of 1947. Khādī was, however, more expensive than mill cloth, and its economic impact was limited; its political and symbolic significance was immense. C. A. Bayly has shown how the politics of khādī drew on older Indian ideas about the moral and physical properties of cloth (Bayly 1986).

docs.title: 14.12 The Charkhā and the Making of Khādī
docs.text: The khādī movement was a craft programme as well as a political one. To make cloth by hand on a national scale, the movement had to recover skills that had almost disappeared. It had to organise spinners, carders and weavers, improve their tools, fix prices and wages, and guarantee to buyers that the cloth was what it claimed to be. This section looks at that practical work. Gandhi’s economic and political thought, and the arguments of his critics, are treated in Volumes 19 and 24.

docs.title: 14.12.1 Recovering a Lost Skill
docs.text: Gandhi recalled in his autobiography that when he praised the spinning wheel in Hind Swaraj in 1909, he had not yet seen one (Gandhi 1927). His ashram at Ahmedabad, founded in 1915, began by weaving on handlooms with mill-spun yarn, because neither a wheel nor a spinner could be found. In 1917 or soon after, Gangabehn Majmundar, a widow who had joined his work, found spinning wheels lying unused in the lofts of houses at Vijapur in the princely state of Baroda. She also found women there who were willing to spin again if someone supplied them with slivers (pūnī) of carded cotton and bought their yarn. At first the slivers came from a mill. Only later was a carder engaged, so that the whole process, from raw cotton to cloth, could be done by hand. Within a century, hand-spinning had declined so far in western India that a national movement had to search for it (Section 14.3); yet the skill had survived in the hands of older women, who taught it to the movement’s volunteers.

docs.title: 14.12.2 From Ashram to Organisation
docs.text:
During the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–22, khādī became the visible sign of commitment to the national cause. Foreign cloth was burned in public bonfires, and in September 1921, at Madurai, Gandhi gave up the shirt and cap for a loincloth and shawl. He explained that while khādī was scarce, those who could not obtain enough of it should make do with less. Congress office-holders were expected to wear khādī, and in 1924 the Congress briefly made the spinning of a monthly quota of yarn a condition of membership.

The All India Spinners’ Association (Akhil Bhāratīya Carkhā Saṅgh), founded in 1925, turned these commitments into an organisation. It bought cotton and distributed it to spinners, often as slivers, and paid for their yarn according to its count and evenness. It gave the yarn to weavers to be woven for a wage, and sold the cloth through its own shops (khādī bhaṇḍār) and at exhibitions held alongside the annual sessions of the Congress. It also certified producers and shops, so that buyers could trust that “khādī” was hand-spun as well as hand-woven, a guarantee that mill cloth sold under nationalist labels could not give. Lisa Trivedi has shown how the Association’s exhibitions, travelling displays, photographs and printed images created a shared visual language of the nation, in which the spinning wheel, the white cap and the hand-spun cloth stood for self-rule (Trivedi 2007). Some regions produced khādī of great fineness. At Ponduru in coastal Andhra, fine yarn is still spun from local cotton that, as in Dhaka, is cleaned with the jaw-bone of a fish (Section 4.7).

The economics were difficult. Spinning paid very little, and khādī cost more than mill cloth. In the mid-1930s Gandhi persuaded the Association to raise spinners’ wages towards a “living wage”, even though this raised prices and reduced sales. He also placed growing weight on self-sufficiency (svāvalambana): households and villages spinning for their own needs rather than for the market.

docs.title: 14.12.3 Improving the Wheel
docs.text:
The village spinning wheel had a single spindle driven by a cord from a large hand-turned wheel. The spinner turned the wheel with one hand and drew out the yarn with the other, and her output was small. The movement spent much effort on improving the tools. Maganlal Gandhi, a younger kinsman of Gandhi and the manager of the Sabarmati ashram until his death in 1928, worked on the wheel and on carding. In 1929 the Association offered a prize of one lakh rupees for a wheel that would allow a spinner to earn substantially more at home under stated conditions; it does not appear to have been awarded. Gandhi’s own contribution was the compact box wheel (peṭī carkhā; Figure 14.1), associated with his imprisonment at Yeravda in the early 1930s, which folded into a case small enough to carry on journeys. For schoolchildren and travellers the movement promoted the simple hand spindle (takalī), which became part of the curriculum of Gandhian basic education (Chapter 15).

Figure 14.1. A box spinning wheel (peṭī carkhā) of the 1920s or 1930s, opened out. The pair of wheels on the right drives, by a cord, the spindle on the left, where the spun yarn is wound (Textile Museum, George Washington University, Washington). Photo: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

After independence the most important change was the multi-spindle Ambar charkhā. It was developed by E. Ekambaranathan of Tamil Nadu, whose name it carries, and adopted in the mid-1950s by the All India Khadi and Village Industries Board, the predecessor of the Commission. With four spindles and drafting rollers it greatly increased output. It needed evenly prepared slivers, which were made by machine, and this raised the question of how much machinery khādī could include while remaining khādī. Later models added more spindles. The debate, about where the line between hand and machine should be drawn, continues in handloom policy today (Section 15.2).

docs.title: 14.12.4 Meanings and Limits
docs.text:
Khādī had critics from the start. Rabindranath Tagore’s essay “The Cult of the Charka” (1925) questioned whether mechanical spinning could free the mind, and Gandhi replied in “The Poet and the Charkha” in Young India later that year (Bhattacharya 1997). Economists pointed to the low returns of hand-spinning, and B. R. Ambedkar rejected the idealisation of the village economy (Volume 19). Even among nationalists, wearing coarse, heavy khādī was a sacrifice. Emma Tarlo has shown how men and women negotiated it, and how khādī was refined over the following decades into finer and more varied cloths (Tarlo 1996). Its achievement was not economic. It brought very large numbers of people, many of them women, into the national movement through a daily act of making. It joined the politics of independence to the fate of the poorest craft workers, and it gave Indian handmade cloth a symbolic standing that it has kept. After independence khādī remained the customary dress of politicians. Until the Flag Code was amended at the end of 2021, the national flag itself had to be made of hand-spun, hand-woven khādī.

Modern Relevance: At Independence

At independence in 1947, millions of Indians still depended on handicrafts and handloom weaving, most of them in poverty. The new state created the All India Handicrafts Board (1952), the All India Handloom Board, and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (1957), and reserved certain products for the handloom sector. The story of these institutions and of the craft revival they supported is taken up in the next chapter.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the Company and the Bengal weavers, Hossain (1988); for south India, Parthasarathi (2001); for the global context, Parthasarathi (2011) and Riello (2013); for the deindustrialisation debate, Bagchi (1976) and Roy (1999); for the nationalist critique, Dutt (1902); for colonial and nationalist ideas of craft, McGowan (2009); for Svadeśī, Sarkar (1973); for the beginnings of khādī, Gandhi (1927); for khādī and the visual culture of the nation, Trivedi (2007).

docs.title: Chapter 15: Living Crafts: Revival, Protection and the Present
docs.text: India still has one of the largest populations of craftspeople and handloom weavers in the world. Their crafts survive in very different conditions: some prosper in national and international markets, some are sustained by government and voluntary support, and many are declining as younger people leave for other work. This chapter surveys the institutions and movements of the craft revival since independence, the design schools, the legal protection of craft names through Geographical Indications, the markets and enterprises that sell crafts today, and the problems that remain.

docs.title: 15.1.1 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and the Handicrafts Board
docs.text:
The central figure of the post-independence craft revival was Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay (1903–1988), a nationalist, socialist and feminist who had worked in the freedom movement and for refugee resettlement after Partition. As the first chair of the All India Handicrafts Board (1952), she directed surveys of crafts across the country, established emporia and marketing organisations, and promoted the recognition of master craftspeople; she was also a founder of the Crafts Council of India (1964) and a leading figure in the World Crafts Council. Her books, such as Handicrafts of India, describe crafts region by region (Chattopadhyay 1975), and her memoir Inner Recesses, Outer Spaces (1986) records her work (Chattopadhyay 1986). Pupul Jayakar, who organised exhibitions of Indian textiles and crafts in India and abroad, from the Museum of Modern Art exhibition of 1955–56 (Jayakar and Irwin 1956) to the Festivals of India of the 1980s, was another influential figure.

Kamaladevi’s work for crafts began with the refugees of Partition. The Indian Co-operative Union, which she founded in 1948, helped to resettle refugees from the North-West Frontier and western Punjab in a co-operative township at Faridabad, near Delhi. To sell the work of refugee and other craftspeople it opened a cottage industries emporium in New Delhi, which the government later took over as the Central Cottage Industries Emporium. At the Handicrafts Board she argued that the artisan should be treated as a creator and not as a source of cheap labour, and that craftspeople should be organised in co-operatives they controlled themselves. She travelled widely to find crafts on the edge of extinction, and many of the makers honoured by the early national awards were people she had sought out. Her approach also had limits that later writers have noted. By presenting crafts above all as national heritage, the programmes she inspired could cast artisans as custodians of tradition rather than as workers with interests of their own (Chapter 13). She received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1966.

docs.title: 15.1.2 Institutions
docs.text:
The state created a network of institutions for crafts and handlooms:

  • the All India Handicrafts Board (1952), later the office of the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), and the All India Handloom Board;

  • the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (1957), for khādī and village industries;

  • state handicrafts and handloom development corporations and cooperative societies, with their emporia;

  • the Crafts Museum in New Delhi, founded in the 1950s and now the National Crafts Museum and Hastkala Academy;

  • the Weavers’ Service Centres, set up from the 1950s to provide designs and technical support to handloom weavers;

  • the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad (1961), and later craft-design schools (Section 15.8);

  • national awards for master craftspersons (from the 1960s) and, from 2002, the Shilp Guru awards.

These institutions sustained many crafts through difficult decades. They have also been criticised for bureaucracy, for favouring cooperatives dominated by traders, and for promoting products designed for urban tastes rather than for the needs of artisans themselves.

docs.title: 15.1.3 Voluntary Organisations and Enterprises
docs.text: From the 1970s, voluntary organisations, designers and private enterprises became increasingly important.
