The Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA), founded by Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad in 1972, organised home-based women workers, including embroiderers and other craftswomen, and helped them to market their work. Dastkar, founded in Delhi in 1981, has worked with craft groups across India and organised craft bazaars that bring artisans directly to urban buyers. Fabindia, founded in 1960 as an exporter of handloom textiles, became a large retailer of hand-made and hand-printed goods, and from the 2000s experimented with companies in which artisan suppliers hold shares. Anokhi, founded in Jaipur in 1970, worked with block-printers in Sanganer and Bagru and established a Museum of Hand Printing at Amber. In Kutch, organisations such as Khamir, founded after the 2001 earthquake, and Kala Raksha (Section 15.8) have worked with embroiderers, weavers and printers.

docs.title: 15.2 Artisans and New Technology
docs.text:
Artisans have never been simply “traditional”; they have adopted new tools, materials and designs whenever these served them. In the early twentieth century handloom weavers took up the fly-shuttle, which allowed one weaver to weave wider cloth faster, and the Jacquard attachment; colonial and princely governments and missionaries promoted improved looms. Weavers adopted mill-spun yarn, artificial silk and synthetic dyes. After independence, many weavers moved from handlooms to power looms, especially in towns such as Bhiwandi and Malegaon in Maharashtra and Surat in Gujarat, which became huge centres of power-loom weaving. Potters have adopted electric wheels and kilns, metalworkers electric blowers and lathes, embroiderers sewing machines, and printers screen-printing.

These changes raise difficult questions. When does a craft cease to be “hand-made”? Does technology that increases productivity help artisans, or does it hand the market to those with capital? Policy has often tried to protect a sharp boundary between handloom and power loom, while many weavers have moved across it in search of a living, and some of the most admired “traditional” textiles of the twentieth century were woven with tools, such as the fly-shuttle and the Jacquard, that had once been new.

docs.title: 15.3 Handloom Policy
docs.text:
Handloom weaving remains the largest single craft occupation in India. Since independence the state has tried to protect it from the competition of mills and power looms through cooperatives, subsidies on yarn, rebates on sales, and the reservation of certain products for the handloom sector under the Handlooms (Reservation of Articles for Production) Act of 1985. Enforcement of the reservation has been weak, and power looms producing imitations of handloom saris and fabrics have taken much of the market. Labelling schemes, such as the Handloom Mark (2006) and the India Handloom brand (2015), certify that products are genuinely hand-woven. Since 2015, 7 August, the anniversary of the launch of the Svadeśī movement in 1905, has been observed as National Handloom Day.

State governments have also promoted crafts through programmes such as Uttar Pradesh’s “One District One Product” scheme (2018), which identifies a characteristic product of each district, many of them crafts, for support with credit, training and marketing; and in 2023 the central government launched the PM Vishwakarma scheme of credit, training and toolkits for artisans in eighteen traditional trades (Chapter 2). Such schemes are recent, and their effects remain to be assessed.

Policy for handicrafts and handlooms has often swung between two views: that crafts are a heritage to be preserved, and that they are an economic sector to be modernised. Artisans themselves have generally wanted both: respect for their skills and traditions, and access to credit, raw materials, markets, education, social security and new technology on their own terms.

docs.title: 15.4 Craft and Education
docs.text:
Gandhi’s scheme of “basic education” (Nayī Tālīm), adopted at a conference at Wardha in 1937, proposed that children should learn through productive work, especially spinning and weaving, and that schools should become partly self-supporting through the sale of their products. The scheme was adopted by several provinces and, after independence, became the model for “basic schools”, but it was gradually abandoned in favour of conventional academic schooling. Its central idea, that manual skill is a form of knowledge to be valued in education, has been revived in recent discussions of school curricula and vocational training.

Artisan families themselves now face a choice between transmitting the craft to their children and giving them a formal education that may lead them away from it. Many craft organisations run schools, scholarships and training programmes, and some, such as the design schools for working artisans described below, try to combine the two.

docs.title: 15.5 Museums
docs.text: Museums have played an important part in the documentation and revival of Indian crafts. The Victoria and Albert Museum in London holds one of the largest collections of Indian textiles and decorative arts, formed largely in the colonial period; its 2015 exhibition The Fabric of India surveyed the whole history of Indian textiles (Crill 2015). In India, the Calico Museum of Textiles in Ahmedabad, founded in 1949 by Gautam and Gira Sarabhai, holds outstanding collections of historic textiles and has published a series of scholarly catalogues (Irwin and Hall 1971, 1973); the National Crafts Museum in Delhi combines collections with demonstrations by living craftspeople; and many state and private museums, such as the Anokhi Museum of Hand Printing at Amber, document particular crafts. Museums face the question of how to present craft objects: as anonymous “ethnographic” specimens, as works of art, or as the products of named individuals and communities with their own histories.

docs.title: 15.6 Geographical Indications
docs.text:
The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act was passed in 1999 and came into force in 2003. A Geographical Indication (GI) is a name identifying goods as originating in a particular place, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to that origin. Registration prevents others from using the name for goods that do not come from the registered area or meet its specification. The first Indian GI was Darjeeling tea (2004); since then several hundred GIs have been registered, a large proportion of them handicrafts and handloom products.

Among the craft and handloom GIs are Pochampally ikat, Kancheepuram silk, Banaras brocades and saris, Chanderi fabric, Muga silk of Assam, Kashmir pashmina and the Kani shawl, Phulkari, Lucknow chikan, Madhubani paintings, Thanjavur paintings, Orissa paṭṭacitra, Bidrī ware, Channapatna toys, Kondapalli toys, Āṟanmuḷa mirrors, Kannauj perfume, the block prints of Sanganer, Bagru and Bagh, and Kolhapuri chappals.

Scholarly Note: What GIs Can and Cannot Do

A GI protects a name, not a technique or a design, and not the livelihood of the makers. It can prevent machine-made saris from Surat from being sold as “Kancheepuram silk”, and it can help to build a reputation for quality. But enforcement depends on producers’ organisations with the resources to take action; a registered GI may be held by an association dominated by traders rather than artisans; and a GI cannot by itself address the low earnings, poor working conditions and social stigma that lead young people to leave crafts. Its value depends on what producers and their organisations do with it.

docs.title: 15.7 Markets Today
docs.text:
Indian crafts reach their buyers through many channels: local markets and fairs, government emporia and craft bazaars (such as the Dilli Haat in Delhi, opened in 1994, and the Shilpgram centres), private shops and brands, exporters, and increasingly online platforms and social media, which allow some artisans to sell directly to customers. Craft tourism has grown in places such as Kutch, Raghurajpur, Pochampally and Swamimalai; Pochampally was named one of the “Best Tourism Villages” of the UN World Tourism Organization in 2021. Jaipur (2015) and Srinagar (2021) have been designated UNESCO Creative Cities of Crafts and Folk Art.

The structure of the market often works against the artisan. Between the maker and the final buyer stand contractors, traders, exporters and retailers, each taking a share; artisans who lack working capital must accept advances from traders who then fix the price. Hand production cannot compete with machines on price, and where buyers do not value the difference between hand-made and machine-made goods, artisans are squeezed. Power looms imitating handloom designs have taken much of the market for handloom saris, despite legal reservations for handloom.

docs.title: 15.7.1 Who Buys Crafts?
docs.text: The buyers of Indian crafts have changed several times. Village households once bought pots, cloth and tools from local artisans; courts and temples commissioned luxury goods; foreign merchants bought for export. Today, much of the market for handmade goods is among the urban middle classes in India and among buyers abroad, including the Indian diaspora, who buy crafts as expressions of taste, identity and support for artisans. Handloom saris, khādī and regional textiles are worn by many Indians as a statement of national or regional identity, and politicians often wear them in public. This market values “authenticity” and “tradition”, but it also demands novelty, consistency and convenience; artisans must negotiate between these expectations.

docs.title: 15.8 Design Schools and the Crafts
docs.text: Since independence, the professional designer has become one of the main intermediaries between India’s craftspeople and their markets. The institutions that trained designers grew out of a long argument about the relation between art, craft and industry, an argument that began in the colonial art schools (Chapter 14) and at Santiniketan (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 15.8.1 The Bauhaus in Calcutta
docs.text: In December 1922 the Indian Society of Oriental Art in Calcutta exhibited works by artists of the Bauhaus, the German school of art, architecture and design founded at Weimar in 1919. Among them were Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, Lyonel Feininger and Johannes Itten, and their works were hung alongside paintings of the Bengal school. The exhibition was arranged through Stella Kramrisch, who had come to India at Rabindranath Tagore’s invitation. Partha Mitter treats it as the moment at which Indian artists first met the European avant-garde in their own city (Mitter 2007). The Bauhaus programme called for artists and craftsmen to work together in the workshop, with no barrier of rank between them. This had obvious affinities with Tagore’s experiments at Santiniketan and Sriniketan. At the time, however, its influence on Indian crafts was slight. Its lasting influence came forty years later, through design education.

docs.title: 15.8.2 The Eameses’ India Report
docs.text: In 1958, at the invitation of the Government of India and with the support of the Ford Foundation, the American designers Charles and Ray Eames spent several months travelling in India. Pupul Jayakar had a large part in bringing them. Their India Report, submitted in April 1958, argued that India faced rapid change, in which traditional ways of making and modern industrial production would collide. It called for a new kind of designer who understood both, and it recommended an institute for training, research and service in design (Eames and Eames 1958). The report’s famous praise of the humble brass loṭā as a model of good design was not nostalgia. The Eameses used the vessel to show how a form refined by generations of makers and users can answer many demands at once, of material, use, cost and beauty. They asked designers to approach every new product with the same seriousness.

docs.title: 15.8.3 The National Institute of Design
docs.text:
The National Institute of Design was set up in Ahmedabad in 1961 as an autonomous institution. Gira Sarabhai and Gautam Sarabhai, of the family that had founded the Calico Museum (Section 15.5), were its guiding figures, and the Ford Foundation gave support. Its early teaching drew on European modernist design education, including the foundation course of the Bauhaus and the methods of the Ulm School of Design, and on visiting teachers from Europe, America and Japan. It also sent its students to study crafts. The documentation of a craft became a regular exercise in Indian design education: recording, in a village or workshop, the materials, tools, processes, products, makers and markets of a living craft. Such studies, accumulated over decades, form an important archive of crafts as they were practised in the second half of the twentieth century.

In January 1979 the Institute hosted an international meeting, held by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization and the International Council of Societies of Industrial Design, which adopted the Ahmedabad Declaration on Industrial Design for Development. The Declaration called on designers in developing countries to serve basic needs and to build on local resources and skills rather than imitate the products of the industrial West. A National Institute of Design Act of 2014 declared the Institute an institution of national importance, and further campuses have since been opened in other states.

docs.title: 15.8.4 Designers in the Handloom Sector
docs.text: The Weavers’ Service Centres of the All India Handloom Board (Section 15.1) employed artists and designers to create new designs for handloom weavers and to record old ones. The painter K. G. Subramanyan, later a leading teacher at Baroda and Santiniketan, worked as a designer for the Board’s Bombay centre around 1960. In the 1980s the Weavers’ Service Centres, under the direction of Martand Singh, prepared a series of exhibitions of handwoven textiles called Vishwakarma. Weavers re-created historical designs and techniques from museum pieces and old samples for these shows, which were seen in India and at the Festivals of India abroad. These projects showed that skills thought to be lost could often be recovered when weavers were given the time, materials and payment to do so.

docs.title: 15.8.5 Crafts on Show: The Festivals of India
docs.text: In the 1980s the Festivals of India, a series of cultural festivals organised by the Indian government under the direction of Pupul Jayakar, presented Indian crafts abroad on an unprecedented scale. They began in Britain in 1982 and continued in the United States and France in the mid-1980s and later in the Soviet Union, Japan and other countries. Besides exhibitions of sculpture and painting, they brought living craftspeople and performers to work in public. The exhibition Aditi, designed by Rajeev Sethi and first shown in London in 1982, followed the cycle of life, from birth and childhood to marriage, through objects, with potters, painters, puppeteers and other makers working in the galleries. Other exhibitions paired international designers with Indian craftspeople to make new objects. The festivals opened export markets and made some master craftspeople known by name. They also revived an old problem. Saloni Mathur has described how, at the Colonial and Indian Exhibition in London in 1886, Indian artisans were brought to work before visitors as living exhibits of a timeless India (Mathur 2007). Critics of the 1980s festivals asked whether showing artisans at work, however respectfully, still presented them as specimens of “tradition” rather than as contemporary makers.

docs.title: 15.8.6 Surveys and Documentation
docs.text: Designers were not the only documenters. The Census of India of 1961 included a series of surveys of handicrafts, published as monographs on particular crafts and villages, which recorded processes, tools, communities and incomes across the country. The art magazine Marg, founded in Bombay in 1946 by the writer Mulk Raj Anand, published special numbers on regional crafts and textiles that brought them to a wide educated readership. Together with the catalogues of the Calico Museum, the reports of the handicrafts and handloom boards and the work of design students, these surveys make the crafts of the mid-twentieth century unusually well recorded.

docs.title: 15.8.7 New Schools
docs.text: From the 1980s the number of design schools grew. The National Institute of Fashion Technology was founded in New Delhi in 1986, and the Indian Institute of Crafts and Design in Jaipur followed in the 1990s. A different model put the artisan in the classroom. The design school opened by Kala Raksha in Kutch in 2005, led by Judy Frater, taught working artisans from embroidering, weaving, printing and other communities to design new work within their own traditions and to understand the markets they sold to. Frater later founded Somaiya Kala Vidya on the same principles. Its graduates are recognised as designers in their own right, not as executors of other people’s designs.

docs.title: 15.8.8 Design for Whom?
docs.text:
Collaboration between designers and artisans has been one of the main strategies of the revival. At its best it brings new products and markets to artisans while respecting their skills and their own design traditions; at its worst it treats them as anonymous labour executing the designs of others. The design schools have also changed how craft knowledge is judged. Ethnographic studies, such as Soumhya Venkatesan’s work on the Pattamadai mat-weavers (Chapter 13), show how the views of designers, officials and buyers about what counts as good craft can override the makers’ own (Venkatesan 2009). The language of “design intervention”, common in development programmes, assumes that a craft needs correcting from outside. Many designers and institutions now prefer to speak of collaboration, to name the artisans they work with, and to share authorship and income. The ideal set out in the India Report and the Ahmedabad Declaration, of design that starts from the knowledge already present in a community, is easier to state than to carry out.

Some artisans have become well-known artists in their own right. Mithilā painters such as Sita Devi, Ganga Devi and Dulari Devi, the Warli painter Jivya Soma Mashe, the Gond painter Jangarh Singh Shyam and the rogan painter Abdul Gafur Khatri (Chapter 12) have been recognised with national awards and international exhibitions. Their success has raised its own disputes: whether a painting made for the market by a named artist is still “folk” or “tribal” art, who may use a community’s styles and motifs, and how much of the price paid in a city gallery returns to the village. Jangarh Singh Shyam’s early death in Japan in 2001, where he had gone to paint for a museum, became for many critics a symbol of the inequalities of that market.

docs.title: 15.9 Fair Trade and Certification
docs.text: Since the 1970s, “alternative trade” organisations in Europe and North America have bought Indian crafts directly from producer groups on terms intended to give artisans a fair price, advance payment and long-term relationships. Indian organisations have joined international fair-trade networks, and certification schemes, such as those against child labour in carpet-weaving (Chapter 4) and the Handloom Mark, try to assure buyers of the conditions under which goods are made. Such schemes have helped some producer groups, but they reach only a small part of the craft sector, and certification adds costs that small producers find hard to bear.

docs.title: 15.10 Shocks and Resilience
docs.text: Craft economies are vulnerable to sudden shocks. The Gujarat earthquake of 2001 destroyed homes and workshops across Kutch; craft organisations and communities rebuilt, and the earthquake led to new initiatives such as the village of Ajrakhpur and the organisation Khamir. The lockdowns imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 closed markets and fairs, cut off orders from exporters and left many artisans without income; online sales and relief from craft organisations helped some, but many artisans turned to other work. Craft communities have survived many such crises, but livelihoods that depend on long chains of intermediaries and on distant markets are the first to fail when those chains break.

docs.title: 15.11.1 Livelihoods and Status
docs.text: The most serious problem is that many craftspeople earn too little to live decently from their work. Surveys of handloom weavers and handicraft artisans conducted by the Government of India have repeatedly found low household incomes and high levels of debt. Young people from artisan families often prefer other occupations, both because they pay better and because craft work still carries the low status that caste attached to manual work. Any revival that does not improve artisans’ incomes and social standing will not last.

docs.title: 15.11.2 A Note on Numbers
docs.text: Figures for the number of artisans in India, the value of craft production and exports, or the number of Geographical Indications are often quoted, but they should be used with care. The most systematic counts are the All India Handloom Censuses conducted for the Ministry of Textiles, the most recent of them in 2019–20, and the surveys of handicraft artisans of the office of the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts). The handloom censuses count households and persons engaged in weaving and in “allied” work such as winding, warping and sizing, and distinguish full-time from part-time workers, so that totals change greatly according to which categories are added together; successive censuses have recorded a declining number of handloom workers, a large majority of them women. Handicraft surveys use different definitions again, and many artisans work part-time or seasonally, combine craft with agriculture or wage labour, or are counted as “helpers” rather than workers. This volume has therefore avoided precise statistics where reliable, sourced figures could not be given. Readers who need numbers should consult the census reports themselves and note how each figure was obtained.

docs.title: 15.11.3 Raw Materials
docs.text: Crafts depend on materials whose supply is often uncertain: the indigenous “desi” cottons suited to hand-spinning, now a small fraction of India’s cotton area, which since 2002 has been dominated by genetically modified Bt hybrids; the host trees of tasar and mugā silk; natural dye plants; sandalwood and other carving woods (Chapter 7); clay from village commons; and bamboo and cane from forests governed by laws that have not always recognised the rights of forest communities.

docs.title: 15.11.4 Knowledge and Its Ownership
docs.text: Traditional designs and techniques are easily copied by industrial producers in India and abroad, and existing intellectual property law protects them only partly. GIs protect names; design registration protects individual new designs; copyright protects individual works. Collective, inherited knowledge falls between these categories. Documentation by museums, design schools and craft organisations helps preserve knowledge of techniques and designs, but documentation cannot replace living transmission from one practitioner to another.

docs.title: 15.11.5 Health and Safety
docs.text: Many crafts carry occupational hazards: silicosis among stone-carvers and agate-workers, lung disease among glass and metal workers, injuries and eye strain among weavers and embroiderers, exposure to toxic dyes, mordants and metals among dyers, printers and jewellers. Child labour, once widespread in carpet weaving, glass-bangle making and other crafts, has been reduced but not eliminated. A craft revival that ignores these issues romanticises hardship.

docs.title: 15.11.6 Women Artisans
docs.text: Women make up a large part of the craft workforce, especially in embroidery, weaving in the North-East, basketry, pottery preparation, bead-work and the processing of fibres; yet they are often recorded as “helpers” rather than artisans, paid less, and excluded from the control of markets and from organisations dominated by men. Many of the most successful craft initiatives of recent decades, such as SEWA, the embroidery collectives of Kutch and Bihar and many self-help groups, have been organised by and for women. Their experience shows that income from craft can increase women’s independence and standing in their families, but also that the double burden of household and craft work can be heavy (Wilkinson-Weber 1999; Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 15.11.7 Caste and Dignity
docs.text: Many of the communities that practise crafts, especially those working with leather, bamboo, fibre and clay, are Dalit, Ādivāsī or “backward” castes, and the stigma attached to manual work and to their identities has not disappeared. Revival efforts that present crafts as timeless “heritage” can ignore this history, or even reinforce it by expecting artisans to remain in their hereditary occupations. Respect for craft must include the freedom of artisans’ children to choose other work, and the dignity of those who choose to stay.

docs.title: 15.12 Conclusion
docs.text: The crafts described in this volume embody one of the great bodies of practical knowledge in human history: the knowledge of how to transform cotton into muslin, iron into crucible steel, ore into zinc, clay into a temple’s terracotta skin, and threads into paṭolā whose patterns appear only when warp and weft meet. That knowledge was created and carried mostly by people whom the dominant texts ranked low and whose names were rarely recorded. To value Indian craft knowledge truly is to value its makers: to record their achievements accurately, without myth or exaggeration; to recognise the injustices of caste and colonial exploitation that shaped their lives; and to ensure that those who practise crafts today can do so with dignity and a fair reward.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For crafts region by region, Ranjan and Ranjan (2007); for the work of the post-independence revival, Chattopadhyay (1975); for the making of the idea of Indian craft, McGowan (2009); for the Fabric of India exhibition of 2015, Crill (2015); for the origins of the National Institute of Design, Eames and Eames (1958); for the Bauhaus exhibition in Calcutta, Mitter (2007).

docs.title: A Guide to Further Reading
docs.text: The short notes at the end of each chapter list the main sources for that chapter. This guide is selective and evaluative: it suggests where a reader should begin, what each work does best, and where its limits lie. Full details are given in the Select Bibliography.

docs.title: Where to Begin
docs.text:
For what is made where today, the indispensable work is Handmade in India, edited by M. P. and Aditi Ranjan (Ranjan and Ranjan 2007). It is a regional encyclopaedia, richly photographed and organised state by state, with descriptions of processes and products; it has little history and almost no social analysis, and is best used beside a historical account such as this one. For textiles as objects, Rosemary Crill’s catalogue The Fabric of India (Crill 2015) is the best single illustrated introduction, and Gillow and Barnard (1991) is a reliable practical survey of techniques. Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay’s Handicrafts of India (Chattopadhyay 1975) belongs to the revival it describes and should be read as a document of that movement as well as a survey.

On the idea of the Indian craftsman, the classic statements are Coomaraswamy’s The Indian Craftsman (Coomaraswamy 1909) and Kramrisch’s essay on the traditions of the Indian craftsman (Kramrisch 1958). Both are eloquent and both largely leave caste aside. George Birdwood’s The Industrial Arts of India (Birdwood 1880) is a Victorian source, valuable for what it records and for its attitudes. Abigail McGowan’s Crafting the Nation in Colonial India (McGowan 2009) is the best modern account of how the category of “Indian crafts” itself was made, and is the natural corrective to all three.

docs.title: Early History and Texts
docs.text: Kenoyer (1998) is the clearest introduction to Indus crafts by the archaeologist who has studied them most closely; Allchin and Allchin (1982) remains a sound general archaeology. For guilds and trade in early India, Chakravarti (2002) is concise and reliable, and Kosambi (1956) is still stimulating, though its model of post-Gupta decline is debated. The translations of the Arthaśāstra by Olivelle (2013) (with up-to-date notes and dating) and Kangle (1960–1965) (with fuller commentary), of Manu by Olivelle (2005), of the Periplus by Casson (1989) and of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā by Bhat (1981–1982) are the primary texts most often cited here. For Tamil literature, Ramanujan (1985) gives a selection of Caṅkam poetry in fine translations and Parthasarathy (1993) a complete translation of the Cilappatikāram. Irfan Habib’s Technology in Medieval India (Habib 2008) is a compact, well-documented account of the period from about 650 to 1750, the one most thinly covered in general surveys.

docs.title: Metals
docs.text: Metallurgy is treated in detail in Volume 14. Srinivasan and Ranganathan (2004) and Bronson (1986) are the best starting points on crucible steel, Balasubramaniam (2002) on the Delhi pillar and Craddock (2017) on zinc, lead and silver; all are written by specialists who also correct popular exaggerations. Verrier Elwin’s The Agaria (Elwin 1942) is a classic ethnography of iron-smelters made just before the craft disappeared.

docs.title: Textiles and Dress
docs.text: For the global trade, Riello (2013) is the most important recent synthesis, arguing that Indian cottons shaped European industrialisation; Parthasarathi (2011) makes a related case on comparative grounds, and Beckert (2014) sets both in a world history of cotton. The essays in Riello and Roy (2009) and Riello and Parthasarathi (2009) are uneven but cover markets from Japan to West Africa. Gittinger (1982) and Irwin and Brett (1970) remain the best accounts of the dyer’s technique; Guy (1998) and Barnes (2005) are essential for the Indian Ocean, and Barnes (1997) for the finds from Egypt. On weavers and the Company, Hossain (1988) and Parthasarathi (2001) are detailed and complementary; on medieval south Indian weavers, Ramaswamy (1985). Tirthankar Roy’s Artisans and Industrialization (Roy 1993) and Traditional Industry (Roy 1999) are the indispensable revisionist accounts of handloom weaving and other industries under colonial rule. For Africa, Machado (2014) and Prestholdt (2008) write from the side of the consumers. On dress, Goswamy (1993) is the best guide to surviving garments, Tarlo (1996) the best study of what clothing meant to those who wore it, and Cohn (1996) the classic essay on dress and colonial rule.

docs.title: Other Crafts
docs.text: On jewellery, Untracht (1997) is encyclopaedic and based on long fieldwork. On instruments and their makers, Deva (1978) describes the instruments, and Krishna (2020) shows, for the mṛdaṅgam, how much the makers’ history has been left out. On leather, there is still no full history; Roy (1999) covers the colonial industry, Lynch (1969) the shoe-makers of Agra and Rawat (2011) the history of the “leather-working” caste label. On painting as a craft, Goswamy (1997) reconstructs a family of hill painters with exceptional care, and Mitter (1994) traces the split between artist and craftsman in colonial India. Losty (1982) is a well-illustrated introduction to the arts of the book, and Topsfield (2006) to board and card games.

docs.title: Caste, Society and Economy
docs.text: Bayly (1999) is the best general history of caste in the eighteenth to twentieth centuries. Ambedkar’s Annihilation of Caste (Ambedkar 1936) is short and should be read whole; Chakravarti (2003) explains why caste and gender cannot be studied apart, and Omvedt (2008) and Zelliot (1992) trace the traditions of anti-caste thought and movement. On artisan communities, Brouwer (1995) presents a Viśvakarma world-view on its own terms and Mines (1984) a weaving caste’s long history. For the jajmānī debate, read Wiser (1936) with the critique in Fuller (1989). On the colonial economy, Dutt (1902) and Naoroji (1901) state the nationalist case, Bagchi (1976) and Morris (1963) the two sides of the deindustrialisation debate, and Haynes (2012) carries the story of artisans and merchants into the twentieth century. On Svadeśī and khādī, Sarkar (1973), Bayly (1986) and Trivedi (2007).

docs.title: Craft Knowledge and Design
docs.text: On tacit knowledge, Polanyi (1958) is the philosophical source; on the place of theory and practice in Sanskrit learning, Pollock (1985). Dharampal (1971) collects European accounts of Indian technology and should be read critically, Raj (2007) for the circulation of knowledge, and Venkatesan (2009) for what development programmes do to craft knowledge. On design and the crafts, the Eameses’ India Report (Eames and Eames 1958) is short and still worth reading, and Mitter (2007) covers the Bauhaus exhibition of 1922.

Robe of a Buddhist monk, sewn from cut pieces in a pattern likened to rice-fields dābū (Hi.) Mud-resist paste used in Rajasthani printing dantakāra Ivory-carver darzī (Hi.) Tailor (from Persian darz, “seam”) deg (Hi.) Copper still used in Kannauj perfume distillation Dhokra, Dokra Lost-wax brass casting of central and eastern India, and the communities who practise it dhvaja Standard or flag-staff; the Delhi iron pillar was a dhvaja of Viṣṇu dhyāna Meditation verse describing the posture, attributes and colour of a deity, memorised by image-makers ekāṇḍa “Single-piece”: a vīṇā whose bowl, neck and head are carved from one log gāmochā (Assamese) White cotton cloth with red borders and woven motifs, used as towel and scarf and given at Bihu gañjīfā (Pe.) Circular playing cards made at Sawantwadi and elsewhere harḍa (Hi.) Myrobalan fruit (Terminalia chebula), a source of tannin used in dyeing haritāla Orpiment, a yellow arsenic sulphide pigment (poisonous) hiṅgula Vermilion (mercury sulphide), a red pigment (poisonous) injiri (Kalabari) “Real Madras handkerchief”: checked cotton woven in the Madras region for the Kalabari of the Niger Delta iṭaṅkai, valaṅkai (Ta.) “Left-hand” and “right-hand” caste divisions of south India jajmānī (Hi.) Customary relationship in which village artisans and service castes served patron households for annual payments in kind jāma (Pe.) Long coat with a fitted bodice and full skirt, tied at the side; formal court dress of Mughal and Rajput India jāmdānī (Bengali) Figured weaving in which motifs are inserted by hand as discontinuous supplementary wefts into a fine cotton ground jāti Hereditary, endogamous occupational community; “caste” in the narrower sense jawārī (Hi.) The buzzing resonance produced by the broad, curved bridge of the sitār and tānpurā; also the bridge itself jūtī, mojaṛī (Hi., Panjabi) Closed leather slipper with a pointed or upturned toe, often embroidered, of Rajasthan and Punjab kāca Glass kalā An art or accomplishment; the Kāmasūtra lists sixty-four kalamkārī (Pe.) “Pen-work”: painted and printed cottons of Andhra Pradesh kalaśa Water-filled pot used as an auspicious symbol and in ritual kalī (Hi.) Triangular gore let into the side of a garment to give fullness kāṃsya Bell metal, a high-tin bronze kānī (Kashmiri) Small bobbin; the twill-tapestry technique of the finest Kashmir shawls kaniki (Swahili) Dark indigo-dyed cotton cloth, a staple of the Indian cloth trade to East Africa kānthā (Bengali) Quilt or wrap of layered old cloth, embroidered in running stitch karmāra Smith kārpāsa Cotton kāru In the Ṛgveda, a singer or poet; later, an artisan kasūti (Kannada) Counted-thread embroidery of the Dharwad region, worked in four stitches khādī (Hi.) Hand-spun and hand-woven cloth, especially as promoted by the national movement kimkhāb (Pe.) Brocade woven with gold and silver thread koftgarī (Pe.) Gold or silver wire inlaid into a cross-hatched iron or steel surface korvai (Ta.) Interlocked-weft technique for contrasting borders in Kāñcīpuram saris kulāla, kumbhakāra Potter kundan (Hi.) Highly refined gold foil; the technique of setting stones with it kuppā (Hi.) Large jar of raw hide for storing and carrying oil or ghee lākṣā Lac, the resin of the lac insect madhūcchiṣṭa-vidhāna “The method of beeswax”: lost-wax casting mañjiṣṭhā Indian madder (Rubia cordifolia), a red dye mashak (Hi.) Goatskin water-bag carried by the water-carrier (bhishtī) masī Ink mīnākārī (Pe.) Enamelling on metal mot (Mar.) Large leather bucket drawn up from a well by bullocks; charsā or pur in parts of north India mugā, erī, pāṭ (Assamese) The golden, castor-fed and mulberry silks of Assam naqqāsh (Pe.) Pattern-drawer, designer naqsha (Pe.) Design; the pattern harness of a drawloom naqshaband (Pe.) Pattern-maker who ties a design into the harness of a drawloom nauvārī (Marathi) Nine-yard sari, worn with a portion passed between the legs and tucked at the back navaratna The “nine gems” associated in astrology with the nine planets nīlī Indigo pādukā Wooden sandal; the footwear of ascetics and the object of worship as the feet of gods and teachers pañcaloha “Five metals”: an alloy prescribed in ritual texts for images paṭolā (Gu.) Double-ikat silk of Patan, Gujarat patrorṇā “Leaf-wool”: in the Arthaśāstra, apparently a silk from caterpillars fed on the leaves of trees paṭṭacitra Painting on prepared cloth, especially in Odisha pelete bite (Kalabari) “Cut-thread cloth”, made by Kalabari women by cutting and pulling threads from imported Indian checks peshwāz (Pe.) High-waisted gown worn by women at the Mughal and later courts phulkārī (Panjabi) “Flower-work”: darning-stitch embroidery in silk floss prāṇapratiṣṭhā Rite of “establishing the breath” in a consecrated image pūnī (Gu., Hi.) Sliver of carded cotton, prepared for spinning puruṣamedha Symbolic “human sacrifice” of the Yajurveda, whose victim-list names many occupations rājakāriya (Sinhala) Service owed to the king in return for land, under which the Kandyan royal craftsmen worked rallī (Sindhi) Pieced and appliquéd cotton quilt of Sindh, Rajasthan and Kutch rathakāra Chariot-maker ratnaparīkṣā The testing of gems; title of several lapidary treatises rogan (Pe.) Painting on cloth with a paste of boiled castor oil and pigments sāñcipāt (Assamese) Prepared inner bark of the agaru tree, used for manuscripts in Assam satra (Assamese) Vaiṣṇava monastery of the tradition of Śaṅkaradeva śilpa Skill, art, craft; a work of art śilpaśāstra Treatise on architecture, image-making and allied crafts śilpin Skilled craftsman śītalpāṭi (Bengali) “Cool mat”: mat woven from split stems of the murtā plant, especially in Sylhet śreṇī (Pa. seṇi) Guild, an association of people following the same occupation sthapati Master builder or sculptor strīdhana A woman’s own property, especially gifts and ornaments received at marriage sūcī, saucika Needle; tailor (“needle-man”) sūtradhāra, sūtragrāhin “Holder of the cord”: surveyor, architect or carpenter svadeśī “Of one’s own country”: the movement to boycott foreign goods and use Indian ones svāvalambana Self-reliance; in the khādī movement, spinning for one’s own cloth rather than for sale takalī (Hi.) Small hand spindle, promoted by the khādī movement for schoolchildren and travellers takṣan, takṣaka Carpenter, carver tāla Module of proportion in image-making, roughly the length of the face tālīm (Kashmiri) Coded pattern-script used by Kashmir kānī shawl and carpet weavers tānā, bānā (Hi.) Warp; weft. Together, tānā-bānā, a figure for the interwoven fabric of a society tantuvāya Weaver tārkashī (Hi.) Brass-wire inlay in wood tolu bommalāṭa (Telugu) Shadow theatre of Andhra Pradesh, performed with large painted puppets of translucent leather ukku (Kannada, Telugu) Steel; source of the English “wootz” ustād, shāgird (Pe.) Master and apprentice vardhakin Joiner; one of the four craftsmen of the śilpaśāstra team vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala Diagram of the “person of the site” used to lay out buildings vāstuśāstra The science of building and of sites Viśvakarman “Maker of all”: the divine craftsman; ancestor claimed by the Viśvakarma artisan communities zardozī (Pe.) Embroidery with metal thread and sequins zarī (Pe.) Gold or silver thread, usually silver-gilt wire wrapped round silk
